 2  GW(64:d1:54…)     PC               ARP    192.168.10.1 is at 64:d1:54:aa:bb:01
    └ happens only when the gateway's MAC isn't cached — after that, straight to #3 next time
 3  192.168.10.37     192.168.10.5     DNS    Standard query A www.capgemini.com
 4  192.168.10.5      192.168.10.37    DNS    Response A 92.123.140.10  (TTL 300)
    └ UDP, one round trip. Slow page loads often hide HERE, not in the download
 5  192.168.10.37     92.123.140.10    TCP    51712 → 443 [SYN]  Seq=0 Win=64240 MSS=1460
 6  92.123.140.10     192.168.10.37    TCP    443 → 51712 [SYN, ACK] Seq=0 Ack=1
 7  192.168.10.37     92.123.140.10    TCP    51712 → 443 [ACK]
    └ the handshake. #5 with no #6 = filtered; #6 as RST = nothing listening
 8  192.168.10.37     92.123.140.10    TLSv1.3  Client Hello (SNI=www.capgemini.com)
 9  92.123.140.10     192.168.10.37    TLSv1.3  Server Hello, Certificate, Finished
    └ SNI in #8 is how one IP hosts many HTTPS sites — and how URL filters see names
10  192.168.10.37     92.123.140.10    HTTP2  GET / (encrypted — you see it only as app data)
11  92.123.140.10     192.168.10.37    HTTP2  200 OK + page data, many frames
12  …                                  TCP    [FIN, ACK] exchanges — polite close
  • Timing columns turn this into a performance report: gap 3→4 = DNS latency · 5→6 = network round-trip to the server · 9→11 = server think time. "The gap is between request and response, on their side" ends blame games.
  • Where NAT fits (invisible here): between #5 and the internet, the firewall rewrote 192.168.10.37:51712 → public-IP:61003; the capture on the outside interface shows that version — capture on both sides of a firewall to see its work.
  • Edge case worth repeating: everything to #9 succeeds, then silence at #10–11 with retransmissions of full-size frames = the MTU/MSS black hole from D3.1 — small handshake packets fit, big data frames don't.
Module 04 · Networks

Switching & VLANs

How switches actually forward, how VLANs segment a network, and the spanning-tree and port-security topics that ride along.

4.1 How a switch forwards

A switch keeps a MAC address table (CAM table): MAC ↔ port. For every incoming frame it does three things:

  1. Learn — record the frame's source MAC against the arrival port.
  2. Forward — if the destination MAC is in the table, send the frame out only that port.
  3. Flood — if the destination is unknown, or is broadcast/multicast, send it out every port except the one it came in on.

Entries age out (default ~300 s). This is why the first packet to a quiet host is flooded but the reply instantly teaches the switch where everyone is. MAC flapping (same MAC seen on two ports rapidly) signals a loop or a duplicated machine.

4.2 VLANs — one switch, many networks

A VLAN (Virtual LAN, IEEE 802.1Q) logically splits one physical switch into multiple isolated layer-2 networks — separate broadcast domains. Devices in VLAN 10 can't talk to VLAN 20 at layer 2 at all; traffic between them must be routed. Why: security (Finance separated from Guests), smaller broadcast domains, and grouping by function regardless of physical location.

  • Access port — belongs to one VLAN; the connected PC never sees tags.
  • Trunk port — carries many VLANs between switches/routers; each frame gets a 4-byte 802.1Q tag holding the VLAN ID (1–4094).
  • Native VLAN — the one VLAN sent untagged on a trunk (default VLAN 1). Mismatched native VLANs on either end cause leaks — and best practice is to change it off VLAN 1.
  • Voice VLAN — an access port can additionally carry a tagged voice VLAN so an IP phone and the PC behind it live in separate networks on one cable.
  • Each VLAN normally maps to one IP subnet (VLAN 10 ↔ 192.168.10.0/24 is a common convention).

4.3 Inter-VLAN routing

Two ways to let VLANs talk:

  • Router-on-a-stick — one trunk to a router; the router has a subinterface per VLAN (e.g. G0/0.10, G0/0.20), each being that VLAN's default gateway. Simple, but the single link is a bottleneck.
  • Layer-3 switch with SVIs — the modern way: the switch itself gets a virtual interface per VLAN (SVI, e.g. interface vlan 10 with IP 192.168.10.1) and routes between them in hardware at line rate.

4.4 Spanning Tree Protocol (STP)

Redundant links between switches create layer-2 loops: Ethernet frames have no TTL, so a broadcast circulates forever, multiplying into a broadcast storm that melts the network within seconds. STP (802.1D) prevents this by logically blocking redundant paths:

  • Switches elect a root bridge (lowest priority + MAC wins).
  • Every other switch keeps its best path to the root and blocks the redundant ports.
  • If an active link dies, a blocked port comes alive — redundancy without loops.
  • Classic STP converges slowly (30–50 s); RSTP (802.1w) does it in seconds and is the modern default. PortFast makes edge ports (PCs) skip the listening/learning wait; BPDU Guard shuts an edge port if a switch appears on it.

4.5 Link aggregation & port-level security

  • EtherChannel / LAG bundles 2–8 physical links between switches into one logical link — more bandwidth plus redundancy, and STP treats the bundle as a single port so nothing gets blocked. LACP (802.3ad) is the standard negotiation protocol.
  • Port security limits which/how many MAC addresses may appear on an access port ("sticky MAC"), shutting the port (err-disabled) on violation — stops rogue devices and MAC flooding attacks.
  • DHCP snooping blocks rogue DHCP offers on untrusted ports; 802.1X requires authentication before a port passes any traffic (Module 7).

4.6 Commands you can name-drop

# Cisco IOS — the vocabulary interviewers recognize
show mac address-table          # who's on which port
show vlan brief                 # VLANs and their access ports
show interfaces trunk           # trunks + allowed VLANs
show interfaces status          # up/down, speed, duplex, VLAN
show spanning-tree              # root bridge, blocked ports
switchport mode access | trunk  # set port role
switchport access vlan 10       # assign VLAN

Interview questions — Module 4

What is EtherChannel or LACP, and why use it?

Model answer: "It bundles two to eight physical links between two switches, or a switch and a server, into one logical link. You get more bandwidth and redundancy: if one cable fails, traffic carries on over the rest, and STP sees one link so it does not block any of them. LACP is the standard negotiation protocol; both ends must agree on speed, duplex, VLANs and trunk settings or the bundle will not form. Traffic is spread per flow by a hash, so a single large transfer still uses only one member link."

How do devices in different VLANs talk to each other?

Model answer: "Through a layer 3 device, because a VLAN is its own broadcast domain and subnet. The classic way is router on a stick: one trunk to a router with a subinterface and gateway IP per VLAN. In most offices today it is a layer 3 switch with an SVI, interface vlan 10 with the gateway address, and ip routing enabled. Each PC uses the SVI of its own VLAN as its default gateway, and ACLs on the SVIs control which VLANs may talk to which."

What is the native VLAN, and why do people change it?

Model answer: "On an 802.1Q trunk, frames in the native VLAN are sent untagged; all other VLANs are tagged. Both ends must agree on it, otherwise traffic leaks between VLANs and CDP reports a native VLAN mismatch. By default it is VLAN 1, so a common hardening step is to move it to an unused VLAN that carries no users, which blocks VLAN-hopping by double tagging."

A new PC gets a 169.254 address on boot, but ipconfig /renew a minute later works. Why?

Model answer: "Almost always spanning tree: with classic STP a new port spends about 30 seconds in listening and learning before it forwards, and the PC gives up on DHCP and falls back to an APIPA address. The fix is PortFast on access ports, with BPDU Guard so a switch plugged into that port is shut down instead of creating a loop; RSTP also converges in a second or two. I would confirm with show spanning-tree interface and the port's state on the switch."

What is a VLAN and why would you use one?

Model answer: "A VLAN logically divides one physical switch into multiple isolated layer-2 networks — each VLAN is its own broadcast domain, usually mapped to its own IP subnet. We use them for security segmentation — keeping guest, voice, server, and user traffic apart — for shrinking broadcast domains, and for grouping users by role rather than by physical location. Traffic between VLANs must pass through a router or layer-3 switch, which is exactly where we apply access control between segments."

Access port vs trunk port?

Model answer: "An access port carries a single VLAN untagged and connects end devices — the PC has no idea VLANs exist. A trunk carries multiple VLANs between switches or to a router, with each frame tagged with its VLAN ID using 802.1Q; the one exception is the native VLAN, which crosses the trunk untagged. If a user's port is put in the wrong VLAN they'll get an address from the wrong subnet or none at all — one of the most common port-level tickets."

What is STP and what happens without it?

Model answer: "Spanning Tree Protocol prevents layer-2 loops when switches are connected redundantly. The switches elect a root bridge and block redundant paths, unblocking them only if an active link fails. Without it, a single loop causes a broadcast storm — Ethernet frames have no TTL, so broadcasts circulate and multiply until the network is unusable, and the MAC tables flap constantly. Modern networks run RSTP for fast convergence, with PortFast on user ports so PCs don't wait 30 seconds for link-up."

How does a switch build its MAC table?

Model answer: "By learning source addresses: whenever a frame arrives, the switch records its source MAC against the ingress port. Forwarding decisions use the destination MAC — known means forward out one port, unknown or broadcast means flood everywhere except the source port. Entries age out after about five minutes so the table stays current."

Users on the same switch can't reach each other. Different subnets, one switch. Why?

Model answer: "If they're in different VLANs — or the same VLAN but different IP subnets — layer 2 alone won't connect them. Different VLANs need a router or an SVI on a layer-3 switch. Same VLAN but mismatched subnets/masks means each host thinks the other is remote and sends to its gateway. I'd check the port VLAN assignments with show vlan brief and the hosts' IP settings, and confirm whether an inter-VLAN gateway exists."

Level 2 · Deep dive

D4.1 Reading the switch — annotated outputs

SW1# show mac address-table interface Gi1/0/14
Vlan  Mac Address     Type     Ports
  10  3c52.824f.1a9b  DYNAMIC  Gi1/0/14      ← exactly one MAC = a PC. Dozens of MACs =
                                                a rogue switch/AP hangs off this port
SW1# show interfaces Gi1/0/14
GigabitEthernet1/0/14 is up, line protocol is up
  Full-duplex, 1000Mb/s                      ← “100Mb/s, Half-duplex” on a modern PC = trouble
  5 minute input rate 2000 bits/sec
  1234 input errors, 1200 CRC, 0 giants      ← CRC climbing = cabling/duplex; test the run
  0 output errors, 43 late collisions        ← late collisions ⇒ duplex mismatch, classic

SW1# show interfaces status err-disabled
Port      Name    Status        Reason
Gi1/0/22          err-disabled  psecure-violation   ← port security tripped; fix cause, then
                                                       shut/no shut to recover

The everyday workflow you can describe: user gives you their IP → arp on the gateway for the MAC → show mac address-table | include <mac> → port → show interface for errors/speed → show run interface for VLAN. That chain ("IP → MAC → port") is how real engineers physically locate any device.

D4.2 STP one level down

  • Election: lowest bridge ID (priority, default 32768, then lowest MAC) wins root. Unmanaged default = your oldest, slowest switch becomes root. Always set the core switch's priority low (e.g. 4096) deliberately.
  • Port roles: root port (best path to root), designated (forwarding on a segment), alternate/blocked. Legacy states listening→learning→forwarding = the 30 s delay PortFast skips for edge ports.
  • Guards: BPDU Guard (edge port hears a switch → err-disable — stops users looping wall ports), Root Guard (uplink tries to become root → block — stops topology hijack), Loop Guard/UDLD (one-way fiber links).
  • Variants: RSTP (802.1w, seconds), MST (instances per VLAN group), Cisco Rapid-PVST+ (a tree per VLAN).
  • Broadcast-storm incident pattern you can narrate: users report "everything frozen", switch CPUs 100%, all port LEDs solid — someone plugged both wall jacks into a mini-switch under a desk. Find via MAC flap logs, shut one port, network heals instantly. Prevention: BPDU Guard + storm control on all access ports.

D4.3 VLAN security edge cases

  • DTP (Dynamic Trunking Protocol): Cisco ports may auto-negotiate trunking — an attacker's crafted DTP can turn their access port into a trunk and reach every VLAN. Hardening: switchport mode access + switchport nonegotiate everywhere users plug in.
  • Double-tagging attack: outer tag = native VLAN gets stripped, inner tag rides into another VLAN. Mitigation: native VLAN ≠ any user VLAN, and tag it (vlan dot1q tag native).
  • Unused ports: shutdown + parked in a dead "black-hole" VLAN — a standard audit finding when not done.
  • Voice VLAN detail: the phone tags voice frames (learned via CDP/LLDP) and passes PC traffic untagged — one cable, two networks, QoS trust boundary at the phone.
Module 05 · Networks

Routing

How routers pick paths: routing tables, static and dynamic routing, the protocols you'll be asked to compare, and ACLs.

5.1 What a router does with a packet

For every packet, a router: checks the destination IP → looks it up in the routing table → picks the entry with the longest prefix match (most specific network wins) → decrements TTL → rewrites the layer-2 frame for the next hop → forwards. If nothing matches and there's no default route, the packet is dropped and an ICMP "destination unreachable" goes back.

Longest prefix match

If the table holds 10.0.0.0/8, 10.1.0.0/16 and 0.0.0.0/0, a packet to 10.1.2.3 uses the /16 — the most specific route always wins, and the default route 0.0.0.0/0 ("gateway of last resort") only catches what nothing else matches. This one sentence answers several interview questions.

5.2 Where routes come from

  • Connected — subnets on the router's own interfaces (automatic).
  • Static — typed in by an admin: ip route 10.2.0.0 255.255.0.0 192.168.1.2. Predictable, zero overhead — but doesn't adapt to failures and doesn't scale.
  • Dynamic — routers exchange reachability via a routing protocol and recalculate automatically when links fail. Scales, self-heals; costs CPU/bandwidth and complexity.

When several sources offer the same prefix, the router believes the source with the lowest administrative distance (AD) — a trust ranking. Within one protocol, the best path is chosen by that protocol's metric.

SourceADMetric it uses
Connected0—
Static1—
eBGP20path attributes (policy)
EIGRP90bandwidth + delay (composite)
OSPF110cost (∝ 1/bandwidth)
RIP120hop count (max 15)

5.3 The routing protocols compared

Two families: IGPs (Interior Gateway Protocols) route within one organization; EGPs route between organizations — in practice that means BGP, the protocol of the internet. An Autonomous System (AS) is one organization's routing domain.

ProtocolTypeHow it thinksKnow this
RIPIGP, distance-vector"Ask your neighbors how far things are" — hop count only, max 15Legacy; slow convergence; only exam value
OSPFIGP, link-stateEvery router floods link info (LSAs), builds the full topology map, runs Dijkstra SPF for shortest paths by costThe standard enterprise IGP. Open standard. Scales via areas (backbone = area 0); neighbors form adjacencies via hello packets; on a LAN they elect a DR/BDR to reduce chatter
EIGRPIGP, advanced distance-vectorComposite metric (bandwidth+delay); keeps backup routes (feasible successors) for instant failoverCisco-originated; very fast convergence
BGPEGP, path-vectorChooses by policy and AS-path, not speed; peers over TCP 179Runs the internet; what ISPs and multi-homed companies use. "eBGP between ASes, iBGP inside one"

5.4 Reading a routing decision

# Windows: route print   |   Linux: ip route   |   Cisco: show ip route
C   192.168.10.0/24  directly connected, Gi0/1
S   10.50.0.0/16     via 192.168.10.254        # static
O   172.16.4.0/24    via 192.168.10.253 [110/20] # OSPF [AD/metric]
S*  0.0.0.0/0        via 41.33.7.1              # default route → internet

Packet to 172.16.4.9 → the OSPF /24 wins. Packet to 8.8.8.8 → only the default matches. Being able to narrate this makes routing questions easy.

5.5 First-hop redundancy (Depth)

If the default gateway router dies, every host on the subnet is stranded — so two routers share a virtual IP that hosts use as their gateway. Protocols: HSRP (Cisco), VRRP (standard), GLBP (Cisco, load-balances). One is active, the other takes over the virtual IP+MAC on failure. Worth one sentence in an interview: "for gateway redundancy we'd run HSRP or VRRP."

5.6 Access Control Lists (ACLs)

An ACL is an ordered list of permit/deny rules applied to an interface (inbound or outbound). Processing is top-down, first match wins, and every ACL ends with an invisible implicit deny all. Standard ACLs filter by source IP only; extended ACLs match source/destination IP, protocol, and ports:

access-list 110 permit tcp 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255 any eq 443   # let LAN browse HTTPS
access-list 110 deny   ip  any any                              # (implicit anyway)

The order rule is a favorite trick question: if a broad "permit any" sits above a specific deny, the deny never fires. ACLs are also the building block of firewall rules and NAT match lists.

Interview questions — Module 5

Two OSPF routers will not become neighbours. What do you check?

Model answer: "show ip ospf neighbor first: no entry at all, or stuck in a state. Then the things that must match on both sides of the link: the same subnet and mask, the same area, the same hello and dead timers, the same authentication, and the same area type. If they reach EXSTART or EXCHANGE and stop, it is almost always an MTU mismatch. Also check that the interface is not passive and that no ACL is blocking multicast to 224.0.0.5."

What is HSRP or VRRP and what problem does it solve?

Model answer: "A PC has a single default gateway. If that router fails, the PC loses everything off its subnet, even though another router is right there. HSRP, Cisco’s protocol, and VRRP, the open standard, let two routers share a virtual IP and MAC address that hosts use as their gateway. One is active and the other takes over within seconds if it stops hearing hellos. You set priority and preemption so the intended router is active normally, and often track the uplink so a router whose WAN is down hands over the role."

What is a floating static route, and where would you use one?

Model answer: "A static route configured with a worse administrative distance than the primary route, for example a default route via a 4G backup with AD 250 while the primary has AD 1 or comes from OSPF at 110. While the primary exists the floating route stays in the config but is not installed; when the primary disappears it is installed automatically, and when the primary returns it is removed again. It is a cheap branch failover; the catch is that it only reacts when the primary route is withdrawn, so pair it with IP SLA tracking if the link can stay up while the path behind it is dead."

Static vs dynamic routing — when is each appropriate?

Model answer: "Static routes are manually configured: predictable, secure, zero protocol overhead — perfect for small networks, stub sites with a single exit, or a default route to the ISP. But they don't react to failures and become unmanageable at scale. Dynamic routing protocols like OSPF let routers advertise networks to each other and reconverge automatically around failures — essential once you have redundant paths or more than a handful of sites. Real networks mix both: OSPF internally, static defaults at the edge."

What is a default gateway, really?

Model answer: "It's the router interface a host sends traffic to when the destination is outside its own subnet. The host decides using its subnet mask: local destinations are ARPed directly, everything else is framed to the gateway's MAC. No gateway or a wrong gateway gives the classic symptom — LAN works, internet doesn't. On the router side, the equivalent concept is the default route, 0.0.0.0/0, which catches all traffic that matches nothing more specific."

Compare OSPF and BGP.

Model answer: "OSPF is an interior gateway protocol for inside one organization: link-state, every router learns the whole area's topology and computes shortest paths by cost, converging in seconds — it optimizes for speed of the best path. BGP is the exterior protocol between organizations — it's what the internet runs on. It's path-vector over TCP 179 and chooses routes by policy and AS-path, not by link speed, because between companies the question is 'which relationship should carry this traffic', not 'which link is fastest'. In an enterprise I'd expect OSPF or EIGRP inside, BGP only toward ISPs or in large multi-site designs."

What is administrative distance?

Model answer: "It's the router's trust ranking between different route sources when they offer the same prefix — connected is 0, static 1, eBGP 20, EIGRP 90, OSPF 110, RIP 120; lowest wins. It's separate from the metric, which compares paths within one protocol. So a static route will override an OSPF-learned route to the same network — useful, but also a source of subtle misconfigurations."

What is an ACL and what's the significance of rule order?

Model answer: "An access control list is an ordered set of permit/deny statements applied to an interface to filter traffic — standard ACLs match source addresses, extended ACLs match protocol, source, destination, and ports. The router evaluates top-down and stops at the first match, and there's an implicit deny-all at the end. Order is everything: put specific rules before general ones, or the general rule swallows the traffic first — and remember that a new ACL with only deny statements blocks everything, because of the implicit deny."

Level 2 · Deep dive

D5.1 OSPF adjacencies — where OSPF problems actually live

Two routers become neighbors through states: Down → Init → 2-Way → ExStart → Exchange → Loading → Full. Support reality: "stuck in a state" maps to a cause:

  • No neighbor at all → hello mismatch: different hello/dead timers, subnet, area number, or authentication — the parameters in the hello must match. This is the OSPF interview trap: "what must match for OSPF neighbors to form?" → area, subnet/mask, timers, authentication, MTU (see next), and unique router IDs.
  • Stuck in ExStart/Exchange → MTU mismatch between interfaces (database packets won't fit). Beautifully obscure until you've seen it once.
  • Stuck in 2-Way on a LAN → normal! Non-DR/BDR routers stay 2-Way with each other by design.
  • Duplicate router ID → flapping LSAs, weird routes. Set router IDs explicitly (loopback /32s).
  • Cost = reference bandwidth ÷ link bandwidth (default reference 100 Mbps — so 1G and 10G both cost 1 until you raise it: auto-cost reference-bandwidth 100000 — a classic design gotcha).
  • Passive interface on user VLANs: advertise the subnet, but don't send hellos toward users (security + noise).
  • Commands: show ip ospf neighbor, show ip ospf interface, show ip route ospf.

D5.2 Static routing tricks worth naming

  • Floating static: a backup default route with worse AD — ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 4G-GW 250 — invisible while OSPF/primary works, takes over when it dies. Cheap failover.
  • ECMP: two equal routes to the same prefix → per-flow load sharing. Per-flow, not per-packet — one big transfer still uses one path.
  • Recursive lookup: a static route pointing at a next-hop IP requires another lookup to find that next-hop's interface; a route to a next hop that's only reachable via itself = blackhole. Point-to-interface + next-hop is the belt-and-braces form.
  • Null0 routes: summarize + discard — also the standard anti-loop companion to summarization.

D5.3 BGP at recognition depth

  • Path selection order (know the first few): highest weight (Cisco-local) → highest local-pref (how we exit) → shortest AS-path → … MED. "BGP prefers policy over speed" is the honest summary.
  • eBGP = between ASes (TTL 1 by default — peers are directly connected); iBGP = same AS (full-mesh or route reflectors — recognition level).
  • The internet's full table is ~1M IPv4 routes in 2026 — why edge routers need serious memory, and why enterprises usually take only a default route from each ISP instead.
  • Multi-homing: two ISPs + your own AS + BGP = survive an ISP failure; influence inbound path with AS-path prepending. One sentence of this = instant credibility.

D5.4 Routing failure patterns in tickets

  • Routing loop: traceroute shows the same pair of hops repeating until TTL dies → two routers each think the other owns the prefix (bad static + dynamic mix, or redistribution done twice).
  • Asymmetric routing: out via router A, back via router B. Legit in principle — but stateful firewalls on one path drop the returning half: "ping works, TCP dies" between specific sites.
  • Blackhole after change: summary or static route pointing somewhere that silently discards. Traceroute stops dead at one hop with no unreachables — compare with the routing table at that hop.
  • One-liner to reuse: "traceroute tells me where; the routing table at that hop tells me why."
Level 3 · Capstone — design a branch network from scratch

Interviewers sometimes flip from quizzing to designing: "You get a new 60-person branch. Design its network." Here's a complete model answer that stitches Modules 1–8 together. Given block: 10.20.0.0/16, branch #4 gets 10.20.4.0/22.

VLANPurposeSubnet (VLSM)HostsGateway (SVI)
10Staff PCs10.20.4.0/2425410.20.4.1
20Voice (IP phones)10.20.5.0/2425410.20.5.1
30Wi-Fi corporate10.20.6.0/2512610.20.6.1
40Wi-Fi guest (isolated)10.20.6.128/2512610.20.6.129
50Printers/servers10.20.7.0/266210.20.7.1
99Management (switches, APs, iLO)10.20.7.64/266210.20.7.65
—P2P links, spare10.20.7.128/25 (carve /30s or /31s)——
  • Hardware: 2 access switches (48-port PoE, for phones + APs) uplinked with an EtherChannel pair to 1 L3 switch (SVIs above) → firewall/router → dual WAN (fiber primary, LTE/second ISP floating static backup). 3–4 ceiling APs, controller-managed.
  • Services: DHCP scopes per VLAN on the central server with IP helpers on each SVI (guest VLAN's DHCP local on the firewall, 1 h leases); reservations for printers; internal DNS via HQ; NTP from the firewall.
  • Security: guest VLAN → internet only (deny to RFC1918); voice and data separated; management VLAN reachable only from the IT jump subnet; BPDU Guard + port security on access ports; unused ports shut in a parked VLAN; WPA2/3-Enterprise on corporate SSID, portal on guest.
  • Routing: default to the firewall; site-to-site IPsec (or SD-WAN overlay) to HQ; OSPF or statics over the tunnel for HQ subnets; QoS: EF priority for the voice VLAN on the WAN uplink.
  • Ops: switch configs backed up, SNMPv3 into monitoring, interface + WAN utilization alerts, and the whole plan in the site runbook — mention documentation and you're ahead.

Practice delivering this in ~2 minutes with a pen — drawing while talking is exactly what strong candidates do.

Level 4 · State of the art & the horizon — networking

What the top networking teams actually run in 2026, what the frontier looks like, and where it's going. One sentence of this in an interview reads as genuine curiosity — never overclaim hands-on experience with it.

What experts run today

  • Data centers left the "core switch" behind: modern fabrics are leaf-spine (every leaf connects to every spine, equal-cost paths everywhere) with VXLAN/EVPN overlays — layer-2 segments tunneled over a routed layer-3 fabric, with BGP EVPN as the control plane. This is what replaced big STP domains: no blocked links, scale-out by adding spines. Vendors: Arista EOS, Cisco Nexus/ACI, Juniper; hyperscalers run disaggregated "white-box" switches on SONiC (Microsoft's open-source switch OS).
  • Speeds: 25/100G to servers is routine, 400G spine links mainstream, 800G shipping — with 1.6T (IEEE 802.3dj) in development. AI GPU clusters drove a new class of lossless fabrics: RoCE tuning and the Ultra Ethernet Consortium (spec 1.0, 2025) building Ethernet to beat InfiniBand for AI training traffic.
  • NetDevOps replaced typing into switches: configs live in Git as source-of-truth data (NetBox/Nautobot inventory), pushed by Ansible/Nornir/Terraform via APIs (RESTCONF/NETCONF), validated before deployment in digital twins (Batfish, Forward Networks) and labbed in Containerlab/GNS3/EVE-NG. "We stopped SSH-ing to devices; the pipeline does" is the cultural shift.
  • Telemetry replaced polling: SNMP's 5-minute polls give way to streaming telemetry (gNMI/gRPC with OpenConfig models — devices push counters every second), analyzed by platforms like Kentik and ThousandEyes (path-aware synthetic monitoring).
  • AIOps is production reality: Juniper Mist's Marvis and Cisco's AI analytics baseline "normal," flag anomalies, and answer natural-language queries ("why was Wi-Fi bad in building 2 yesterday?"). LLM copilots now draft config changes and summarize incidents in NOC workflows.
  • Internet-infrastructure hardening — the "sensitive critical" layer underneath everything: RPKI route-origin validation (cryptographically signing "this AS may announce this prefix") now covers roughly half the internet's routes and is how BGP hijacks get stopped; MANRS is the operator hygiene pact. DNS got DNSSEC (signed answers), DoH/DoT (encrypted queries), and ECH (encrypting even the site name in TLS). NTP got NTS. Expect "how do we trust routing/DNS/time?" to define the next decade of ops work.

The horizon

  • SRv6 (segment routing over IPv6): the path is programmed into the packet itself — carriers are deploying it as the successor to MPLS; IPv6-only data centers (NAT64 at the edge) are already normal at hyperscalers.
  • DPUs/SmartNICs (NVIDIA BlueField, AMD Pensando, Intel IPU): the NIC becomes a computer that runs the firewall, overlay, storage, and telemetry — freeing host CPUs and moving "the network" into the server itself. P4-programmable data planes live on in these.
  • Post-quantum transport: hybrid ML-KEM key exchange is already default-on in major browsers/CDNs (Module 7's Level 4 has the dates) — network engineers will spend years upgrading VPNs, load balancers and TLS termination for it.
  • Research frontier: co-packaged optics (lasers inside the switch ASIC package), hollow-core fiber (light in air — lower latency), quantum key distribution pilots in carrier networks, and "self-driving networks" — intent in, verified config out, closed-loop remediation.
Module 06 · Networks

Wi-Fi, WAN & VPN

Wireless fundamentals and the technologies that connect sites and remote workers — all named explicitly in the job description.

6.1 Wi-Fi fundamentals (IEEE 802.11)

StandardMarketing nameBandMax (theoretical)
802.11nWi-Fi 42.4 + 5 GHz600 Mbps
802.11acWi-Fi 55 GHz~3.5 Gbps
802.11axWi-Fi 6 / 6E2.4 + 5 (+6 GHz for 6E)~9.6 Gbps
802.11beWi-Fi 72.4 + 5 + 6 GHz~46 Gbps
  • 2.4 GHz: longer range, better wall penetration, but crowded (microwaves, Bluetooth) and only 3 non-overlapping channels (1, 6, 11). 5 GHz: faster, many more channels, shorter range. 6 GHz (Wi-Fi 6E+): clean spectrum, shortest range.
  • SSID — the network name broadcast in beacons. BSSID — one AP radio's MAC. One SSID served by many APs = an ESS; clients roam between APs (the client decides when, which is why "sticky clients" cling to far APs).
  • An access point bridges wireless clients into a wired VLAN. Enterprise APs are often managed centrally by a wireless LAN controller (WLC) and powered by PoE.
  • Wireless is half-duplex shared media — clients take turns (CSMA/CA), so heavy per-AP client counts hurt everyone.

Wi-Fi security — the progression

SchemeVerdictWhy
Open / WEPForbiddenNo/broken encryption — WEP cracks in minutes
WPA (TKIP)DeprecatedStop-gap for WEP hardware
WPA2 (AES-CCMP)Still commonPSK mode: shared passphrase (homes, small offices). Enterprise mode: 802.1X — each user authenticates individually against a RADIUS server (e.g. with AD credentials or certificates)
WPA3Current bestSAE key exchange resists offline password cracking; forward secrecy

Common Wi-Fi tickets: weak signal/dead zones (coverage), channel interference (co-channel APs), wrong PSK, 802.1X certificate expired, DHCP scope exhausted on the guest VLAN, and "connected but no internet" (usually DHCP/DNS, not radio).

6.2 WAN technologies

  • Leased line — dedicated point-to-point circuit from a carrier; guaranteed bandwidth, expensive.
  • MPLS — carrier-managed private WAN connecting many sites; traffic is label-switched inside the provider cloud with QoS guarantees. The classic enterprise WAN.
  • Broadband + VPN — ordinary internet (fiber/DSL/cable/4G/5G) with encrypted tunnels over it. Cheap, no SLA.
  • SD-WAN — the modern answer: appliances at each site build encrypted tunnels over multiple cheap links (internet, LTE, MPLS) and steer each application over the best path in real time, managed from one dashboard. Expect the term to come up; one clean sentence about it impresses.
  • Vocabulary: CPE (customer premises equipment), last mile, QoS (Quality of Service — prioritizing voice/video over bulk data using DSCP markings), latency (delay, ms), jitter (variation in delay — kills VoIP), bandwidth vs throughput (capacity vs what you actually get).

6.3 VPNs — private tunnels over public networks

A VPN (Virtual Private Network) creates an encrypted tunnel across an untrusted network so remote traffic behaves like it's on the private LAN. Two shapes:

  • IPsec — the standard suite for site-to-site (and many client) VPNs. IKE negotiates keys in two phases (Phase 1: secure the negotiation channel; Phase 2: the data tunnels/SAs); ESP encrypts and authenticates the packets. Tunnel mode wraps the entire original packet (site-to-site); transport mode protects only the payload (host-to-host).
  • SSL/TLS VPN — runs over TCP 443, so it works from hotel/café networks that block everything else; typical for remote access, sometimes clientless via browser portal.
  • Split tunnel — only corporate destinations use the tunnel, general browsing exits locally (less load, less control). Full tunnel — everything goes through the company (more control/inspection). A favorite interview distinction.
  • Troubleshooting a "VPN connects but nothing works" ticket: check assigned IP and routes (split-tunnel config), DNS servers pushed by VPN, MTU issues, and whether the firewall permits the user's group to the resource. "VPN won't connect at all": credentials/MFA, reachability of the gateway (port blocked on hotel Wi-Fi), certificate expiry, IKE mismatch (site-to-site).

Interview questions — Module 6

What is QoS and when does it matter?

Model answer: "Quality of service only matters where a link is congested, usually the WAN or internet uplink. You classify traffic, mark it with DSCP values, EF for voice, AF classes for business apps and best effort for the rest, and then queue by class: voice goes into a small priority queue so it never waits behind a backup, and bulk traffic gets what is left. QoS does not create bandwidth; it decides who suffers when there is not enough. A typical ticket is choppy Teams calls during the nightly backup over the same link."

Users complain the Wi-Fi drops in one meeting room. How do you approach it?

Model answer: "Measure first: signal strength in the room in dBm, where below about -70 is weak, and the noise and channel use. Common causes are coverage, so the room is between access points or behind a thick wall; co-channel interference, where several APs share a 2.4 GHz channel, fixed by using only 1, 6 and 11 and moving clients to 5 GHz; or too many clients on one AP at meeting time. I would check the controller for the AP's client count, retries and roaming events, then fix with channel and power planning, an extra AP or band steering."

Difference between 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz Wi-Fi?

Model answer: "2.4 GHz travels farther and penetrates walls better, but it's slower, crowded with interference, and has only three non-overlapping channels — 1, 6, and 11 — so dense deployments interfere with themselves. 5 GHz offers far more channels and much higher speeds at shorter range. Modern design uses 5 or 6 GHz for capacity and keeps 2.4 for legacy and IoT devices. When someone complains about 'slow Wi-Fi far from the AP', band and channel planning is usually the story."

What's the difference between WPA2-Personal and WPA2-Enterprise?

Model answer: "Personal uses a single pre-shared key — fine at home, weak in a company because everyone shares one secret that never rotates and leaves with every ex-employee. Enterprise uses 802.1X: each user authenticates individually through the AP to a RADIUS server, typically with their Active Directory credentials or a machine certificate, so access is per-user, auditable, and revocable. WPA3 improves both modes with SAE against offline cracking."

What is a VPN and how does IPsec work at a high level?

Model answer: "A VPN builds an encrypted, authenticated tunnel across an untrusted network so remote sites or users appear to be on the private network. Site-to-site VPNs run between two gateways permanently; remote-access VPNs serve individual clients. IPsec does it in two stages: IKE Phase 1 authenticates the peers and creates a secure negotiation channel, Phase 2 negotiates the data tunnels, then ESP encrypts and integrity-protects the actual traffic — in tunnel mode the whole original packet is wrapped in a new one. SSL VPNs are the alternative for roaming users since they ride TCP 443, which is open almost everywhere."

A remote user's VPN connects, but they can't open internal apps. Diagnose.

Model answer: "Connected-but-broken usually isn't the tunnel itself. I'd check, in order: did the client get an internal IP and the right routes — in split-tunnel setups a missing route means corporate subnets go out the local internet; can they ping an internal IP → if yes but names fail, the VPN isn't pushing internal DNS servers; is the specific app's port allowed for their user group on the firewall; and finally MTU — large packets dying inside a tunnel classically lets ping work while real applications hang."

What is SD-WAN in one minute?

Model answer: "SD-WAN replaces or augments traditional MPLS by putting smart edge appliances at each site that build encrypted tunnels over several cheap transports — broadband, LTE, plus any existing MPLS — and steer traffic per application based on real-time link quality, all managed centrally. The business case is cost and agility: branch connectivity on commodity internet with the reliability engineered in software."

Level 2 · Deep dive

D6.1 Wi-Fi numbers that make you sound experienced

C:\> netsh wlan show interfaces
    SSID           : CORP-WIFI
    BSSID          : a0:3d:6f:11:22:33     ← which exact AP you're on — compare across users!
    Radio type     : 802.11ax
    Channel        : 44                    ← 5 GHz channel
    Signal         : 82%                   ← Windows hides dBm; ~82% ≈ −55 dBm (good)
    Receive rate   : 573 Mbps
  • RSSI targets: −55 dBm excellent · −67 dBm = the design target for voice/video · −75 dBm marginal · −85 dBm unusable. SNR (signal minus noise) should exceed ~25 dB. Two numbers to quote and you sound like you've done surveys.
  • Channel width tradeoff: 80 MHz is faster but eats the 5 GHz band and overlaps neighbors; dense offices run 20/40 MHz on purpose. More width ≠ better in enterprise.
  • DFS channels share spectrum with radar — AP hears radar → must vacate → clients drop for ~60 s. Explains "Wi-Fi blips near the airport/port" tickets.
  • Sticky client / roaming: the client chooses when to roam; laptops cling to a distant AP at −80 dBm while sitting under a fresh one. Fixes: 802.11k/v/r assist, min-RSSI on APs, driver updates.
  • Co-channel interference: two APs on channel 6 don't collide — they politely take turns (airtime sharing), halving throughput. Wrong power settings create this indoors constantly.
  • Captive portal logic: guest joins → HTTP probe intercepted → portal. HTTPS-everywhere breaks interception → "connected, no internet" until the user browses to a plain-HTTP site. Know http://neverssl.com as the trick.
  • Controller architectures: autonomous APs vs controller-based (CAPWAP tunnels to a WLC) vs cloud-managed (Meraki, Mist). In centrally-switched setups user traffic rides the tunnel to the controller — a WLC outage takes Wi-Fi down even with APs powered.

D6.2 VPN internals & failure signatures

  • IKEv2 is the modern default (faster rekey, MOBIKE roaming). Phase-1 mismatch (encryption/hash/DH group/PSK) → tunnel never forms, logs say "no proposal chosen". Phase-2 mismatch (interesting-traffic selectors don't mirror each other) → tunnel up, some subnets unreachable. Reading which phase failed = half of site-to-site troubleshooting.
  • NAT-T: ESP has no ports, so NAT breaks raw IPsec; NAT traversal wraps ESP in UDP 4500. Firewall must pass UDP 500 + 4500 (+ ESP where no NAT). "Tunnel forms, no data passes" behind NAT = NAT-T not negotiating.
  • DPD (dead peer detection) tears down dead tunnels; without it, one side "up", other side rebooted = blackhole until rekey.
  • MTU again: tunnels add 50–80 bytes of overhead. Symptom set from D3.1 applies — clamp MSS ~1350 on tunnel interfaces is the field fix.
  • Alternatives to name: GRE (plain tunnel, no crypto — often GRE-over-IPsec for routing protocols across VPNs), WireGuard (modern, lean, UDP), DMVPN (Cisco hub-and-spoke mesh), ZTNA (per-app access replacing full VPNs — the strategic direction).

D6.3 QoS in three sentences (they may probe once)

Classify traffic (voice, video, business apps, bulk), mark it (DSCP values — EF for voice, AF classes for the middle, best-effort rest), then queue by class on congested links — priority queue for voice, guaranteed shares for the rest, policing/shaping at the WAN edge. QoS only matters where links congest — a quiet 10G LAN needs none; a 20 Mbps branch uplink carrying phone calls absolutely does. Voice needs: latency <150 ms, jitter <30 ms, loss <1%.

Level 4 · State of the art & the horizon — wireless, WAN & remote access

What experts run today

  • Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be) is the current enterprise deployment wave: MLO (multi-link operation — one client using 5 GHz and 6 GHz simultaneously), 320 MHz channels, 4K-QAM. Cloud-managed platforms (Mist, Meraki, Aruba Central) with AI baselining are the operating model — APs phone home, the dashboard tells you which user had a bad hour and why.
  • Wi-Fi 8 (802.11bn) is defined and prototyped (first silicon shown at CES 2026, ratification expected ~2028) — and its headline is telling: not more speed, but Ultra High Reliability — same bands, same ~23 Gbps peak as Wi-Fi 7, all effort into deterministic latency and dense-environment robustness. The industry decided reliability beats headline Mbps.
  • Private 5G networks (factories, ports, hospitals — dedicated spectrum like CBRS) complement Wi-Fi where deterministic coverage and mobility matter; LEO satellite (Starlink-class) became a legitimate branch backup WAN link, steered by SD-WAN like any other transport.
  • SASE/SSE is the WAN-edge end-state many enterprises bought: SD-WAN plus cloud-delivered security (SWG, CASB, ZTNA, FWaaS) from one vendor cloud — Zscaler, Netskope, Palo Alto Prisma Access, Cloudflare One. The branch firewall shrinks to a thin tunnel-terminator.
  • ZTNA is eating the VPN: instead of putting a remote user "on the network," a broker grants per-application access after checking identity + device posture, continuously. Where VPNs remain, WireGuard-based meshes (Tailscale-style) and always-on IKEv2 with MFA are the pattern. QUIC/HTTP-3 (with MASQUE proxying) increasingly carries this traffic — UDP 443 that looks like web browsing.

The horizon

  • Post-quantum VPNs: hybrid ML-KEM key exchange is landing in OpenSSH (default since 10.x), WireGuard experiments and commercial IPsec stacks — remote-access gear you buy now gets judged on PQC roadmaps.
  • Wi-Fi sensing (using Wi-Fi signals to detect motion/presence), OpenRoaming (seamless federated Wi-Fi onboarding), and 6G research (~2030, integrated sensing + communication, AI-native radio) are the visible next decade.
  • The operational future: one policy engine deciding per-session — user, device health, location, sensitivity — across office Wi-Fi, private 5G, home, and mobile identically. "The network perimeter" finishes dissolving into identity.
Module 07 · Networks / Security

Network security & firewalls

The security concepts the job description asks for: firewalls, the attacks you should recognize, and the hardening basics every infra engineer applies.

7.1 Three frameworks to name

  • CIA triad — every security control protects Confidentiality (only authorized eyes — encryption, access control), Integrity (data unaltered — hashing, checksums), or Availability (systems up — redundancy, backups, DDoS protection).
  • AAA — Authentication (prove who you are), Authorization (what you may do), Accounting (log what you did). Implemented by RADIUS or TACACS+ servers for network gear and by AD for users.
  • Least privilege & defense in depth — give the minimum access needed, and layer controls (firewall + segmentation + endpoint + patching) so one failure isn't fatal.

7.2 Firewalls

A firewall enforces rules about which traffic may pass between security zones (outside/internet, inside/LAN, DMZ). Evolution stages — a great structure for an answer:

  • Packet filter (stateless) — judges each packet alone against ACL-style rules (IPs, ports). Fast, dumb: must explicitly allow return traffic.
  • Stateful firewall — the norm. Tracks every connection in a state table; outbound requests automatically admit their replies. Rule logic becomes "who may initiate what."
  • Next-Generation Firewall (NGFW) — adds deep packet inspection: identifies applications regardless of port, filters URLs, inspects TLS, applies IPS signatures, and integrates user identity (AD) into rules. Vendors you can name: Palo Alto, Fortinet FortiGate, Cisco Firepower, Check Point.
  • IDS vs IPS — an Intrusion Detection System watches a traffic copy and alerts; an Intrusion Prevention System sits inline and blocks in real time. NGFWs embed IPS.
  • Proxy / web filter — terminates users' web sessions, applies URL categories and malware scanning.
  • Host firewalls — Windows Defender Firewall, Linux firewalld/iptables/nftables. Defense in depth means the network firewall isn't alone.
  • 802.1X / NAC — port-based network access control: a device must authenticate (EAP → RADIUS) before its switch port or Wi-Fi association passes traffic; NAC can also check device health before admitting it.

7.3 Attacks you must be able to describe

AttackWhat happensPrimary defenses
PhishingFraudulent mail/pages harvest credentials or deliver malware; spear phishing targets specific peopleUser awareness, mail filtering, MFA
DoS / DDoSFlooding a service into unavailability; DDoS uses botnets from many sourcesUpstream scrubbing/CDN, rate limiting, redundancy
Man-in-the-middleAttacker relays and reads traffic between victimsTLS everywhere, certificate validation
ARP spoofingLAN MITM: attacker claims the gateway's IP with their MACDynamic ARP Inspection, DHCP snooping
Brute force / credential stuffingGuessing passwords / replaying leaked onesLockout policies, MFA, strong password policy
RansomwareMalware encrypts data and demands payment; spreads via phishing and unpatched servicesPatching, least privilege, EDR, offline/immutable backups
SQL injection / XSSWeb-app input attacks (know the names)Input validation, WAF
Social engineeringManipulating people — "IT calling, tell me your password"Process discipline: verify identity, never share credentials

7.4 Hardening — what you'd actually do

  • Patch OSes, firmware, and applications on a schedule (the #1 control; ties into Module 13).
  • MFA on everything remote-facing; strong password policy; disable default accounts.
  • Close what's unused — services, ports, protocols (Telnet→SSH, SNMPv2→v3, disable SMBv1); change default credentials on network gear.
  • Segment — VLANs + firewall rules between user, server, management, and guest zones; separate management network for switch/ESXi/iLO interfaces.
  • Back up and test restores; encrypt sensitive data at rest and in transit.
  • Log and monitor — syslog/SIEM, alert on anomalies; NTP so timestamps line up.
  • Zero trust (buzzword worth one line): never trust by network location alone — authenticate and authorize every access explicitly.

7.5 Encryption, hashing and keys

"Encryption" questions test whether you can tell three different tools apart, and say where data is protected in transit (moving over a network) and at rest (stored on a disk or array).

In transitAt rest
What it protects againstSniffing and tampering on the networkA stolen laptop, disk or backup tape; a decommissioned drive
ExamplesTLS (HTTPS, LDAPS, SMTPS), IPsec VPN, SSH, SMB 3 encryption, WPA3BitLocker (with the TPM), LUKS on Linux, self-encrypting drives, array encryption (Dell "D@RE"), database TDE, encrypted backups
Where the key livesNegotiated per sessionTPM, a key manager or HSM, the array — and a recovery key escrowed in AD or Entra ID
  • Lose the key, lose the data: a BitLocker laptop whose recovery key was never escrowed is a wiped laptop. Key management (storage, rotation, recovery) is most of the real work.
  • Passwords are hashed, not encrypted, with a per-user salt and a deliberately slow algorithm (bcrypt, PBKDF2, Argon2), so a stolen database cannot simply be reversed.
  • Algorithms to name: AES-256 (symmetric), RSA and ECC (asymmetric), SHA-256 (hash). Retired: DES/3DES, RC4, MD5 and SHA-1 for security, SSL and TLS 1.0/1.1.
Say it: "Hashing is one-way, for integrity and password storage. Symmetric encryption like AES uses one shared key and is fast, so it protects bulk data — disks with BitLocker, VPN and TLS traffic. Asymmetric uses a public/private pair; it's slow, so it's used to prove identity with certificates and to exchange the symmetric key. HTTPS uses both: certificates and key exchange first, then AES."

Interview questions — Module 7

RADIUS or TACACS+: what is the difference?

Model answer: "Both are AAA protocols, so the switch or access point asks a central server instead of keeping local accounts. RADIUS runs over UDP 1812 and 1813, combines authentication and authorisation in one reply and encrypts only the password; it is what 802.1X, Wi-Fi and VPN logins use for ordinary users. TACACS+ runs over TCP 49, keeps the three A’s separate, encrypts the whole message and can authorise each command, so it is used for engineers logging in to network devices. Either way, keep a local break-glass account in case the AAA server is unreachable."

What is the difference between an IDS and an IPS?

Model answer: "An IDS watches a copy of the traffic, from a SPAN port or tap, and raises alerts; it cannot stop anything. An IPS sits inline, so it can drop or reset a malicious session as it happens, but a false positive also blocks legitimate traffic and a failure can cut the link. Today most next-generation firewalls include IPS signatures. You start in alert-only mode, tune out the false positives, then move the trusted signatures to blocking."

What is port security on a switch?

Model answer: "It limits which and how many MAC addresses may use an access port, for example a maximum of two, learned sticky. If a different device appears, the port can protect, which drops the frames silently; restrict, which drops and logs; or shutdown, which puts the port into err-disabled until someone clears it. It stops casual plugging-in of unknown devices and MAC flooding, but MAC addresses can be spoofed, so for real access control you use 802.1X."

How does 802.1X work?

Model answer: "Three roles: the supplicant is the client, the authenticator is the switch port or access point, and the authentication server is RADIUS, for example NPS backed by Active Directory. Until authentication succeeds the port passes only EAP. The switch relays the client's EAP inside RADIUS on UDP 1812; the server checks the user or the machine certificate, and answers Access-Accept, often with a VLAN assignment, or Access-Reject. WPA2 and WPA3-Enterprise Wi-Fi are the same flow. Typical failures: an expired RADIUS server certificate, a client missing the root CA, or a device that cannot do 802.1X, such as a printer, which needs MAB or its own VLAN."

What's the difference between a stateful and a stateless firewall?

Model answer: "A stateless packet filter evaluates every packet independently against static rules — so you'd have to write explicit rules for return traffic in both directions. A stateful firewall tracks connections in a state table: when an inside host initiates an allowed session, the firewall automatically permits the matching replies, and unsolicited inbound packets are dropped because they belong to no known connection. That's the default architecture today; next-generation firewalls add application awareness, user identity, URL filtering, and intrusion prevention on top."

What is a DMZ and why do we use one?

Model answer: "A DMZ is a separate firewall zone for services the internet must reach — web servers, mail gateways, the VPN concentrator. The rule structure is: internet can reach only the published DMZ services; the DMZ cannot initiate connections into the internal LAN; the LAN can reach out. So if a public-facing server is compromised, the attacker is contained in the DMZ instead of standing inside the corporate network."

What is the CIA triad? Give a real example of each.

Model answer: "Confidentiality, integrity, availability — the three goals of security. Confidentiality: TLS encryption and file permissions keep payroll data readable only to HR. Integrity: checksums and hashing prove a backup or a download wasn't altered. Availability: RAID, clustering, and DDoS protection keep the service reachable — an attack that just takes a system offline is an attack on availability even though nothing was stolen."

How would you protect a small office network? (open-ended)

Model answer: "Layered basics: a stateful firewall at the edge with deny-by-default inbound; NAT for the LAN; separate VLANs for users, servers, guests, and management with rules between them; WPA2/3-Enterprise Wi-Fi; patched systems with automatic updates; endpoint protection; MFA on email and VPN; least-privilege accounts — no daily work as admin; tested backups following 3-2-1; and central logging so we'd actually notice an incident. Security is a stack of boring controls done consistently, not one product."

What is MFA and why does it matter so much?

Model answer: "Multi-factor authentication requires two or more of: something you know (password), something you have (phone app/token), something you are (biometrics). It matters because passwords leak constantly — phishing, reuse, breaches — and MFA makes a stolen password insufficient by itself. It's the single highest-value control for remote access, email, and admin accounts."

Level 2 · Deep dive

D7.1 Firewall rule craft — what good policy looks like

# Anatomy of a clean rulebase (any vendor)
1  permit  LAN-Users     → DMZ-Web        tcp/443           log     # specific first
2  permit  LAN-Users     → Internet       tcp/80,443,53udp  log
3  permit  Mgmt-Subnet   → All-Devices    ssh,https,snmp            # admin plane, tight sources
4  deny    any           → RFC1918        any               log     # stop leaks to private ranges
5  deny    any           → any            any               log     # explicit final deny — logged!
  • Principles you can recite: default-deny both directions; rules reference named objects/groups (host "DC01", group "Web-Servers") not raw IPs; every rule has a comment + ticket reference; log the final deny — it's your best troubleshooting sensor ("the firewall shows drops from your host to port 445 — that's our answer").
  • Common audit findings: temporary "any/any" rules that became permanent, rules for servers decommissioned years ago, shadowed rules (a broad rule above makes a lower one dead).
  • Order of operations trap on many platforms: NAT happens before or after policy depending on vendor — on a "policy allows it but traffic dies" ticket, check whether the rule should match pre-NAT or post-NAT addresses.

D7.2 How a real compromise unfolds — and where each control bites

  1. Phish lands → user opens attachment (controls: mail filter, awareness, macro blocking)
  2. Malware runs, calls out to C2 over 443 (EDR on the endpoint, DNS/URL filtering, NGFW app control)
  3. Attacker dumps cached credentials, scans the LAN (least privilege, LAPS — unique local admin passwords, port security, private VLANs)
  4. Lateral movement over SMB/RDP with stolen creds (network segmentation, MFA on admin accounts, monitoring for odd logons — event 4625/4624 patterns)
  5. Domain admin obtained → ransomware deployed everywhere at 2 a.m., including reachable backups (tiered admin model, immutable/offline backups — the last line that must hold)

Telling this story compactly demonstrates you understand why the boring controls exist — segmentation isn't bureaucracy, it's what turns "company down" into "one laptop reimaged."

D7.3 Identity & crypto vocabulary one level down

  • Kerberos vs NTLM: Kerberos = modern ticket-based AD auth (needs DNS + time sync); NTLM = legacy challenge-response fallback, relayable, being phased out. "Why does auth fall back to NTLM?" is an L2/L3 conversation you can recognize.
  • LDAP vs LDAPS: 389 plaintext (binds expose passwords!) vs 636 TLS. Apps binding to AD should use LDAPS — an easy hardening win to mention.
  • Hashing vs encryption: one-way integrity (SHA-256; passwords stored as salted hashes) vs reversible confidentiality (AES symmetric — fast, shared key; RSA/ECC asymmetric — key pairs, used to exchange the symmetric key). TLS uses both, in that order.
  • PKI chain: root CA (offline) → intermediate → server cert. Missing intermediate on the server = "some clients fail" — the client-dependent TLS bug from D3.4.
  • EDR vs antivirus: signatures vs behavior + telemetry + response actions (isolate host, kill process). Names: Defender for Endpoint, CrowdStrike, SentinelOne.

D7.4 Authorized scanning — what nmap output means

$ nmap -sS -p- 192.168.20.15        # in a lab / with written authorization only
PORT     STATE    SERVICE
22/tcp   open     ssh          ← service answered the SYN
443/tcp  open     https
3389/tcp filtered ms-wbt-server ← no reply at all = a firewall silently dropped it
8080/tcp closed   http-proxy    ← host sent RST = reachable, nothing listening

open vs closed vs filtered is the diagnostic gold: closed proves the network path works (the host itself refused); filtered proves something in between is eating packets. Ethics line for interviews: scanning is for assets you're authorized to test — on client networks that means a ticket/change and written scope.

Level 4 · State of the art & the horizon — security

What top security teams run today

  • Zero trust became the architecture, not the buzzword (NIST SP 800-207): identity + device posture verified per access, microsegmentation between workloads (Illumio, NSX, cloud-native policies), least privilege enforced by policy engines. "Assume breach; verify explicitly; limit blast radius."
  • The endpoint stack is EDR→XDR: CrowdStrike Falcon, Microsoft Defender XDR, SentinelOne — behavioral detection plus response actions (isolate host, kill process), correlated across endpoint + identity + email + cloud. The SOC runs on SIEM/SOAR: Microsoft Sentinel, Splunk, Google SecOps — logs in, detections out, playbooks automating the boring 80%.
  • Identity is the new perimeter: phishing-resistant passkeys/FIDO2 replacing passwords+OTP (the SOTA answer to phishing), conditional access everywhere, ITDR (identity threat detection — watching AD/Entra for golden-ticket-style abuse), privileged access via PAM vaults and just-in-time elevation.
  • The shared language is MITRE ATT&CK — detections, red teams, and reports all map to its tactic/technique IDs; exposure management (CTEM, attack-surface management) continuously asks "what can an attacker reach today?"
  • AI on both sides: SOC copilots (Microsoft Security Copilot, CrowdStrike Charlotte) triage alerts and draft incident summaries; attackers industrialized phishing with LLMs and deepfake voice/video (finance-approval fraud via fake video calls is a real 2024–26 loss category — verification callbacks are the humble control). And securing AI itself — prompt injection, data leakage via chatbots, model supply chains — became its own discipline (OWASP LLM Top 10).

The horizon — including the quantum question

  • Post-quantum migration is now scheduled reality, not sci-fi: the threat is harvest-now-decrypt-later (adversaries record today's encrypted traffic to decrypt on a future quantum computer). NIST standardized the replacements in 2024 — ML-KEM (FIPS 203, key exchange), ML-DSA (FIPS 204, signatures), SLH-DSA (FIPS 205). By 2026 roughly half of web-facing domains already negotiate hybrid X25519+ML-KEM; Akamai defaulted it for customers in Feb 2026, AWS made ML-KEM its default hybrid and Cloudflare targets origin-side PQC by mid-2026. Deadlines to quote: NIST IR 8547 deprecates RSA-2048/ECC-256 by 2030 and disallows them after 2035; Google targets 2029 internally, Microsoft 2033. For an infra engineer this lands as: inventory your crypto (TLS, VPN, SSH, certs), then upgrade endpoints and appliances as vendors ship PQC.
  • Confidential computing (AMD SEV-SNP, Intel TDX, Arm CCA): VMs encrypted while running, so even the cloud/hypervisor operator can't read guest memory — already offered by the big clouds for sensitive workloads.
  • Memory-safe languages (Rust) pushed by CISA/NSA to eliminate the buffer-overflow class entirely; secure-by-design procurement pressure on vendors.
  • Agentic AI SOCs: the near future is AI agents that investigate an alert end-to-end (query logs, check intel, isolate a host) with humans approving — L1 security triage is automating first, which is exactly why the human skill to build is judgment: scoping, escalation, and communication.
Module 08 · Networks

Network troubleshooting

The method, the tools, and rehearsed walkthroughs of the scenarios interviewers actually pose. This module wins interviews — a support role is 80% this.

8.1 The method (say it before you say commands)

  1. Identify the problem — question the user, reproduce it, note exact errors. What changed recently?
  2. Establish scope — one user, one floor, one site, everyone? Scope tells you the layer: one user → their device/port; a whole subnet → its switch/VLAN/DHCP; a whole site → router/WAN/firewall; everyone including other sites → core or central service (DNS, proxy, AD).
  3. Form a theory — work the OSI stack: bottom-up (cable → IP → service) for "no connection", top-down for "app is slow", divide and conquer (start at L3: can we ping?) when experienced.
  4. Test the theory; escalate if wrong.
  5. Plan and implement the fix — with change control if it touches shared infrastructure.
  6. Verify full function — and confirm with the user.
  7. Document — ticket notes, root cause, knowledge-base article.

8.2 The toolkit

Tool (Win / Linux)What it tells youTypical use
ipconfig /all / ip aIP, mask, gateway, DHCP server, DNS, MACFirst look at any client issue; spot APIPA, wrong VLAN's subnet, missing DNS
pingL3 reachability + round-trip time + lossPing loopback → own stack; gateway → LAN; 8.8.8.8 → WAN; name → DNS. That 4-step ladder is the interview answer
tracert / traceroute, pathping / mtrEvery hop to the destination, where loss/latency starts"Site is slow" — find the bad hop; prove it's beyond your edge
nslookup / digDNS answers, which server answeredName resolution failures; test against a different server: nslookup host 8.8.8.8
arp -a / ip neighIP↔MAC cacheDuplicate IP suspicion, "is the gateway resolving?"
netstat -ano / ss -tulpnListening ports and active connections + owning process"Is the service actually listening?" / port conflicts
route print / ip routeHost routing tableVPN/split-tunnel issues, wrong default route
Test-NetConnection host -Port 443 / nc -zv host 443TCP connectivity to a specific portDistinguish "host up but port blocked" from "host down" — much better than ping alone
Wireshark / tcpdumpFull packet captureThe last word: see handshakes fail, resets, retransmissions, DHCP conversations
ipconfig /flushdns, /release, /renew—Clear DNS cache; force a new DHCP lease
# The 4-step ping ladder — memorize as a sequence
ping 127.0.0.1      # my TCP/IP stack works?
ping 192.168.1.1    # my LAN + switch + cable work? (gateway)
ping 8.8.8.8        # routing + WAN + firewall work?
ping google.com     # DNS works?  → fails only here = DNS problem

8.3 Scenario walkthroughs (rehearse these aloud)

Scenario 1 — "A user can't access the internet." The most likely interview scenario of all.

Model walkthrough: "First I scope it: is it just this user or others too? Just this user — I start at their machine. Physical: link light, Wi-Fi associated to the right SSID? Then ipconfig /all: do they have a valid IP for our subnet — a 169.254 address means DHCP failed; wrong subnet could mean wrong VLAN on the port. Then the ping ladder: loopback, gateway, 8.8.8.8, then a name. Gateway fails → local switch/port/VLAN issue. 8.8.8.8 fails but gateway works → routing/firewall/WAN — I check if colleagues are affected and look at the edge device. Name fails but IP works → DNS: nslookup, check configured servers, flush cache. If it's a browser-only problem — ping all good but pages fail — I think proxy settings or content filter. Throughout, I ask what changed: new cable, moved desk, VPN client installed? And I document the fix in the ticket."

Scenario 2 — "Users can ping by IP but not by name."

Model answer: "That isolates the problem to DNS. I'd verify with nslookup — does it time out (server unreachable) or return an error like NXDOMAIN (record missing)? Check which DNS servers the clients have via DHCP; test resolution directly against them and against a public server to split 'our server is down' from 'upstream forwarding broken'. On a domain network, wrong DNS breaks logons and shares too, so it's urgent. Quick client-side checks: ipconfig /flushdns, correct suffix search list. Root causes I've seen described: DNS service stopped, scope handing out a wrong server address, or firewall now blocking port 53."

Scenario 3 — "The network is slow." (the vaguest ticket in IT)

Model answer: "First make it measurable: slow for whom, to what, since when — one app or everything, wired and wireless both? Then localize: speed test from the affected segment vs another; ping -t to the gateway for loss/jitter (clean gateway pings but bad WAN latency moves suspicion outward); tracert to see which hop latency jumps at. Common local culprits: duplex mismatch on a port (huge symptom: slow + errors), a saturated uplink or WAN link (check interface utilization/monitoring), Wi-Fi interference or an overloaded AP, a broadcast storm from a loop, or one machine flooding (backup running at 10am). If it's one application only, the network is usually innocent — look at the server."

Scenario 4 — "Two devices have the same IP address."

Model answer: "Duplicate IPs cause intermittent connectivity for both devices as ARP entries flip between two MACs. Detection: the OS often warns; arp -a shows the IP's MAC changing. Usual cause: someone configured a static IP inside the DHCP pool. Fix: identify both MACs, trace them to switch ports via the MAC table, change the offender to DHCP or an address outside the pool — and prevent it by keeping an exclusion range for statics and documenting IP assignments."

Scenario 5 — "A whole floor lost connectivity at once."

Model answer: "Simultaneous group failure points at shared infrastructure — the floor's access switch, its uplink, or its VLAN. Check the switch: powered, reachable from the management network? Uplink port status and errors? Recent change — someone patching cables, a new device creating a loop (look for STP topology changes and storm symptoms)? If the switch is dead, that's when spare hardware and the escalation path matter: notify, engage the next level with what I've verified, and communicate an ETA to affected users."

Interview questions — Module 8

A user’s connection is slow and drops now and then, but only theirs. Where do you look?

Model answer: "At the physical and data-link layer of that one path. On the switch port: show interfaces for CRC and input errors, late collisions, which point to a duplex mismatch, and the speed it negotiated, since 100 Mb/s on a gigabit port hints at a bad cable. I check whether the port flaps in the log. Then I swap the patch cable and try another port, and on the PC update the NIC driver and check its power-saving settings. If it is Wi-Fi, I look at signal strength and roaming instead."

Walk me through how you troubleshoot "the internet is slow".

Model answer: "First I scope it: one user, one floor or everyone, all sites or one, since when, and what changed. Then I measure instead of guessing: ping the gateway and a public IP to compare latency and loss, check DNS resolution time separately with nslookup, and run tracert or mtr to see where latency starts and whether it persists to the end. If only one PC is slow I look at its NIC speed and duplex, Wi-Fi signal and CPU; if a whole site is slow I check the WAN link utilisation and errors on the edge interfaces. I change one thing at a time, confirm the fix with the user, and write down the cause."

A user cannot open a file share, but colleagues can. How do you narrow it down?

Model answer: "Because others can, the server and network path are probably fine, so I start at the user. Can they reach the server by name and by IP? That splits DNS from connectivity. Test-NetConnection to port 445 checks the path to SMB. Then permissions: the share and NTFS permissions together, their group membership, and whether they logged in before being added to the group, because group changes only apply after a new logon or klist purge. Finally the account itself: locked out, expired password, or a stale mapped drive with cached credentials."

What does a good root cause analysis contain?

Model answer: "A timeline with timestamps from detection to recovery; the impact, meaning who was affected and for how long; the trigger and the root cause, reached by asking why until the answer is a process that can change, not a person to blame; what went well and what slowed us down; and owned actions with dates that stop it recurring, for example monitoring, a runbook update or a change to the change process. It is blameless: the goal is a system that makes the mistake hard, not finding someone to punish."

Ping works to a server but the application on it doesn't respond. What does that mean?

Model answer: "Ping proves layer-3 reachability only — the host is up and routed. The application lives at layer 4+: the service may be stopped, listening on a different port, or a firewall may block that port while permitting ICMP. I'd test the specific port with Test-NetConnection -Port or nc -zv, and on the server check the service state and ss -tulpn / netstat to confirm it's listening. The reverse is also true — ping blocked but app fine — which is why I never rely on ping alone."

What's the difference between tracert and pathping (or traceroute and mtr)?

Model answer: "Tracert maps the path once — each hop and its latency at that moment. Pathping and mtr combine trace and statistics: they keep probing every hop over time and report per-hop packet loss, which is what you need for intermittent problems — a single trace can look clean while mtr shows 15% loss starting at hop 4."

When would you reach for Wireshark?

Model answer: "When the normal tools tell me that it fails but not why — I capture at the client or a switch SPAN port and read the conversation: does the TCP SYN go unanswered (filtered), come back RST (service refusing), do I see retransmissions (loss/MTU), does DHCP's DORA complete, does TLS fail at the certificate step? It's also the honest answer for proving the network innocent — showing the request left us and the server took 30 seconds to answer."

Level 2 · Deep dive

D8.1 Annotated outputs — read them like an engineer

C:\> ping 10.50.1.10
Reply from 10.50.1.10: bytes=32 time=38ms TTL=63
   TTL tells a story: Linux starts at 64, Windows at 128, network gear at 255.
   TTL 63 = a Linux box one router hop away. TTL 116 = a Windows host ~12 hops away.
   Sudden TTL change on repeat pings = the path (or the answering machine!) changed.

C:\> tracert -d www.example.com
  1     1 ms   192.168.10.1        ← my gateway — LAN is fine
  2     3 ms   41.33.7.1           ← ISP edge — our firewall/WAN link fine
  3     4 ms   41.178.0.14
  4     *      *      *            ← one silent hop = usually just ICMP-deprioritized. IGNORE
  5    64 ms   62.115.42.9         ← +60ms jump = the international/submarine leg — normal
  6    65 ms   93.184.216.34       ← destination; end-to-end ~65ms, loss nowhere: path healthy
   Rule: a problem hop affects EVERY hop after it. One starred hop that recovers = cosmetic.
   Stars from hop N to the end = real blackhole at N.

C:\> netstat -ano | findstr :8080
  TCP  0.0.0.0:8080   0.0.0.0:0   LISTENING   4312
C:\> tasklist | findstr 4312
  javaw.exe   4312                 ← who owns the port — “port already in use” solved

D8.2 Wireshark / tcpdump starter kit

# Wireshark display filters that solve 90% of cases
ip.addr == 10.1.2.3                    # one host's conversations
tcp.port == 443 && ip.addr == 10.1.2.3
tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0   # who is opening connections
tcp.analysis.retransmission            # loss somewhere on the path
tcp.flags.reset == 1                   # who is killing connections
dns || dhcp                            # the infrastructure chatter
http.response.code >= 400

# tcpdump on a Linux server (no GUI)
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -n host 10.1.2.3 and port 443
sudo tcpdump -i any -n udp port 67    # watch DHCP DORA live
sudo tcpdump -w /tmp/case123.pcap ... # capture to file, analyze in Wireshark later
  • Capture placement matters more than filters: on the client you see what it sent; on a SPAN/mirror port you see what the switch actually delivered; compare both to find where frames vanish.
  • Three instant reads: SYN, SYN, SYN with no answer = silently filtered. SYN→RST = port closed at the host. Handshake completes then zero-window/long gaps = the application is slow, network innocent — the capture that ends the "it's the network" blame game.

D8.3 Edge cases that make tools lie

  • Ping fine, app broken → MTU/MSS black hole (VPNs!): small packets pass, full-size die. Test with ping -f -l 1472, then 1400, 1350… the boundary reveals the tunnel.
  • Traceroute shows a "bad" hop that isn't → routers deprioritize ICMP generation; latency at a hop with clean latency after it = cosmetic. Only trust patterns that persist to the destination.
  • Asymmetric paths: your traceroute shows the outbound path only — the return may differ (and be the broken half). When two sites disagree about who's down, trace from both ends.
  • DNS caching layers (browser → OS → resolver): a fixed record "still broken" on one machine only = stale cache at some layer; ipconfig /flushdns + browser restart before deeper digging.
  • Wi-Fi roaming mid-test: pings drop every few minutes on a laptop = roams between APs, not a network fault — check BSSID before/after.
  • The observer effect: remote-desktop into a machine to test its network = your session competes with your test. Prefer out-of-band access (console/iLO) for serious loss testing.

D8.4 The escalation package (copy this structure)

Ticket #48211 — P2 — Branch CAI-03 intermittent packet loss
SYMPTOM   Users report app freezes 09:00–11:00 daily; VoIP choppy.
SCOPE     ~40 users, branch CAI-03 only. HQ + other branches clean.
EVIDENCE  mtr HQ→branch: 8% loss starting hop 4 (ISP PE) during window, 0% after 11:00.
          Branch router: WAN interface 95–100% utilization in window (graph attached).
          Top talker: 10.3.7.22 (backup agent) pushing 18 Mbps to cloud during window.
TRIED     Rebooted branch AP (no effect) · confirmed no QoS policy on WAN uplink.
THEORY    Backup job saturating 20M uplink; VoIP unprotected without QoS.
ASK       L2: apply QoS template (EF for voice) + reschedule backup to 22:00. Approve change?

Symptom → scope → evidence → tried → theory → specific ask. An escalation written like this is the single fastest way to be seen as promotable.

Level 4 · State of the art & the horizon — from troubleshooting to observability
  • Today's expert stack: the reactive ping-and-trace workflow is being wrapped in observability — metrics, logs, and traces flowing through the OpenTelemetry standard into Prometheus/Grafana, Datadog, Dynatrace or Elastic; synthetic monitoring (ThousandEyes, Catchpoint) runs your "ping ladder" continuously from dozens of vantage points so you see the DNS/BGP/ISP problem before users call; eBPF agents observe every connection on every host with no packet capture setup.
  • AIOps correlation (Dynatrace Davis, BigPanda, Moogsoft): 500 alerts collapse into one incident — "these 47 alarms are all downstream of switch X" — the machine doing the scoping step of your methodology.
  • LLM copilots in the NOC: summarize the incident so far, draft the customer update, propose next diagnostic steps, write the postmortem skeleton. 2026 reality in large delivery centers — including Capgemini's own AI-augmented operations offerings.
  • Pre-change verification: digital twins (Batfish, Forward) simulate "will this ACL change break anything?" against a model of the whole network before it ships — troubleshooting's future is preventing the ticket.
  • The horizon: closed-loop self-healing (detect → diagnose → remediate via automation with human approval), intent-based verification ("prove every branch can still reach the ERP"), and autonomous L1. Your career read: the tools do the collecting; humans keep the hypothesis-forming and judgment — which is exactly the skill this module trains.
