Module 09 · Storage

Storage

Disks, RAID, and the three ways servers get storage — DAS, NAS, and SAN — plus the backup concepts every operations team lives by.

9.1 The disks themselves

TechnologyHow it worksPerformanceWhere used
HDD (hard disk drive)Spinning magnetic platters + moving heads; 7.2k/10k/15k RPM~100–200 IOPS, ms-level latencyBulk capacity, backups, archives — cheap per TB
SSD (solid state)NAND flash, no moving partsTens of thousands of IOPS, sub-msOS disks, databases, VMs
NVMe SSDFlash attached via PCIe with the NVMe protocol instead of legacy SATA/SAS100k–1M+ IOPS, lowest latencyHigh-performance tiers, vSAN caches
  • Interfaces: SATA (consumer, 6 Gbps), SAS (enterprise — dual-ported, deeper queues), NVMe/PCIe (fastest).
  • The three performance metrics — use them precisely: IOPS (I/O operations per second — how many reads/writes), throughput (MB/s — how much data), latency (ms — how long each operation takes). A database cares about IOPS and latency; a backup job cares about throughput.

9.2 RAID — surviving disk failure

RAID (Redundant Array of Independent Disks) combines disks for performance and/or fault tolerance. Done by a hardware RAID controller (with battery-backed cache) or in software (Windows Storage Spaces, Linux mdadm/ZFS).

LevelMin disksSurvivesUsable capacityCharacter
RAID 020 failures100%Stripes for speed; any disk death loses everything — never for production data
RAID 121 disk50%Mirror; simple, fast reads; standard for OS/boot drives
RAID 531 diskn−1 disksEfficient; write penalty (parity calc); risky rebuilds on huge disks
RAID 642 disksn−2Double parity; the safe default for big-capacity arrays
RAID 1041 per mirror pair50%Best mix of speed + resilience; databases and VM datastores
  • A hot spare is an idle disk the controller automatically rebuilds onto when a member dies. During a rebuild the array is degraded and vulnerable — RAID 5's weakness on multi-TB drives (a second failure or read error mid-rebuild is fatal) is why RAID 6 exists.
  • RAID is not a backup — it protects against disk hardware failure only, not deletion, corruption, or ransomware, all of which are faithfully mirrored. Say this sentence in the interview.

9.3 Block vs file vs object — the three access models

ModelThe server sees…ProtocolsBest for
BlockA raw disk (a LUN) it formats with its own filesystemiSCSI, Fibre Channel, (local: SATA/SAS/NVMe)Databases, VM datastores — lowest latency, most control
FileA ready-made shared folder over the networkSMB/CIFS (Windows, port 445), NFS (Linux/VMware, port 2049)Home directories, department shares, ISO libraries
ObjectAn HTTP API storing objects with metadata in flat bucketsS3 API, Azure BlobCloud-scale unstructured data, backup targets, archives

9.4 DAS, NAS, SAN

  • DAS (Direct-Attached Storage) — disks inside or cabled to one server. Fast and simple; capacity is trapped in that server.
  • NAS (Network-Attached Storage) — an appliance that owns its filesystem and serves files over the LAN via SMB and NFS. Users, permissions, quotas built in.
  • SAN (Storage Area Network) — a network (usually dedicated) that delivers blocks: the array carves RAID pools into LUNs (Logical Unit Numbers) and presents them to servers, which format them like local disks. Shared block storage is what makes VMware clustering (vMotion/HA) possible.

SAN transport options

TransportRuns onKey vocabulary
Fibre Channel (FC)Dedicated fabric: HBAs in servers → FC switches → array; 8/16/32 GbpsWWN (World Wide Name — FC's MAC address), zoning (fabric ACLs: which HBA sees which array port), LUN masking (array-side: which host sees which LUN)
iSCSIBlock SCSI over ordinary TCP/IP — port 3260; ideally a dedicated VLAN with jumbo framesInitiator (client), target (array), IQN (iSCSI name), CHAP auth. Cheaper than FC — no special hardware
FCoE / NVMe-oFFC frames on converged Ethernet / NVMe over fabricsRecognize the names; NVMe-oF is the modern high-end

Multipathing (MPIO): every serious server has two paths (two HBAs/NICs, two fabric switches, two array controllers) to the same LUN, for failover and load balancing. In VMware this appears as path policies (Round Robin etc.).

9.5 Provisioning, snapshots, tiering

  • Thick provisioning — allocate all promised space up front (predictable). Thin provisioning — allocate on demand; you can promise more than you have (oversubscription) — efficient, but monitor actual usage or a full pool takes every thin volume down at once.
  • Storage snapshot — an instant point-in-time image implemented copy-on-write; cheap to create, great for "restore the share to before the bad script ran", but it lives on the same array — not a backup by itself.
  • Deduplication & compression — arrays store repeating blocks once; huge savings on VM farms and backups.
  • Tiering — hot data automatically lives on flash, cold data on big slow disks.

9.6 Backup — the concepts interviews test

TypeWhat's copiedRestore needsTrade-off
FullEverything1 setSlow to take, fastest to restore
IncrementalChanges since the last backup of any typeFull + every incremental sinceFastest daily, slowest/most fragile restore chain
DifferentialChanges since the last fullFull + newest differential onlyMiddle ground; grows through the week
  • 3-2-1 rule: 3 copies of data, on 2 different media/systems, 1 offsite (or offline/immutable — the anti-ransomware copy).
  • RPO (Recovery Point Objective) — how much data you may lose = time since last backup. RTO (Recovery Time Objective) — how fast you must be back. These two numbers drive the whole design.
  • A backup that was never test-restored is a hope, not a backup. Interviewers love hearing about restore testing.
  • Tools worth naming: Veeam (the VMware world's favorite), Commvault, Windows Server Backup, Linux rsync/tar.

9.7 The Dell storage portfolio — names you must recognise

Dell bought EMC in 2016 and sold storage as Dell EMC until about 2021–22. The brand is now plain Dell (Dell Technologies), but job descriptions still say "Dell EMC". Current products follow one pattern: Power + what it does. Interviewers expect you to place each name: which access model (block, file or object, 9.3), which tier, and what it replaced.

ProductWhat it isTypical useOlder name
PowerStoreMidrange all-NVMe unified array: block (FC, iSCSI, NVMe/TCP), file (SMB, NFS) and VMware vVols; always-on deduplication and compressionThe default general-purpose array for VMware clusters and databasesReplaces Unity XT and SC (Compellent)
Unity XTMidrange unified array, hybrid or all-flash, managed in UnisphereStill in many estates you will supportEMC VNX before it
PowerMaxHigh-end block array; SRDF replication between sites; mainframe supportBanks, telcos: workloads that must not stopVMAX, Symmetrix
PowerScaleScale-out NAS running OneFS: add nodes and one filesystem grows; SMB, NFS, HDFS, S3File shares at petabyte scale, media, AI datasetsIsilon
PowerVault ME5Entry-level block array (iSCSI, FC, SAS), simple web managementSmall sites, direct-attached to a few serversPowerVault ME4
PowerFlexSoftware-defined block storage over many x86 serversLarge, scale-out block at high performanceScaleIO, VxFlex
ObjectScale / ECSS3-compatible object storageBackups, archives, cloud-native appsElastic Cloud Storage
PowerProtect DDBackup target appliance with inline deduplication; DD Boost speeds backups; retention lock makes copies immutableWhere Veeam, NetWorker or PowerProtect Data Manager write backupsData Domain
VxRailHyperconverged appliance: PowerEdge servers + VMware vSAN, updated as one unitTurnkey VMware clusters without a separate SAN—
  • Management: Unisphere (Unity, PowerMax, PowerVault) and PowerStore Manager on the array; CloudIQ for fleet health and predictions across arrays, servers and switches. Arrays also "phone home" to Dell support through Secure Connect Gateway, like servers do (18.9).
  • The day-to-day vocabulary is the same on every array: create a pool, carve a volume (LUN), map it to a host or host group (masking), check the host sees it over iSCSI or FC (multipathing!), and watch capacity and latency.
  • Data reduction ratio (for example 4:1) is how much logical data fits per physical TB after deduplication and compression. It depends on the data: VDI and VM images reduce well, already-compressed video and encrypted data barely at all.
Say it: "Dell's current midrange array is PowerStore — unified block and file on NVMe, replacing Unity XT. PowerMax is the high-end block tier with SRDF replication, PowerScale is the scale-out NAS that used to be Isilon, and PowerProtect DD — formerly Data Domain — is the deduplicating backup target. Whatever the model, the workflow is pool, volume, host mapping, multipath check."

Interview questions — Module 9

iSCSI or Fibre Channel: when would you pick each?

Model answer: "Both carry SCSI block commands to a LUN. iSCSI runs over ordinary Ethernet and TCP on port 3260, so it is cheaper and uses skills the team already has; it wants a dedicated VLAN or switches, jumbo frames end to end, and two paths with MPIO. Fibre Channel is a separate, lossless fabric with its own HBAs, switches, WWN-based zoning and very predictable latency, which is why large databases and high-end arrays still use it. For a small or mid-size VMware estate on 25 GbE, iSCSI is usually the sensible choice; where FC already exists, you keep it."

A datastore or LUN is almost full. What do you do?

Model answer: "First stop it getting worse and find out why: check for forgotten VMware snapshots, which grow silently, old ISO files and VMs that were powered off but never deleted. Then short term, Storage vMotion a VM or two to a datastore with space. Longer term, grow the LUN on the array and expand the VMFS datastore, or add a new datastore. Because thin pools can be overcommitted, I would also check the pool on the array, since a full pool stops every LUN in it, and set alerts at 80 percent so it never comes as a surprise."

Explain the difference between NAS and SAN.

Model answer: "Both are shared network storage; the difference is what they serve. A NAS owns its own filesystem and serves files — SMB or NFS shares over the ordinary LAN; clients see a network folder. A SAN serves raw blocks: the array presents LUNs over Fibre Channel or iSCSI, and each server formats the LUN with its own filesystem as if it were a local disk. NAS is simpler and perfect for user shares; SAN gives the low latency and shared block access that databases and VMware clusters need — vMotion and HA depend on every host seeing the same LUNs."

Compare RAID 0, 1, 5, 6, and 10. Which for a database?

Model answer: "RAID 0 stripes across disks for speed with zero redundancy — one failure loses all, so it's only for scratch data. RAID 1 mirrors two disks — simple, survives one failure, 50% capacity, classic for OS drives. RAID 5 stripes with one distributed parity — survives one disk at n−1 capacity, but has a write penalty and risky long rebuilds on large disks. RAID 6 adds a second parity and survives two failures — the safe choice for big arrays. RAID 10 mirrors pairs and stripes across them — best combined read/write performance and quick rebuilds at 50% capacity. For a busy database I'd choose RAID 10, because random write performance and fast recovery matter more than capacity efficiency."

Why isn't RAID a backup? And why isn't a snapshot a backup?

Model answer: "RAID protects only against disk hardware failure — deletion, corruption, and ransomware are replicated to every member instantly. Snapshots do give you point-in-time rollback, but they live on the same array and usually depend on the base data, so an array failure or a full pool takes them with it. A real backup is an independent copy on separate media, ideally offsite and offline per the 3-2-1 rule, and it's only proven when you've tested a restore."

What is a LUN? What are zoning and masking?

Model answer: "A LUN is a logical unit — a slice of the array's RAID pool presented to hosts as a block device. Zoning is configured on the Fibre Channel switches and controls which server HBAs can even see which array ports — like an ACL for the fabric. LUN masking is on the array and controls which specific hosts may access which LUN. Together they ensure only the right cluster sees a given LUN — two unrelated hosts writing one LUN without cluster awareness corrupts it."

What are IOPS, throughput, and latency — and thick vs thin provisioning?

Model answer: "IOPS is operations per second — the currency of random workloads like databases and VDI; throughput is MB/s — what sequential workloads like backups care about; latency is per-operation delay, where SSDs win by orders of magnitude. Thick provisioning reserves all space up front; thin allocates as data is written, letting you oversubscribe the pool — efficient, but you must monitor real consumption, because a thin pool hitting 100% takes every volume on it offline simultaneously."

Design a backup scheme for a small company (RPO 24h).

Model answer: "A weekly full backup, nightly incrementals — or differentials if restore simplicity matters more than backup window — satisfying a 24-hour RPO. Retention: daily for two weeks, weekly for a couple of months, monthly for a year, per policy. Follow 3-2-1: primary copy on a backup server or NAS, a second copy replicated offsite or to cloud object storage, with one copy immutable or offline against ransomware. Monitor job success daily and do a test restore on a schedule — quarterly at minimum — because an unverified backup isn't one."

Level 2 · Deep dive

D9.1 iSCSI end to end — the flow you can narrate

  1. Array side: create the volume/LUN → map it to the host's IQN (e.g. iqn.1991-05.com.microsoft:srv01) → optionally require CHAP.
  2. Network: dedicated storage VLAN, ideally two (path A/B), jumbo frames end-to-end (host NIC 9000 = switch 9198+ = array 9000 — one mismatched hop causes silent fragmentation or drops), flow control on, no routing if avoidable.
  3. Host: iSCSI initiator (Windows iscsicpl; Linux iscsiadm -m discovery -t st -p 10.9.9.10 then --login) → discover portal → log in over two NICs → enable MPIO → new raw disk appears → format and use.
$ sudo multipath -ll
mpatha (3600a098038303f...) dm-2 NETAPP,LUN
size=2.0T features='3 queue_if_no_path' hwhandler='1 alua'
|-+- policy='round-robin 0' prio=50 status=active
| `- 3:0:0:1 sdb 8:16 active ready running     ← path via fabric/NIC A
`-+- policy='round-robin 0' prio=10 status=enabled
  `- 4:0:0:1 sdc 8:32 active ready running     ← path via fabric/NIC B — lose one, I/O continues

Real ticket pattern: "datastore/disk latency alarms every day at 13:00" → one iSCSI path down for weeks (nobody noticed — MPIO masked it) and the surviving link saturates at lunch-hour load. Moral you can quote: redundancy hides failures; monitor the paths, not just the service.

D9.2 Why RAID 5 fell out of favor — the math in one paragraph

Consumer/nearline disks quote an unrecoverable read error (URE) rate around 1 per 1014 bits ≈ one bad sector per ~12.5 TB read. Rebuilding a failed disk in a RAID 5 of large drives forces reading every surviving bit — 10 TB × 5 disks approaches or exceeds that expectation, so the rebuild itself may hit an unreadable sector, and with zero remaining redundancy the array (or at least data) is lost. Hence: RAID 6 or RAID 10 for big disks, enterprise drives with better URE (1015), scrubbing (periodic full-array reads that catch latent bad sectors early), and hot spares to shrink the exposed window. Bonus vocabulary: SMART monitoring predicts failures; replace on pre-fail attributes, don't wait.

D9.3 Controller cache, queues, and the performance conversation

  • Write-back cache: controller ACKs the write once it's in RAM cache → fast, but needs a BBU/flash-backed cache to survive power loss; a dead battery silently flips arrays to write-through (ACK only after disk) → "everything got slow last week" = check the RAID battery. A genuinely impressive answer for an associate.
  • Queue depth: how many I/Os can be in flight; deep queues raise throughput and latency. High IOPS + high latency = saturated; low IOPS + high latency = something sick (path, cache, failing disk).
  • Real numbers for intuition: 7.2k HDD ≈ 80–120 IOPS · 10k SAS ≈ 140–180 · SATA SSD ≈ 50–90k · NVMe ≈ 200k–1M+. A 20-disk HDD RAID 10 ≈ ~2,000 IOPS total — one modern SSD beats it.

D9.4 File-protocol versions & edge cases

  • SMB: v1 = ancient, wormable (WannaCry) — disabled everywhere; never re-enable it to "fix" an old scanner, isolate the device instead. v2/v3 current; SMB3 adds encryption and multichannel. Port 445.
  • NFS: v3 = host-based trust (export lists, UID mapping — "why does user 1001 own these files?"), v4 = stateful, Kerberos-capable, single port 2049. VMware NFS datastores typically v3 — locking and permissions behave differently than v4, an L2-level detail worth recognizing.
  • Mixed-protocol gotcha: the same NAS folder shared over SMB (Windows ACLs) and NFS (POSIX bits) has two permission models — mismatches create "I can see it from Windows but not from Linux" tickets.

D9.5 Backup engineering vocabulary (Veeam-era)

  • Crash-consistent (as if power was pulled) vs application-consistent (app flushed via VSS on Windows / pre-freeze scripts): databases and AD need the latter — restoring a crash-consistent DC or SQL box invites corruption. This distinction is a favorite senior filter question.
  • CBT (Changed Block Tracking): the hypervisor marks changed blocks so incrementals read only deltas — why nightly VM backups take minutes.
  • Synthetic full: build a new "full" from existing increments on the backup server — full-restore convenience without re-reading production.
  • Immutability: object-lock (S3), hardened Linux repos — backups that ransomware with admin credentials still can't delete. The modern non-negotiable.
  • Replication ≠ backup: replication copies changes fast — including the encryption/deletion. Replication answers RTO (fast failover); backups answer RPO/history. You want both, for different reasons.
  • Restore drills: file-level, VM-level, and the full "restore AD + app tier in the DR site" exercise. Mentioning you'd time the restore against RTO shows operational maturity.
Level 3 · Expert corner — arrays, replication & the performance flow

Inside a storage array (so the words mean pictures)

  • A midrange array = two controllers (active/active, mirrored write cache, each with FC/iSCSI front-end ports) + disk shelves (JBODs) on redundant SAS back-end loops. Every component dual — a controller reboot (firmware upgrade) is designed to be invisible if multipathing on every host is healthy. Pre-upgrade check: "all hosts show ≥2 paths" — a real change-task an associate gets.
  • ALUA: both controllers accept I/O but each LUN has an "owning" controller with optimized paths — why multipath output shows prio 50 vs prio 10 path groups.
  • Modern refinements: storage pools instead of fixed RAID groups (wide striping), always-on compression/dedupe on all-flash, QoS per LUN (cap the dev box's IOPS so it can't starve production).

Replication & DR — the level above backups

  • Synchronous: write ACKed only after the remote array has it → RPO = 0, but distance-limited (~100 km; light is slow) and the WAN's latency becomes your write latency. For metro DR / stretched clusters.
  • Asynchronous: ship deltas every N seconds/minutes → RPO = N, any distance. The standard for country-to-country DR.
  • Failover realities interviewers respect: replication also replicates corruption (still need backups); failback is its own project; and an untested DR plan is theater — name "annual DR test" and you sound like operations, not theory.
  • vSAN specifics (bridges to Module 10): disk groups (cache SSD + capacity devices), policies per-VM — FTT=1 mirrors objects across 2 hosts (+witness), RAID-5/6 erasure coding on all-flash; a host in maintenance triggers resync traffic — why vSAN clusters want 10/25G networking.

The storage-performance troubleshooting flow (recite this)

  1. Define: which VMs/hosts, reads or writes, since when, latency number vs baseline (GAVG 5 ms → 80 ms is a story; "feels slow" isn't).
  2. Locate the layer: guest (one VM only → its queue/filesystem/app) → host (KAVG > 2 ms = host queueing) → path (dead path, saturated fabric port) → array (DAVG high for many hosts = controller/disk side).
  3. Classic culprits: a backup or antivirus scan storm (look at the time pattern), one "noisy neighbor" VM flooding IOPS, thin pool nearing full (arrays slow down defensively), RAID rebuild in progress, dead cache battery → write-through, misaligned/undersized cache tier.
  4. Prove it: correlate esxtop/array performance graphs timestamps with the complaint window before changing anything.
Level 4 · State of the art & the horizon — storage

What experts run today

  • All-flash won; NVMe end-to-end is the new normal: arrays like Pure Storage FlashArray, Dell PowerStore/PowerMax and NetApp AFF are all-NVMe inside, and increasingly speak NVMe-oF outward — NVMe over Fabrics, with NVMe/TCP as the pragmatic mainstream (SAN semantics on ordinary Ethernet, replacing iSCSI) and RoCE where ultra-low latency pays. Cheap-and-huge QLC flash made "flash for everything but archives" economical.
  • Software-defined and scale-out took the high end: HCI (vSAN ESA, Nutanix) for general estates; for AI and analytics, parallel scale-out platforms — VAST Data, Weka, plus Ceph/MinIO in open source — feed GPU clusters at hundreds of GB/s (GPUDirect Storage moves data NVMe→GPU bypassing the CPU). The S3 object API became the universal storage language — backup targets, data lakes, archives all speak it.
  • Ransomware reshaped the field: immutable snapshots, object-lock, anomaly detection in the array ("entropy spike = encryption in progress"), and clean-room recovery are now standard array features, not add-ons — storage admins became part of the security team.
  • Capacity frontier: HAMR (heat-assisted recording) pushed hard drives past 30 TB with ~50 TB on the roadmap — disks live on as the cold/capacity tier; 61–122 TB QLC SSDs exist for dense flash; LTO-10 tape (~30+ TB native) keeps tape alive as the cheapest air-gapped ransomware-proof tier. Fun frontier: Microsoft's Project Silica (data in glass) and DNA storage research target century-scale archives.
  • Autonomous storage ops: fleets phone home to AIOps clouds (Pure1, HPE InfoSight) that predict failures and pre-open support cases — many storage tickets now start from the vendor, not the customer.

The horizon

  • CXL (Compute Express Link): memory pooling and tiering over a fast fabric — servers borrowing RAM from a shared pool; the line between "memory" and "storage" blurs this decade.
  • DPUs and computational storage: compression, encryption, even query filtering executed on the NIC or the drive itself — data processed where it lives.
  • Zoned storage (ZNS SSDs, host-managed SMR) squeezing more from media; storage-as-code (provisioning via Terraform/K8s CSI) as the default operating model — the associate-level takeaway: the concepts you learned (LUNs, RAID-thinking, snapshots, paths) survive every one of these waves; only the transport and management planes keep changing.

Tier 2 — Build & grow: partitions, filesystems, LVM, software RAID

# New disk end-to-end (Linux, simple path)
parted /dev/sdb mklabel gpt mkpart data xfs 0% 100%
mkfs.xfs /dev/sdb1
mkdir /data && mount /dev/sdb1 /data
echo "UUID=$(blkid -s UUID -o value /dev/sdb1) /data xfs defaults,nofail 0 0" >> /etc/fstab
mount -a          # ALWAYS test fstab before the next reboot does it for you

# The LVM working set (grow online — the real-world daily task)
pvcreate /dev/sdc            ; pvs ; pvdisplay
vgcreate vg_data /dev/sdc    ; vgs ; vgextend vg_data /dev/sdd
lvcreate -n lv_app -L 100G vg_data       # or -l 100%FREE
lvs ; lvdisplay
lvextend -r -L +50G /dev/vg_data/lv_app  # -r grows the filesystem too (xfs_growfs/resize2fs)
lvremove /dev/vg_data/lv_old

# Software RAID (mdadm) & swap
mdadm --create /dev/md0 --level=1 --raid-devices=2 /dev/sdb /dev/sdc
mdadm --detail /dev/md0 ; cat /proc/mdstat        # rebuild progress lives here
mkswap /dev/vg_data/lv_swap && swapon -a ; swapon --show

Module 10 · VMware

VMware & virtualization

Virtualization from zero, then the vSphere stack you'd administer: ESXi, vCenter, vMotion, HA, DRS, snapshots, and virtual networking.

10.1 What virtualization is and why everyone does it

Virtualization runs multiple isolated virtual machines (VMs) — each with its own OS, virtual CPU, memory, disk, and NIC — on one physical server. The layer that makes this possible is the hypervisor: it owns the hardware and schedules each VM's access to it. Before virtualization, servers ran one app each at 5–15% utilization; virtualization consolidated them, and it's the foundation cloud computing is built on.

Benefits to recite: consolidation (fewer physical boxes → less power/cooling/space), fast provisioning (new server in minutes from a template), isolation (one VM crashing doesn't touch others), hardware independence (a VM is just files — portable between hosts), high availability and live migration, easy lab/testing, snapshot-based rollback, simpler DR (replicate VM files).

VM vs container

A VM virtualizes hardware and carries a full guest OS. A container (Docker, Kubernetes) virtualizes at the OS level — all containers share the host kernel, isolated by namespaces — so they're megabytes instead of gigabytes and start in seconds. One line for interviews: "VMs isolate at the hardware level with a full OS each; containers share the kernel and package just the app and its dependencies."

10.2 The vSphere product map — get the names exactly right

NameWhat it is
vSphereThe overall suite (ESXi + vCenter + features). "We run vSphere 8."
ESXiThe type-1 hypervisor installed on each physical server ("host"). Tiny footprint; managed via vCenter or its own Host Client web UI; console = DCUI; SSH for support.
vCenter ServerThe central management appliance (VCSA — a Linux-based appliance VM). Manages many hosts: inventory, permissions, and it's required for vMotion, HA, DRS. If vCenter is down, VMs keep running — you just lose central management (top trick question).
ClusterA group of ESXi hosts pooled together so HA and DRS can treat their CPU/RAM as one resource pool.
vSphere ClientThe HTML5 web UI to vCenter.
vSANVMware's hyper-converged storage: the cluster pools its hosts' local disks into one shared datastore (flash cache + capacity tiers).
NSX, Aria, Horizon, VCFNetwork virtualization / management & automation / VDI desktops / the whole private-cloud bundle (VMware Cloud Foundation). Name-recognition level is enough. (Context point: Broadcom acquired VMware in 2023 and reorganized licensing around VCF subscriptions.)

10.3 Anatomy of a VM

  • Virtual hardware: vCPUs, memory, virtual disks (VMDK), virtual NIC (vmxnet3 is the paravirtual/fast type), virtual SCSI controller (PVSCSI), CD-ROM mapping an ISO.
  • VMware Tools — drivers + agent installed inside the guest OS: better graphics/mouse, the vmxnet3/PVSCSI drivers, heartbeats to the host, graceful shutdown/restart from vCenter, time sync, and the memory balloon driver. "VM shows 'Tools not running'" = degraded manageability; installing/upgrading Tools is a routine associate task.
VM fileContents
.vmxConfiguration (hardware, options) — plain text
.vmdk / -flat.vmdkVirtual disk descriptor / the actual data
.nvramBIOS/UEFI state
.vswpSwap file created at power-on (size = unreserved RAM)
.vmsn / -delta.vmdkSnapshot memory state / snapshot delta disks
.logVM logs — where support looks first

10.4 Storage in vSphere

  • A datastore is where VM files live. Types: VMFS (VMware's clustered filesystem on block LUNs — FC/iSCSI/local; multiple hosts mount it simultaneously, which is what enables vMotion/HA), NFS (file-based datastore on a NAS), vSAN.
  • Disk provisioning: thin (grows on demand), thick lazy-zeroed (space reserved), thick eager-zeroed (pre-zeroed — needed for clustering/FT, best write performance).
  • RDM (Raw Device Mapping) hands a VM a raw LUN directly — legacy clustering cases.
  • Storage vMotion moves a running VM's disks between datastores with no downtime (evacuating an array, rebalancing space).

10.5 Virtual networking

  • vSS (standard switch) is configured per host; vDS (distributed switch) is configured once in vCenter and spans all hosts — consistent and required at scale.
  • A port group = a set of virtual ports with the same settings (VLAN ID, teaming, security policy). VM traffic and infrastructure traffic are separated by port groups + VLANs.
  • VMkernel ports are the host's own IP interfaces, one per service: management, vMotion, iSCSI/NFS storage, vSAN, replication. "Host disconnected from vCenter but VMs fine" → management network problem.
  • Classic ticket: VM moved to a host where the port group's VLAN isn't trunked → VM has no network on that host only.

10.6 The flagship features (the certain questions)

FeatureWhat it doesGotchas to mention
vMotionLive-migrates a running VM between hosts — memory is copied over the vMotion network while the VM runs, then a sub-second switchover. Zero downtimeNeeds shared storage (classic), a vMotion VMkernel network, and CPU compatibility (EVC masks CPU differences)
Storage vMotionMoves a running VM's disks between datastoresCombine both = migrate host+storage at once
HA (High Availability)If a host dies, its VMs are automatically restarted on surviving cluster hostsIt's a restart — minutes of downtime, not zero. Uses heartbeats (network + datastore) to detect failure; admission control reserves failover capacity
DRS (Distributed Resource Scheduler)Load-balances VMs across cluster hosts using vMotion, automatically; affinity/anti-affinity rules (keep the two DCs apart)HA = availability after failure, DRS = performance balancing. They complement, don't overlap
FT (Fault Tolerance)Runs a live shadow copy of a VM on a second host — zero downtime on host failureExpensive (lockstep execution, vCPU limits) — for the few truly critical small VMs
SnapshotsPoint-in-time state of a VM (disk + optionally memory). Writes go to a delta file; revert = discard deltasNot backups; deltas grow and slow I/O; policy: keep max 24–72 h; deleting ("consolidating") a huge old snapshot is slow and fills datastores — a legendary outage cause
Templates & cloningA template is a golden VM image; deploy new VMs from it with guest customization (new hostname, IP, SID). Full clone = independent copy; linked clone shares the parent's diskHow real estates deploy servers in minutes; OVF/OVA are the portable appliance formats

10.7 Resource management (Depth, but high-yield)

  • Shares / Reservations / Limits per VM: shares = relative priority under contention; reservation = guaranteed minimum; limit = hard cap.
  • Memory overcommitment works via: transparent page sharing, the balloon driver (Tools asks the guest OS to give up idle pages), compression, and — worst case — host swapping (terrible performance; the sign of true memory pressure).
  • CPU Ready time — how long a VM waited for physical CPU; the metric that catches oversized VMs ("more vCPUs isn't always faster" — scheduling gets harder).
  • Watch in the client / esxtop: CPU ready, ballooning/swap, datastore latency, and alarms in vCenter.

10.8 Everyday associate tasks & troubleshooting

  • Deploy VM from template; adjust CPU/RAM; extend a VMDK then grow the partition in the guest; mount an ISO; install/upgrade VMware Tools; take/delete snapshots around changes; put a host in maintenance mode (DRS evacuates VMs) for patching via Lifecycle Manager.
  • VM won't power on → check datastore free space (snapshot/delta growth, swap file creation fails), resource reservations, and the VM's log.
  • Host shows disconnected → VMs may be fine; check management network, restart management agents from DCUI, then investigate.
  • VM slow → check CPU ready, ballooning/swapping, datastore latency, snapshot chain length — in that order.

10.9 Hyper-V — the Microsoft hypervisor, mapped to vSphere

Hyper-V is Microsoft's Type 1 hypervisor, installed as a role on Windows Server (or enabled on Windows 10/11 Pro for labs). When you add the role, the hypervisor slides underneath Windows: the Windows you log into becomes the parent (root) partition that manages the hardware drivers, and each VM is a child partition. Since Broadcom's VMware licensing changes (see "the Broadcom era" at the end of this module), many companies run or evaluate Hyper-V, so expect at least one comparison question.

ConceptVMware vSphereMicrosoft Hyper-V
HypervisorESXiHyper-V role on Windows Server (or Azure Local for HCI)
Central managementvCenterFailover Cluster Manager, Windows Admin Center, System Center VMM (SCVMM)
Guest driversVMware ToolsIntegration Services (built into modern Windows and Linux)
Disk fileVMDKVHDX (up to 64 TB; fixed, dynamically expanding or differencing)
Shared storage for a clusterVMFS datastore, vSANCluster Shared Volumes (CSV), Storage Spaces Direct (S2D), SMB 3 file shares
Live move of a running VMvMotionLive Migration
Move a VM's disks liveStorage vMotionStorage Live Migration
Restart VMs after host failurevSphere HAFailover Clustering
Load balancingDRSDynamic Optimization (SCVMM), cluster VM load balancing
Point-in-time copySnapshotCheckpoint — production (VSS, application-consistent, the default) or standard (saves memory state)
Async replication for DRvSphere ReplicationHyper-V Replica (every 30 s, 5 min or 15 min to another host)
Memory overcommitBallooning, TPSDynamic Memory (startup, minimum and maximum RAM per VM)
Virtual switchvSS / vDSHyper-V virtual switch: External, Internal or Private (below); SET for NIC teaming
  • VM generations: Generation 2 VMs use UEFI firmware, Secure Boot and boot from virtual SCSI (use them for anything modern); Generation 1 emulates legacy BIOS and IDE for old guests. You can't convert one to the other in place.
  • The classic Hyper-V ticket: "the VM has no network". Check the virtual switch type (Private or Internal by mistake), the VLAN ID on the VM's adapter versus the physical switch port (it must be a trunk carrying that VLAN), and whether the External switch was bound to the right physical NIC.
  • Checkpoints are not backups — the same rule as VMware snapshots: they chain AVHDX differencing disks on the same storage, and old ones grow and slow the VM. Back up with a VSS-aware tool (Veeam, Windows Server Backup, DPM).
  • PowerShell runs everything: Get-VM, Start-VM / Stop-VM, Checkpoint-VM, Get-VMSwitch, New-VMSwitch -Name Ext -NetAdapterName "NIC1", Move-VM (live migration), Measure-VM (resource use).
  • Licensing in one line: Windows Server Datacenter allows unlimited Windows VMs on a licensed host; Standard covers two. The free standalone Hyper-V Server stopped with the 2019 version.
Say it: "Hyper-V is Microsoft's Type 1 hypervisor. The concepts map one-to-one with vSphere: Live Migration is vMotion, Failover Clustering with Cluster Shared Volumes is HA, checkpoints are snapshots, and Hyper-V Replica gives asynchronous DR replication. Its virtual switch comes in three types — External to reach the physical network, Internal for host and VMs, Private for VMs only."

Interview questions — Module 10

How do VMs get onto the right VLAN in vSphere?

Model answer: "The physical switch ports facing the ESXi hosts are trunks carrying the VLANs. On the host, a standard or distributed switch has port groups, each tagged with a VLAN ID, say VM-Staff on VLAN 20 and VM-Servers on VLAN 30. A VM’s virtual NIC is connected to a port group, and the virtual switch tags its frames with that VLAN on the way out. If a VM gets no network after a move, I check that the port group exists with the same name and VLAN on the new host and that the VLAN is allowed on that host’s uplink trunk."

Users say a VM is slow. How do you troubleshoot it?

Model answer: "I narrow it to a resource. CPU: in esxtop, CPU ready above about 5 percent per vCPU means the VM waits for physical CPU, often because it has too many vCPUs or the host is overcommitted. Memory: ballooning or swapping on the host. Storage: latency, splitting GAVG into KAVG for the host queue and DAVG for the array. Network: dropped packets on the vNIC. Inside the guest I check its own CPU, memory and disk queue. Then I fix the actual constraint, for example right-size the VM or move it with vMotion, rather than just adding resources."

What is a hypervisor? Type 1 vs Type 2?

Model answer: "A hypervisor is the software layer that lets multiple virtual machines share one physical server, allocating CPU, memory, disk, and network to each while keeping them isolated. Type 1 runs directly on the hardware — ESXi, Hyper-V, KVM — and is the data-center standard for performance and stability. Type 2 runs as an application on a desktop OS — VMware Workstation or VirtualBox — and is for labs and development. In production I'd only ever expect Type 1."

Difference between ESXi and vCenter? What happens if vCenter goes down?

Model answer: "ESXi is the hypervisor installed on each physical host — it's what actually runs the VMs. vCenter is the central management server that aggregates hosts into clusters and enables everything cluster-wide: vMotion, DRS, HA configuration, templates, permissions. If vCenter fails, the VMs keep running untouched — ESXi doesn't need vCenter to operate — and even HA restarts still work since HA agents run on the hosts; what you lose is central management, vMotion and DRS until it's back. That distinction is exactly why vCenter itself runs as a VM protected by HA."

Explain vMotion, HA, DRS, and FT — and how they differ.

Model answer: "vMotion live-migrates a running VM between hosts with zero downtime by copying memory across the vMotion network and switching over in a fraction of a second — used for maintenance and balancing. DRS uses vMotion automatically to keep the cluster load-balanced. HA is failure recovery: when a host dies, its VMs are restarted on surviving hosts — automatic, but it's a reboot, so there are minutes of downtime. FT goes further for critical VMs, running a lockstep shadow copy on another host so a host failure causes zero downtime — at significant resource cost. So: vMotion/DRS are planned movement and balance; HA/FT are failure protection at two different service levels."

Are VMware snapshots backups? How should they be used?

Model answer: "No. A snapshot freezes the base disk and writes changes to a delta file on the same datastore — it depends on the original files and dies with them. It's a short-term undo button: take one before a patch or upgrade, verify, then delete it within a day or so. Left to grow, delta files degrade I/O and can fill the datastore, and deleting a huge old snapshot takes hours of heavy I/O. Real backups are separate copies taken by a backup product like Veeam — which, ironically, uses temporary snapshots internally to get consistent images."

What is VMware Tools and why does it matter?

Model answer: "It's the driver-and-agent package installed inside the guest OS: paravirtual drivers like vmxnet3 for fast networking, the balloon driver for memory management, heartbeat so the host knows the guest is healthy, time sync, and the ability to shut the guest down gracefully from vCenter instead of pulling virtual power. A VM without Tools runs, but slower and half-blind to management — so checking Tools status is part of any VM health check."

A VM has no network after being migrated to another host. Why?

Model answer: "Classic cause: the VM's port group exists on the new host but its VLAN isn't trunked to that host's uplinks — or with standard switches, the port group is named or configured differently per host. I'd check the port group's VLAN ID, the physical switch trunk allowed-VLAN list for that host's NICs, and NIC teaming status. This whole class of problem is why distributed switches exist — one consistent config across all hosts."

What is a datastore and what types exist?

Model answer: "A datastore is the storage container where VM files live — the VMX config, VMDK disks, swap and logs. Main types: VMFS on block storage — a clustered filesystem on FC or iSCSI LUNs that many hosts mount at once, which is the foundation for vMotion and HA; NFS datastores served by a NAS; and vSAN, where the cluster pools local disks of the hosts into one distributed datastore. Shared access by all cluster hosts is the key property — it's what lets a VM restart or migrate anywhere in the cluster."

Level 2 · Deep dive

D10.1 esxtop — the four metrics that diagnose any slow VM

~ # esxtop            # c=CPU  m=memory  d=disk  n=network views
  GID NAME       %USED  %RDY   %CSTP
  1234 SQL01     380.2  14.30  6.10
        │          │      │      └ %CSTP high (>3): too MANY vCPUs — they must be co-scheduled;
        │          │      │          the fix is REMOVING vCPUs. Counter-intuitive = memorable.
        │          │      └ %RDY (CPU Ready) >5–10% per vCPU: VM wants CPU, host can't schedule it
        │          │          → host oversubscribed or limits set. THE slow-VM metric.
        │          └ %USED high alone is fine — it's just working.
LayerMetric (esxtop)HealthyMeaning when bad
CPU%RDY< 5%/vCPUContention — too many vCPUs on the host, or a limit strangling the VM
MemoryMCTLSZ (balloon)0Host under pressure, reclaiming guest memory via Tools balloon
MemorySWCUR (host swap)0Emergency — hypervisor paging guest RAM to disk; performance falls off a cliff
DiskDAVG / KAVG / GAVG<20 / ~0 / <25 msDAVG = the array is slow · KAVG = the host/queueing is the problem · GAVG = what the guest feels (D+K)

That one table lets you say: "I'd check CPU ready, ballooning, and DAVG before blaming the guest OS" — an L2 sentence from an associate's mouth.

D10.2 Host-level tools & commands

~ # vmkping -I vmk1 -s 8972 -d 10.9.9.10   # test the STORAGE VMkernel path with jumbo-size,
                                              don't-fragment: proves MTU 9000 end-to-end or not
~ # esxcli storage core adapter list       # HBAs/initiators
~ # esxcli storage nmp device list         # paths + policy per LUN (should be 2+ active)
~ # esxcli network vswitch standard list
~ # services.sh restart                    # restart mgmt agents (or DCUI: Restart Management Agents)
                                              — the standard fix for “host disconnected, VMs fine”
~ # vim-cmd vmsvc/getallvms                # VM inventory from the host shell when vCenter is down

D10.3 HA internals & storage failure states

  • HA elects a master host; slaves send network heartbeats; on silence the master checks datastore heartbeats to distinguish "host dead" (restart VMs) from "host isolated" (network-only problem — apply the isolation response: leave powered on / shut down). Two-layer heartbeating = fewer false failovers.
  • Admission control reserves cluster capacity so failover is guaranteed — the reason you "can't power on" a VM in a cluster that looks half-empty.
  • Storage loss states: APD (All Paths Down — array vanished without saying goodbye; hosts keep retrying, VMs hang) vs PDL (Permanent Device Loss — array said "gone"; HA can kill and restart affected VMs elsewhere). Recognizing APD/PDL in logs is a real L2 skill worth name-dropping.
  • vSphere 7+ can also restart vCenter itself via vCLS agent VMs (those tiny "vCLS" VMs confuse juniors — they belong there; don't delete them).

D10.4 vMotion & snapshot edge cases from real life

  • vMotion prerequisites checklist: shared storage (or storage vMotion combo), vMotion VMkernel on both hosts same subnet, same/compatible CPUs (EVC masks generational differences — but only within a vendor: Intel↔AMD never), matching port groups/VLANs, no CD-ROM mapped to a host-local ISO (the #1 silly blocker), no anti-affinity conflict.
  • Slow vMotion = 1G vMotion network. Modern practice: 10G+, multiple NICs, or vMotion fails its precopy convergence on busy VMs.
  • Snapshot horror pattern to tell: backup software takes nightly snapshots, deletion silently fails for weeks → 40-deep delta chain → datastore hits 100% → every VM on it pauses. Detection: "Needs Consolidation" column, du on the datastore folder. Prevention: alarm on snapshot age/size and datastore ≥85%.
  • Deleting a huge snapshot ≠ instant: committing deltas can take hours and briefly stun the VM — schedule it, never fire it at 11 a.m. on the ERP server.
  • Orphaned VM (grayed italic) after host crash → remove from inventory, re-register the .vmx from the datastore browser. Locked .vmdk ("unable to access file since it is locked") → another host still holds the lock — find it via the lock owner MAC in the error, restart its mgmt agents.
  • PSOD (Purple Screen of Death) = ESXi's kernel panic — usually hardware/driver; note the code, check HCL/firmware, engage vendor. VMs restart elsewhere via HA — which is exactly the story to tell about why clusters exist.

D10.5 vSwitch security policies (the three toggles)

  • Promiscuous mode (default Reject): Accept = the port sees all the port group's traffic — needed only for IDS/packet-capture VMs.
  • MAC address changes / Forged transmits (default Reject on vDS): whether a VM may use a MAC different from its configured one — needed for NLB/clustering/nested labs; otherwise keep rejected (stops MAC spoofing from inside VMs).
  • Traffic shaping and NIOC (Network I/O Control on vDS) keep vMotion from starving VM traffic on shared 10G uplinks — recognition level.
Level 3 · Expert corner — vCenter internals, cluster patching & rightsizing

vCenter (VCSA) one level down

  • The appliance runs its own Photon-OS Linux with services: SSO (vmdir — logins, including AD integration), inventory, vpxd (the core), and its database. Management UI on :5480 (VAMI) — where you patch/backup vCenter itself. File-based VCSA backup ≠ optional.
  • The failure everyone eventually meets: expired vCenter/host certificates — services won't start or hosts won't reconnect; recognized by dates in the error. Also: vCenter's disk partitions fill (logs/db) → services stop; VAMI shows per-partition usage.
  • Login chain worth knowing: vSphere Client → SSO token → vpxd → host's vpxa agent → hostd. "Host not responding" but pings fine = agents (restart via DCUI/services.sh); hostd dead = even direct Host Client fails.

Patching a cluster with zero VM downtime — the model answer

  1. Baseline/image in Lifecycle Manager (vLCM); check vendor hardware compatibility (HCL) and driver/firmware pairing.
  2. Snapshot nothing — hosts aren't VMs; instead confirm N+1 capacity and HA admission control.
  3. Host 1 → maintenance mode → DRS evacuates VMs live (vMotion) → remediate (patch + reboot) → verify (paths, networks, vSAN resync done) → exit maintenance.
  4. Repeat host by host — a "rolling upgrade". Users never notice; that's the entire point of clusters. vSAN adds: wait for resync between hosts; witness/quorum awareness.

Rightsizing & capacity — the conversations behind the tickets

  • Oversized VMs hurt: more vCPUs → co-scheduling pain (%CSTP) + bigger memory footprint + longer vMotions. Method: measure real usage over 30 days (peak + 95th percentile), size to peak+headroom, review quarterly. "8 vCPU because the vendor PDF said so" is how estates rot.
  • Overcommit norms: CPU 3–5:1 vCPU:pCore for general workloads is routine; memory overcommit close to 1:1 in practice (ballooning is a symptom, not a strategy). NUMA edge: a VM bigger than one CPU socket's cores/RAM spans nodes — align sizes to socket boundaries for the picky apps.
  • Capacity triggers you'd alarm on: cluster CPU/mem >70–80% sustained, datastore >85%, failover capacity below N+1, snapshot age >72 h, host uptime > patch cycle (means it's missing patches).
  • Recognition extras: VM encryption/vTPM (Windows 11 guests need vTPM), GPU passthrough/vGPU for VDI/AI, content libraries for template distribution, tags + custom attributes for ownership — the metadata that makes 2,000-VM estates governable.

From vSphere to cloud — the context of "Cloud Infrastructure Services"

Your business line has "Cloud" in its name; one paragraph of fluency goes a long way. The cloud is this module's ideas rented at scale:

On-prem VMware conceptAWS nameAzure name
Virtual machineEC2 instanceVirtual Machine
Virtual disk / datastoreEBS volume / S3 (object)Managed Disk / Blob storage
vSwitch + VLANs + subnetsVPC + subnets + security groupsVNet + subnets + NSGs
Firewall rulesSecurity groups / NACLsNSGs / Azure Firewall
TemplateAMIImage (Gallery)
Site-to-site VPN / MPLS to siteVPN Gateway / Direct ConnectVPN Gateway / ExpressRoute
HA/DRS clusterAuto Scaling + AZsAvailability sets/zones + VMSS
  • Service models one-liner: IaaS = rent VMs/networks (you patch the OS — this job, in the cloud); PaaS = rent the platform (managed database); SaaS = rent the finished app (M365).
  • Hybrid reality at clients: AD synced to Entra ID, some workloads in Azure/AWS, the rest on vSphere, connected by ExpressRoute/Direct Connect or IPsec — one estate, and the same OSI-model troubleshooting applies; the "data center" is just farther away.
  • Migration vocabulary: "lift and shift" (rehost VMs as-is), replatform, refactor — CIS teams run all three. VMware-in-cloud offerings (Azure VMware Solution etc.) literally run vSphere clusters inside hyperscalers — your skills transfer 1:1.

State of the art & the horizon — virtualization in the Broadcom era

  • The market context you should know walking in: since Broadcom acquired VMware (Nov 2023), perpetual licenses are gone — everything is subscription, bundled mainly as VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) 9 (vSphere+vSAN+NSX+Aria, list ~$350/core/year) — and vSphere 8's general support ends October 2027, forcing every customer to choose: commit to VCF 9, or migrate. This is arguably the biggest infrastructure story of the decade, and Capgemini CIS teams run both sides of it.
  • The migration wave is real: Nutanix AHV (a 2026 Gartner leader) for enterprises wanting a comparable stack; Proxmox VE (KVM-based, ~1.5M hosts, built-in VMware import tooling) storming the SMB/mid-market; Hyper-V, XCP-ng, OpenStack (sovereign clouds/providers), and OpenShift Virtualization / KubeVirt — running VMs inside Kubernetes so containers and VMs share one platform. Interview gold: being able to name these calmly, plus the honest caveat that migrations cost testing, tooling, and retraining — which is why many estates still standardize on vSphere.
  • Inside the SOTA stack: vSAN ESA (all-NVMe rewrite), DPU offload (running the vSwitch/NSX on BlueField-class cards), confidential VMs + vTPM as default hygiene, GPU virtualization (NVIDIA vGPU/MIG time-slicing GPUs for AI/VDI), and image-based fleet management (golden images via Packer, config via Ansible/Terraform — "pets → cattle" applied to hosts too).
  • MicroVMs & the light end: AWS Firecracker boots a stripped VM in ~125 ms (it's what runs Lambda) — the research direction where VM isolation meets container speed; Kata Containers wraps each container in a tiny VM.
  • The horizon: Kubernetes as the universal control plane (VMs, storage, even clouds managed as K8s objects via Crossplane); AI-driven placement and self-tuning clusters; liquid-cooled, GPU-dense AI data centers reshaping facility design; and platform engineering — infra teams productizing "paved roads" for developers instead of handling tickets one by one.
Command compendium · VMware — foundation → state of the art

Tier 1 — Foundation: the interfaces and where the logs live

  • vSphere Client (HTML5 → vCenter): deploy from template, edit settings, web console, Snapshot Manager, Migrate wizard (host and/or datastore), datastore file browser, Events/Tasks/Alarms tabs — know these by name.
  • DCUI (the host's yellow console): Configure/Test Management Network, Restart Management Agents, enable ESXi Shell/SSH — the "host disconnected" first-aid kit.
  • Host Client (https://esxi-host/ui): manage one host directly when vCenter is down.
ESXi logWhat's in it

/var/log/vpxa.logThe vCenter↔host agent — "host disconnected" clues
/var/log/fdm.logHA agent — election, heartbeats, restarts
