Module 11 · Linux

Linux

The Linux an infrastructure engineer actually uses: the filesystem, the commands, permissions, services, networking, disks, and logs — with the exact syntax.

11.1 Orientation

  • Linux is a free, open-source, Unix-like OS kernel; a distribution ("distro") bundles the kernel with tools and a package manager. Two families dominate servers: Red Hat family (RHEL, CentOS/Rocky/Alma, Fedora — package manager dnf/yum, packages .rpm) and Debian family (Debian, Ubuntu — apt, packages .deb). SUSE (SLES) matters in SAP shops — relevant at Capgemini.
  • Servers run headless — you work in the shell (usually bash) over SSH. Everything below is command line.
  • root is the superuser (UID 0). Daily practice: log in as yourself and prefix admin commands with sudo — audited, revocable, safer.
  • Get help: man command, command --help. Case-sensitive everywhere. Everything in Linux is a file — devices, sockets, even process info.

11.2 The filesystem hierarchy

One tree starting at / (no drive letters — disks are mounted onto directories):

DirectoryHolds
/etcConfiguration files — the directory you'll live in (/etc/ssh/sshd_config, /etc/fstab, /etc/hosts)
/homeUsers' home directories (/home/ahmed); root's is /root
/varVariable data — /var/log (logs!), spools, web roots, databases
/bin, /sbin, /usrPrograms and system binaries; /usr/bin holds most commands
/tmpTemporary files, world-writable, often cleared on boot
/devDevice files — disks are /dev/sda, /dev/sdb, partitions /dev/sda1, NVMe /dev/nvme0n1
/proc, /sysVirtual filesystems exposing kernel/process state (/proc/cpuinfo, /proc/meminfo)
/opt, /srvThird-party software; served data
/bootKernel and bootloader (GRUB)
/mnt, /mediaManual and removable mount points

11.3 Core commands by job

# WHERE AM I / MOVING AROUND
pwd                     # print working directory
ls -lah                 # list: long, all (incl. hidden .files), human sizes
cd /var/log ; cd ~ ; cd -   # go there / home / back

# FILES & DIRECTORIES
touch f.txt             # create empty / update timestamp
mkdir -p a/b/c          # make nested dirs
cp -r src/ dst/         # copy (recursive)
mv old new              # move / rename
rm -rf dir/             # delete recursively, no prompt — DANGEROUS, double-check path
ln -s target linkname   # symbolic link

# READING FILES
cat file                # whole file
less file               # pager (q quits, / searches)
head -20 file ; tail -20 file
tail -f /var/log/syslog # FOLLOW live — the troubleshooting staple

# SEARCHING
grep -i "error" app.log         # lines containing (case-insensitive)
grep -rn "listen" /etc/nginx/   # recursive, with line numbers
find / -name "*.conf" 2>/dev/null   # find files by name
find /var -size +100M -mtime -2     # big files changed in last 2 days

# PIPES & REDIRECTION — the shell's superpower
command > out.txt        # overwrite file with stdout
command >> out.txt       # append
command 2> err.txt       # redirect errors (stderr)
cmd1 | cmd2              # pipe output into next command
history | grep ssh       # example: search your history
ps aux | grep nginx | wc -l   # chain: count nginx processes

# SYSTEM INFO
uname -a ; hostnamectl   # kernel / host info
uptime                   # load averages (rule of thumb: compare to CPU count)
free -h                  # memory (buff/cache is reclaimable — not "used up")
df -h                    # disk space per filesystem
du -sh /var/*            # what's eating space
top / htop               # live processes

11.4 Permissions — guaranteed interview topic

Every file has an owner, a group, and three permission sets — user/group/others — each read/write/execute:

chmod 640 report.txt        # numeric: rw- r-- ---
chmod u+x deploy.sh         # symbolic: add execute for user
chown ahmed:devops file     # change owner and group
umask                       # default-permission mask for new files

Depth: special bits — SUID (run as file's owner, like passwd), SGID (dirs: new files inherit the group), sticky bit (on /tmp: only owners delete their own files). Recognize the names.

11.5 Users & groups

sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash sara    # create (with home dir)
sudo passwd sara                     # set password
sudo usermod -aG sudo sara           # add to group (-a APPEND — forgetting -a replaces!)
id sara ; groups sara                # check identity
sudo userdel -r olduser              # remove incl. home
  • Accounts live in /etc/passwd (world-readable, no passwords despite the name), password hashes in /etc/shadow (root-only), groups in /etc/group. Sudo rights: /etc/sudoers, edited only via visudo.

11.6 Processes & services

ps aux                       # all processes (USER, PID, %CPU, %MEM, COMMAND)
ps aux | grep java
top                          # live view — P/M sort by CPU/mem; load average top right
kill 1234                    # polite stop (SIGTERM 15)
kill -9 1234                 # force kill (SIGKILL) — last resort, no cleanup
nohup ./job.sh &             # run in background, survive logout

Modern distros use systemd; services are units:

systemctl status sshd        # state + recent log lines — first move on "service down"
sudo systemctl start|stop|restart nginx
sudo systemctl enable nginx  # start at boot (disable = don't)
systemctl list-units --type=service --state=failed
journalctl -u nginx -e       # unit's log, jump to end
journalctl -b -p err         # this boot, errors and worse
Interview one-liner: "enable vs start" — start is now, enable is at boot; a service that "keeps disappearing after reboot" was started but never enabled.

11.7 Software packages

# Debian/Ubuntu                      # RHEL/Rocky/CentOS
sudo apt update                      sudo dnf check-update
sudo apt install nginx               sudo dnf install nginx
sudo apt upgrade                     sudo dnf update
apt search / apt show pkg            dnf search / dnf info pkg
dpkg -l | grep nginx                 rpm -qa | grep nginx

11.8 Networking on Linux

ip a                        # addresses (replaces ifconfig)
ip r                        # routing table — check default via ...
ping -c4 8.8.8.8 ; traceroute host
ss -tulpn                   # listening sockets + owning process (replaces netstat)
dig google.com ; dig @8.8.8.8 google.com    # DNS, and DNS via specific server
nmcli device status         # NetworkManager overview
cat /etc/resolv.conf        # DNS servers in use
cat /etc/hosts              # static name overrides (checked BEFORE DNS)
curl -I https://site.com    # test an HTTP service directly
sudo firewall-cmd --list-all     # RHEL firewall  |  Ubuntu: sudo ufw status

Persistent IP config lives in: Ubuntu → /etc/netplan/*.yaml (apply with netplan apply); RHEL → NetworkManager profiles (nmcli con mod ... ; nmcli con up ...). An interface with an address but state DOWN, a missing default route, or an empty resolv.conf are the three classic "Linux box offline" findings.

11.9 Disks, mounts, LVM

lsblk                       # block devices tree: disks → partitions → LVM
df -h                       # mounted filesystems + usage
sudo mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/data ; sudo umount /mnt/data
cat /etc/fstab              # permanent mounts (bad line here = server won't boot cleanly)
sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb1    # format (xfs is the RHEL default)

LVM (Logical Volume Manager) adds flexibility between disks and filesystems: physical volumes (PV) pool into a volume group (VG), carved into logical volumes (LV) that can be grown online:

sudo pvcreate /dev/sdc                     # new disk → PV
sudo vgextend vg_data /dev/sdc             # grow the pool
sudo lvextend -r -L +20G /dev/vg_data/lv_var   # grow LV AND filesystem (-r)

That three-step flow — often after first extending the disk in VMware — is one of the most common real tasks in this job: "extend the VM's disk in vCenter → rescan → grow PV/LV → grow filesystem, all online."

11.10 Logs, cron, SSH, vi

  • Logs: /var/log/syslog (Debian) / /var/log/messages (RHEL), auth.log/secure (logins), dmesg (kernel/hardware), plus journalctl. Troubleshooting = tail -f the right log while reproducing the issue.
  • cron: crontab -e; five fields: min hour day month weekday. 0 2 * * 0 /opt/backup.sh = Sundays 02:00. System-wide: /etc/cron.d, cron.daily. (systemd timers are the modern alternative — know the name.)
  • SSH: ssh user@host, files copy with scp file user@host:/path or rsync -av. Key auth: ssh-keygen → ssh-copy-id user@host → private key stays with you, public key goes in the server's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. Server config /etc/ssh/sshd_config: disable root login & password auth for hardening. Keys must be 600 — SSH refuses loose permissions.
  • vi/vim survival (you will be dropped into it): i insert mode → type → Esc → :wq save+quit, :q! quit without saving, /text search, dd delete line, u undo.

11.11 Three rehearsed scenarios

Scenario — "Disk full" on a Linux server (root filesystem 100%)

Model walkthrough: "Confirm with df -h — which filesystem is full? Then hunt the space: du -sh /var/* | sort -h, usually landing in /var/log (a runaway log) or an application spool. Check for one giant file with find / -size +500M. Fix the cause, not just the symptom: rotate/compress the log (logrotate config), clean package caches, remove old kernels. Edge case worth mentioning: if a process holds a deleted log open, df stays full while du looks fine — lsof | grep deleted finds it, restart that service to release the space. If it's LVM and genuinely needs space, extend the LV online."

Scenario — "A service is down" (web server not responding)

Model walkthrough: "systemctl status nginx — is it running, crashed, or never started? If failed, journalctl -u nginx -e for the reason: config syntax error (nginx -t to validate), port already in use (ss -tulpn | grep :80), missing file permissions, or disk full. Restart, verify with curl -I localhost, then confirm externally — if local works but remote doesn't, it's the host firewall or network path, not the service. Finally systemctl is-enabled nginx so it survives the next reboot, and document the root cause."

Scenario — "Server is slow / high load"

Model walkthrough: "uptime first — load average versus CPU count (load 8 on 8 cores is busy; on 2 cores it's drowning). top: is it CPU (a process at 400%), memory (low available + swap in use — check free -h), or neither — then it's often I/O wait (high %wa in top; iostat to confirm the busy disk). Identify the offending process, decide with the owner whether to renice, restart, or schedule it off-hours. On a VM, also check the host layer — CPU ready or ballooning in vCenter can make an innocent guest look slow, which ties Linux and VMware troubleshooting together."

Interview questions — Module 11

A service will not start because its port is already in use. How do you find out what has it?

Model answer: "On Linux, ss -tulpn shows every listening socket with the process name and PID; lsof -i :8080 does the same for one port. On Windows, netstat -ano lists the PID and Get-Process -Id gives its name, or Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort 8080 in PowerShell. Then I decide whether that process should be there: an old instance that never stopped, a second copy of the service, or a different app that needs moving to another port."

How do you check disk space, and what's the difference between df and du?

Model answer: "df -h reports free space per mounted filesystem from the filesystem's own accounting — the 'is the disk full' view. du -sh path walks a directory tree and sums actual file sizes — the 'what is eating it' view. They disagree in one famous edge case: a deleted file still held open by a process is invisible to du but still counted by df — found with lsof | grep deleted and released by restarting the process."

Explain chmod 755. What do the numbers mean?

Model answer: "Each digit is a sum of read 4, write 2, execute 1 — for owner, group, and others in order. 755 gives the owner read-write-execute, and group and others read-execute. It's the standard for directories and scripts: everyone can enter or run, only the owner can modify. By contrast 644 is a normal file, 600 a private file like an SSH key, and 777 means anyone can do anything — almost always a mistake or a lazy 'fix' that becomes a security hole."

A service stops working after every reboot. First thing you'd check?

Model answer: "Whether it's enabled: systemctl is-enabled servicename. Starting a service only runs it now — enabling creates the boot-time link. If it is enabled but fails at boot, journalctl -b -u servicename shows why — commonly it starts before a dependency like the network or a mount is ready, which is fixed with unit dependencies like After= or a mount requirement in the unit file."

How does SSH key authentication work, and why is it better than passwords?

Model answer: "You generate a key pair; the public key goes into the server's authorized_keys, the private key never leaves your machine. At login the server issues a challenge only the private key can sign, so no secret crosses the network. It's better because it can't be brute-forced or phished like a password, it enables safe automation, and combined with disabling password authentication in sshd_config it kills the constant bot login attempts you see in auth.log."

What is the load average? Is 4.0 bad?

Model answer: "The three numbers from uptime are the average count of processes running or waiting to run — or in uninterruptible I/O wait — over 1, 5, and 15 minutes. It's only meaningful relative to core count: 4.0 on an 8-core server is half capacity; on a 2-core VM it means constant queuing. The three values also show trend — 12, 6, 2 means it's getting worse right now; 2, 6, 12 means it's recovering."

How would you add a new disk to a Linux VM and make it available?

Model answer: "Add the virtual disk in vCenter, rescan the SCSI bus or reboot, confirm with lsblk — say it appears as /dev/sdb. Then either simple: partition, mkfs.xfs, mount, add to /etc/fstab by UUID so it survives reboots. Or the better practice, LVM: pvcreate, add to the volume group, lvextend -r the logical volume — which grows the filesystem online with zero downtime. I'd always test mount -a after editing fstab, because a bad fstab line can leave the server in emergency mode at next boot."

Level 2 · Deep dive

D11.1 Reading top and free like a professional

top - 14:02:11 up 41 days,  load average: 6.12, 5.80, 3.40
                                          └ worsening: now-ish 6.1 vs 15-min 3.4 → getting worse NOW
%Cpu(s): 12.0 us,  3.0 sy,  0.0 ni, 22.0 id, 62.0 wa
          │         │                        └ wa = I/O WAIT. 62% wa = CPUs idle, stuck waiting for disk.
          │         │                          The server isn't “busy”, its STORAGE is. → iostat -x 2
          │         └ sy high = kernel/interrupt churn (network storms, bad driver)
          └ us high = normal application work
MiB Mem: 15843 total, 320 free, 14200 used, 1323 buff/cache
                      └ “free” low is NORMAL — Linux uses spare RAM as cache.
                        The number that matters is “available” (free -h) ≈ free + reclaimable cache.
  • D-state processes (uninterruptible I/O sleep) inflate load without CPU use — ps aux | awk '$8 ~ /D/'; usually a dead NFS mount or dying disk. Even kill -9 can't remove them — fix the I/O, not the process. Legendary edge case: a hung NFS server makes clients' load average climb to hundreds while CPUs sit idle.
  • Zombies (Z state) are already dead — they cost a process-table slot only; a few are cosmetic, thousands mean a buggy parent.
  • OOM killer: kernel out of memory → kills the biggest offender; app "randomly died overnight" → dmesg | grep -i oom or journalctl -k. The fix is memory sizing/limits, not just restarting.
  • Inode exhaustion: df -h shows space free but writes fail "No space left on device" → df -i shows 100% inodes — millions of tiny files (mail queues, session files). The trick question interviewers who know Linux love.

D11.2 Boot, targets, and rescue — when a server won't come up

  1. Firmware (BIOS/UEFI) → GRUB bootloader → kernel + initramfs → systemd reaches a target (multi-user.target ≈ headless server, graphical.target, rescue.target).
  2. Bad /etc/fstab entry (typo'd UUID, missing disk) → boot drops to emergency mode. Fix: comment the line, mount -a to verify, reboot. Prevention: nofail option on non-critical mounts — say this and you've clearly broken a server before (a good thing).
  3. Lost root password: reboot → edit GRUB entry → rd.break or init=/bin/bash → remount rw → passwd → (SELinux: touch /.autorelabel). Recognition level is fine.
  4. systemd-analyze blame — what made boot slow; systemctl list-dependencies — why a unit starts (or doesn't).

D11.3 Config-file literacy — the files you'll actually edit

# /etc/fstab — one line, six fields
UUID=3f5e...  /data  xfs  defaults,noatime,nofail  0 0
  device      mount  fs   options                  dump fsck-order

# crontab — five fields + command; THE classic gotcha: cron has a minimal PATH,
# so always use absolute paths in scripts (works in shell, “fails in cron” = this)
0 2 * * 0  /usr/local/bin/backup.sh >> /var/log/backup.log 2>&1

# /etc/ssh/sshd_config hardening trio (then: systemctl reload sshd — and keep a session open
# while testing, so a typo doesn't lock you out of a remote box)
PermitRootLogin no
PasswordAuthentication no
AllowGroups ssh-users

# logrotate — why /var/log doesn't eat the disk (usually)
/var/log/myapp/*.log { daily; rotate 14; compress; missingok; notifempty; postrotate systemctl reload myapp; endscript }

D11.4 Networking & firewall on Linux — the practical layer

# Set a static IP properly (RHEL family, NetworkManager)
nmcli con mod "ens192" ipv4.addresses 10.20.30.41/24 ipv4.gateway 10.20.30.1 \
      ipv4.dns "10.20.30.5 10.20.30.6" ipv4.method manual
nmcli con up "ens192"

# Ubuntu netplan (/etc/netplan/00-installer.yaml) — YAML: indentation is syntax!
network: {version: 2, ethernets: {ens192: {addresses: [10.20.30.41/24],
  routes: [{to: default, via: 10.20.30.1}], nameservers: {addresses: [10.20.30.5]}}}}
sudo netplan try      # applies with auto-rollback — use TRY on remote boxes, not apply

# Firewalls
sudo firewall-cmd --add-service=https --permanent && sudo firewall-cmd --reload   # RHEL
sudo ufw allow from 10.20.0.0/16 to any port 22 proto tcp                          # Ubuntu
# “service unreachable from outside, fine locally” checklist: ss -tulpn (bound to 127.0.0.1
# instead of 0.0.0.0?) → host firewall → network firewall → SELinux (ausearch -m avc)
  • SELinux/AppArmor: mandatory access control beyond file permissions. The signature: permissions look perfect, service still gets "permission denied" (e.g. nginx reading /srv/www or binding a non-standard port) → check getenforce, audit log, fix the context (restorecon/semanage) — never just disable it; that's the answer that separates candidates.
  • Edge cases: script from Windows fails with bad interpreter ^M → CRLF line endings → dos2unix. "Command not found" as root for a tool a user can run → different PATH/secure_path. Timezone/locale drift making logs "wrong" — timedatectl + chrony/ntpd.
Level 3 · Expert corner — scripting, deep debugging & a real unit file

A small bash script, fully annotated (say you automate; prove it)

#!/bin/bash
# diskwatch.sh — warn when any filesystem crosses a threshold; cron-safe
set -euo pipefail                      # die on errors/undefined vars — professional reflex
THRESHOLD=${1:-85}                     # first argument, default 85%
HOST=$(hostname -s)
df -P | awk 'NR>1 {gsub("%","",$5); print $5, $6}' | while read use mnt; do
  if [ "$use" -ge "$THRESHOLD" ]; then
    echo "$(date '+%F %T') WARN ${HOST}:${mnt} at ${use}%" | tee -a /var/log/diskwatch.log
    logger -t diskwatch "${mnt} at ${use}%"      # also into syslog → central monitoring
  fi
done

Concepts it demonstrates in 12 lines: shebang, arguments with defaults, pipes, awk field handling, loops, conditionals, logging to file and syslog. Cron it: */15 * * * * /usr/local/bin/diskwatch.sh 90 — absolute path, remember D11.3.

One-liners that solve tickets

grep -c "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log                    # count brute-force attempts
awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head # top IPs hammering the web server
sed -i.bak 's/^#Port 22/Port 22/' /etc/ssh/sshd_config         # edit-in-place with backup
find /var/log -name "*.gz" -mtime +30 -delete                  # purge ancient rotated logs
tar czf /backup/etc-$(date +%F).tar.gz /etc                    # dated config backup
rsync -avz --delete /srv/www/ backup01:/srv/www/               # mirror with deletions

When normal tools aren't enough

  • lsof -p PID / lsof :443 — every file/socket a process holds (also finds the deleted-file space leak, and "who is using this mount" before umount fails with target is busy).
  • strace -p PID — live syscalls: see the exact file a program fails to open or the address it can't connect to. The "why does it hang" microscope.
  • /proc/PID/ — environ, limits, fd/ — a process's world without restarting it. ulimit -n: "too many open files" errors = file-descriptor limit, raised via systemd LimitNOFILE.
  • sysctl tuning names to recognize: vm.swappiness (swap eagerness), net.core.somaxconn (listen backlog), fs.file-max. Persisted in /etc/sysctl.d/.

A real systemd unit file (what "the service" actually is)

# /etc/systemd/system/reportapi.service
[Unit]
Description=Internal report API
After=network-online.target postgresql.service    # start order — fixes boot races
[Service]
User=svc-report                                    # least privilege, never root
ExecStart=/opt/reportapi/bin/server --port 8081
Restart=on-failure                                 # self-healing
RestartSec=5
LimitNOFILE=65536
[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
# then: systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl enable --now reportapi

Container awareness (one breath): Docker runs apps in kernel-shared containers — docker ps, docker logs, docker restart; Kubernetes orchestrates them across nodes. Infra teams increasingly host the VMs those clusters run on — knowing the words earns a nod.

State of the art & the horizon — Linux

  • eBPF is the biggest Linux revolution of the decade: safe programs injected into the running kernel now do networking (Cilium — Kubernetes networking at Google/AWS scale), security (Falco, runtime detection), and observability (bpftrace — ask the kernel questions live, no reboots, no kernel modules). If an interviewer asks "what's exciting in Linux," this is the answer.
  • Rust entered the kernel (drivers since 6.x) to kill memory-corruption bug classes; io_uring rewrote high-performance I/O; live kernel patching (kpatch/KernelCare) means security fixes without reboots on critical fleets.
  • Immutable, image-based servers are the new fleet model: Fedora CoreOS, Ubuntu Core, Bottlerocket, Talos (Kubernetes-only Linux with no shell at all), and RHEL's image mode — the OS ships as a versioned image you replace rather than patch in place; config drift becomes impossible, rollback is a boot-menu entry. Declarative NixOS carries the same idea to its extreme.
  • The ops toolchain around Linux: Ansible remains the config-management standard; observability standardized on Prometheus/Grafana/OpenTelemetry; Podman/containerd quietly replaced the Docker daemon in enterprises; systemd absorbed ever more (timers, networkd, sd-boot).
  • Horizon: OpenSSH already defaults to hybrid post-quantum key exchange (ML-KEM-based since 10.x) — your SSH sessions are quantum-hardened before most people noticed; confidential containers (workloads encrypted even from the host); AI copilots at the shell (natural language → commands, with the obvious "review before running as root" discipline); and more of the kernel's attack surface rewritten in memory-safe code.
Command compendium · Linux — foundation → state of the art

Tier 1 — Foundation (11.3 covered the core; these complete it)

stat file            # timestamps, inode, perms in full
file mystery.bin     # what IS this file?
which cmd / type cmd # where a command comes from (alias? /usr/bin?)
man -k keyword       # search all man pages (= apropos)
history | tail -30 ; !105 ; !!   # rerun by number / repeat last (sudo !!)
alias ll='ls -lah'   # personal shortcuts (~/.bashrc)
wc -l file ; diff -u old new ; cmp a b
ln -s /srv/app/current /opt/app  # symlink; ls -l shows the arrow
watch -n2 'df -h /data'          # rerun any command every 2s
date +%F_%H%M ; cal ; uptime -p

Tier 2 — Text & data: the awk/sed toolbelt (where Linux gets its power)

# grep beyond -i: -r recursive, -n line numbers, -v invert, -E regex, -c count, -l files-only, -A3/-B3 context
grep -E "error|fail|crit" -i app.log | grep -v "healthcheck"
# awk = column surgeon
awk '{print $1,$5}' file                    # pick columns
awk -F: '$3 >= 1000 {print $1}' /etc/passwd # real users (UID≥1000)
awk '{sum+=$10} END {print sum/NR}' access.log   # average of column 10
# sed = stream editor
sed -n '100,120p' big.log                   # print a line range
sed -i.bak 's/DEBUG/INFO/g' app.conf        # in-place replace WITH backup
sed '/^#/d;/^$/d' config                    # strip comments+blank lines (read configs fast)
# The pipeline classics
cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
sort -h ; sort -k2 -n ; uniq -c ; tr 'a-z' 'A-Z' ; column -t
xargs: find /tmp -name "*.tmp" -print0 | xargs -0 rm -f      # -0 survives spaces in names
find /var/log -name "*.log" -size +100M -mtime +7 -exec gzip {} \;
tar -czf etc-$(date +%F).tgz /etc ; tar -tzf x.tgz ; tar -xzf x.tgz -C /restore
rsync -avz --delete --dry-run src/ dst/     # ALWAYS dry-run a --delete first
jq '.items[] | {name, status}' api.json     # JSON is data; jq is its awk
sha256sum file ; md5sum -c sums.txt         # integrity checks
tee: long_cmd | tee output.log              # see it AND save it

Tier 3 — Administration: the full working set

# Users/groups beyond 11.5
chage -l sara ; chage -M 90 sara            # password aging
last | head ; lastb | head ; who ; w        # logins, FAILED logins, who's on now
getfacl f ; setfacl -m u:sara:r f           # ACLs beyond rwx
chattr +i /etc/resolv.conf ; lsattr         # immutable flag (also a classic “why can't root edit this?!”)
# Processes beyond 11.6
pgrep -af nginx ; pkill -f runaway.py
kill -l                                     # the signal list (15 TERM default, 9 KILL, 1 HUP=reload)
nice -n10 bigjob.sh ; renice 5 -p 4312 ; ionice -c3 -p 4312
jobs ; fg %1 ; bg %1 ; disown -h %1
# systemd beyond 11.6
systemctl cat nginx ; systemctl edit nginx  # see/override a unit safely
systemctl mask badservice                   # impossible to start (stronger than disable)
systemctl list-timers                       # the modern cron
journalctl --since "1 hour ago" -p warning ; journalctl --disk-usage ; --vacuum-size=500M
# Packages beyond 11.7
dpkg -S /usr/sbin/nginx  |  rpm -qf /usr/sbin/nginx    # which package owns this file
dpkg -L nginx            |  rpm -ql nginx              # what files a package installed
apt list --upgradable ; dnf history ; dnf needs-restarting -r
# Hardware & identity
lscpu ; free -h ; lsblk ; lspci ; lsusb ; dmidecode -t system   # serial numbers for tickets!
timedatectl ; chronyc sources -v ; localectl

Tier 4 — Performance, deep debugging & state of the art

# The USE sweep: Utilization, Saturation, Errors — in four commands
uptime                      # load vs cores + trend
vmstat 2                    # r=run queue, b=blocked, si/so=swapping(!), wa=I/O wait, cs=context switches
iostat -x 2                 # per-disk %util, await
sar -n DEV 2                # NIC throughput (sar also has history: -q, -r, -b for past days)
# Deep instruments (recognize + one use each)
lsof -i :443 ; lsof -p 4312 ; lsof +D /data      # who holds ports/files/dirs
strace -f -e trace=openat,connect -p 4312        # exact syscall where it fails/hangs
perf top                                          # which function burns the CPU
# eBPF era (bcc tools) — the SOTA microscope
execsnoop        # every process exec'd, live — “what keeps running?!”
opensnoop -p 4312 ; tcpconnect ; biolatency       # file opens / TCP connects / disk latency histogram
bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_openat {printf("%s %s\n",comm,str(args->filename))}'
# Security & transport
openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host | openssl x509 -noout -dates  # cert expiry!
ssh -L 8443:internal:443 jumphost   ; ssh -J jump user@target   # port-forward / jump hosts
ausearch -m avc -ts recent ; restorecon -Rv /srv/www            # SELinux denials → fix contexts
# Session survival — non-negotiable ops habit
tmux new -s work → C-b d → tmux attach -t work    # your session survives VPN drops

Edge-case index — Linux

SymptomFirst suspicion
df full, du innocentDeleted-but-open file → lsof | grep deleted
"No space left" with space freedf -i — inodes gone
Load sky-high, CPU idleD-state processes: dead NFS/dying disk (vmstat b column)
App died overnight, no crash logOOM killer — dmesg | grep -i oom
Service dies at every rebootEnabled? Or races the network → After=network-online.target
Boot lands in emergency modefstab typo/missing disk → comment line, nofail next time
Script works by hand, fails in croncron's minimal PATH/env → absolute paths, log stderr
"bad interpreter ^M"Windows CRLF → dos2unix
Perms look right, still "permission denied"SELinux context (ausearch -m avc), or missing x on a parent dir, or chattr +i
Can't bind port / service unreachable remotely, fine locally<1024 needs root/capability; bound to 127.0.0.1; host firewall
SSH suddenly refuses key authPermissions drifted: ~/.ssh 700, keys 600, authorized_keys 600
usermod -G removed the user's other groupsForgot -a (append) — the classic self-inflicted wound
Deleted user's files show numeric UIDOwnership survives users — plan orphaned-file cleanup
"Free memory" looks tiny, app people panicbuff/cache is reclaimable — read available in free -h
Module 12 · Windows

Windows & Active Directory

Windows Server administration basics and the Active Directory concepts the job description flags as "a plus" — easy points if you know the vocabulary.

12.1 Windows Server & the domain model

  • Windows Server (2016/2019/2022/2025) adds roles to the OS: AD DS, DNS, DHCP, File Services, Print, IIS (web), Hyper-V — installed via Server Manager or PowerShell.
  • Workgroup = standalone machines, each with local accounts. Domain = centralized: one directory of users/computers, single sign-on everywhere, central policy. Any real company runs a domain.
  • Support staples: RDP (port 3389) for remote administration, Event Viewer (System/Application/Security logs) as the Windows equivalent of /var/log, Task Manager / Resource Monitor, services.msc, and PowerShell (Get-Service, Test-NetConnection, Get-EventLog/Get-WinEvent).

12.2 Active Directory structure

Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) is Microsoft's directory: a database of objects — users, computers, groups, printers — hosted on domain controllers (DCs), which authenticate every logon using the Kerberos protocol.

  • Domain controller — a server running AD DS; always deploy at least two, they replicate the database. (Special single-owner roles exist — FSMO roles — recognize the term.)
  • AD depends on DNS absolutely: clients locate DCs via SRV records. Wrong DNS on a client = "can't contact domain" even with perfect network. Clients in a domain must use the internal DNS servers, never 8.8.8.8 directly.
  • Kerberos issues time-stamped tickets — clock drift >5 minutes breaks logons (hence NTP).
  • Groups: security groups grant permissions (share ACLs, GPO filtering); distribution groups are mail lists only. Best practice pattern to name-drop: AGDLP — Accounts → Global groups → Domain Local groups → Permissions.

12.3 Group Policy (GPO)

  • A GPO is a bundle of settings (password policy, mapped drives, desktop lockdown, software deployment, firewall rules) linked to a domain, site, or OU — applying automatically to all users/computers beneath it.
  • Processing order: Local → Site → Domain → OU ("LSDOU"), last writer wins unless enforced.
  • Tools: gpupdate /force (apply now), gpresult /r (what applied — first stop when "policy isn't applying"), Group Policy Management Console (gpmc.msc).

12.4 Daily AD tasks (what "user account management" means)

# GUI: Active Directory Users and Computers (dsa.msc / ADUC)
# PowerShell equivalents worth name-dropping:
Unlock-ADAccount -Identity a.hassan
Set-ADAccountPassword -Identity a.hassan -Reset
Get-ADUser a.hassan -Properties LockedOut,PasswordExpired,MemberOf
Add-ADGroupMember -Identity "VPN-Users" -Members a.hassan
  • The classic ticket: account locked out (too many bad passwords — often a saved old password on a phone or a mapped drive retrying). Unlock, find the source in the DC security log (event 4740).
  • Others: password resets (verify identity first!), new-hire onboarding from a template user, disabling leavers (disable → grace period → delete), group membership for access requests, computer account rejoins ("trust relationship failed" → rejoin domain).

12.5 Patching & endpoint basics

  • Windows Update centrally managed via WSUS or cloud (Intune/Autopatch); monthly "Patch Tuesday" cycle; test group → broad deployment; reboots in maintenance windows.
  • Know the names: Defender/EDR agents, BitLocker (disk encryption), UAC, NTFS permissions vs share permissions (effective access = the more restrictive of the two).

Interview questions — Module 12

What are the FSMO roles?

Model answer: "Five operations that only one domain controller may perform. Per forest: the schema master, which changes the schema, and the domain naming master, which adds or removes domains. Per domain: the RID master, which hands out pools of IDs for new objects; the PDC emulator, which handles password changes, account lockouts and is the time source; and the infrastructure master, which updates cross-domain references. netdom query fsmo shows who holds them. If a holder fails for good, you seize the role on another DC; otherwise you transfer it."

A PC will not join the domain. What do you check?

Model answer: "DNS first: the PC must use the domain controllers as its DNS servers, not the router or a public DNS, because it finds a DC through SRV records. nslookup the domain name and _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.domain to prove it. Then reachability to the DC on the needed ports, the time being within five minutes, whether the account doing the join has the rights, and whether a computer object with that name already exists. The error message and the NetSetup.log in Windows\debug usually name the actual cause."

Explain the difference between share permissions and NTFS permissions.

Model answer: "Share permissions apply only when the folder is accessed over the network through the share; NTFS permissions apply to every access, local or remote, and can be set per file and folder. Over the network the effective access is the more restrictive of the two. Common practice is to set the share to Authenticated Users or Everyone with Change or Full Control, and do the real control with NTFS permissions granted to groups, never individual users. To check what someone actually gets, use the Effective Access tab."

What is Active Directory and why do companies use it?

Model answer: "Active Directory is Microsoft's centralized directory service: a replicated database of users, computers, and groups hosted on domain controllers. It gives single sign-on — one identity for every PC, share, and application — central control through Group Policy, and delegation of administration through OUs. Without it you'd manage local accounts on every machine separately. It authenticates with Kerberos and depends completely on DNS, which is why AD problems are so often DNS problems in disguise."

Domain vs workgroup?

Model answer: "A workgroup is peer-to-peer: every machine keeps its own local accounts, fine for a handful of PCs. A domain centralizes identity on domain controllers: users log on anywhere with one account, admins apply policy from one place, and access to resources is controlled by group membership. Any organization beyond a small office runs a domain."

What is a GPO? Give practical examples.

Model answer: "A Group Policy Object is a set of managed settings linked to a domain or OU, applied automatically to computers and users under it. Real examples: enforcing password complexity and screen lock, mapping the department's network drive, deploying the VPN client, disabling USB storage, configuring Windows Firewall. Processing is Local, Site, Domain, then OU — closest OU wins conflicts. When someone says a policy isn't applying, I run gpupdate /force, then gpresult /r to see what the machine actually received."

A user calls: "my account is locked out." Walk me through it.

Model answer: "Verify identity per procedure first — lockout calls are also what attackers sound like. Unlock via ADUC or Unlock-ADAccount, and if they've forgotten the password, reset with 'change at next logon'. If it re-locks repeatedly, something is replaying an old password — a phone's saved Wi-Fi or mail profile, a mapped drive, a scheduled task, a cached credential — so I'd check the DC security log for event 4740 to find the source machine and clean the stored credential. Then note it in the ticket, because repeat lockouts are a pattern worth a knowledge-base entry."

Why does Active Directory need DNS?

Model answer: "Clients find domain services by querying DNS SRV records — 'which server is a domain controller for this domain?' — before any authentication happens. That's why domain-joined machines must point at the internal DNS servers; give a client a public resolver like 8.8.8.8 and it can't find its DCs: logons fall back to cached credentials, group policy fails, shares break — with the network itself looking perfectly healthy."

Level 2 · Deep dive

D12.1 Event IDs and commands — the Windows support toolkit

Event ID (Security/System)MeaningUse
4740Account locked out (names the source computer!)Find what's replaying the old password
4625Failed logon (+ failure sub-code: 0xC000006A bad password, 0xC0000234 locked)Brute-force patterns, app misconfig
4624Successful logon (+ type: 2 console, 3 network, 10 RDP)Who's on this server and how
6008Unexpected shutdownCrash forensics starting point
1074Who/what initiated a restart"Why did the server reboot?"
C:\> whoami /groups              # my effective group memberships (access questions start here)
C:\> gpresult /r                 # which GPOs applied, which were filtered out, from which DC
C:\> nltest /dsgetdc:corp.local  # which DC am I talking to — the AD “ping”
C:\> dcdiag /v                   # DC health suite (on a DC)
C:\> repadmin /replsummary       # AD replication health — deltas + fail counts per DC pair
C:\> klist                       # my Kerberos tickets (klist purge to refresh after group changes)

"Group membership changes take effect at next logon" — the Kerberos ticket (with its group list) was issued at logon; user added to a group but "still no access" → log off/on (or klist purge). Tiny fact, enormous number of tickets.

D12.2 AD one level down — the pieces behind the words

  • FSMO roles (5): Schema Master, Domain Naming (forest-wide); PDC Emulator (time source, password-change hub, lockout arbiter — the one you'll feel when it's down), RID Master, Infrastructure Master (per-domain). netdom query fsmo shows holders.
  • Global Catalog: DCs holding a partial copy of every domain's objects — needed for forest-wide search and logons (universal group lookups). Port 3268.
  • Sites & replication: AD maps subnets → sites so clients pick a local DC and replication respects WAN links (change notification within a site, scheduled between sites). Wrong subnet→site mapping = "logons slow at the branch because they authenticate to a DC across the ocean."
  • SYSVOL/NETLOGON shares on every DC carry GPO files and scripts (DFSR-replicated). GPO applies for some users but not others → check SYSVOL replication first.
  • Kerberos flow in one breath: logon → KDC (a DC) issues a TGT; accessing a server → present TGT, receive a service ticket for that server's SPN; the server validates it — passwords never cross the wire. Requires DNS + time within 5 minutes (both again!).
  • Trust relationship failed: the computer account's password (rotated every 30 days) fell out of sync — commonly after restoring an old VM snapshot of the machine. Fix: Reset-ComputerMachinePassword or rejoin. And that's why you don't revert old snapshots of domain controllers or domain members casually — and never DCs (USN rollback).

D12.3 NTFS vs share permissions — the worked example

Folder: D:\Finance     Share: \\FS01\Finance
NTFS:   Finance-Team = Modify        Share:  Everyone = Read
→ Over the network: effective = MOST RESTRICTIVE of the two = READ ONLY  ← ticket:
  “I can open files but can't save!”  Fix: raise SHARE to Change/Full, control via NTFS.
Best practice: Share = Authenticated Users:Full Control, do all real control with NTFS ACLs.
Tools: icacls D:\Finance /t (dump ACLs), Effective Access tab, takeown for orphaned dirs.
  • More edge cases: Deny beats Allow (a stray Deny entry breaks one user mysteriously); moving a file within a volume keeps its ACL, copying inherits the destination's — "why did permissions change after the move?"; user profile issues → temporary profile logons (fix the corrupt profile registry key/rename profile folder).
  • Mapped drives via GPO Preferences (item-level targeting by group) — the modern answer vs logon scripts.
  • DNS scavenging: stale dynamic A records answer for machines that changed IPs → "RDP lands on the wrong machine" weirdness; scavenging + correct DHCP/DNS aging fixes it.
Level 3 · Expert corner — PowerShell toolbox & hybrid identity

The associate's PowerShell dozen

Get-ADUser a.hassan -Properties * | Select Enabled,LockedOut,PasswordExpired,LastLogonDate
Search-ADAccount -LockedOut | Select Name,SamAccountName          # all current lockouts
Get-ADGroupMember "VPN-Users" | Measure-Object                    # how many members
Get-ADComputer -Filter {OperatingSystem -like "*Server*"} | Select Name
Get-Service -ComputerName FS01 | Where Status -eq "Stopped" | Where StartType -eq "Automatic"
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security';Id=4740} -MaxEvents 5   # recent lockouts
Restart-Service Spooler -Force                                    # the print-fix classic
Get-Volume | Select DriveLetter,SizeRemaining,Size                # disk space, scriptable
Test-NetConnection FS01 -Port 445                                 # reach + port in one
Get-Process | Sort CPU -Descending | Select -First 5
Copy-Item \\FS01\it\agent.msi C:\Temp\; Start-Process msiexec "/i C:\Temp\agent.msi /qn"
Get-HotFix | Sort InstalledOn -Descending | Select -First 5       # patch level check

The meta-skill to voice: "anything I do twice in a GUI, I look for the PowerShell version" — that sentence signals automation mindset, which delivery centers prize.

Hybrid identity — the modern AD conversation

  • Most client estates are hybrid: on-prem AD synced to Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD) via Entra Connect — one identity for both the domain and Microsoft 365/cloud apps.
  • Consequences you can reason about: password changes sync (password hash sync) or pass through; MFA and Conditional Access live in the cloud layer; a user "can log into the laptop but not Teams" = cloud-side (license, sync, CA policy), while "can't log into the laptop at all" = on-prem side (DC, DNS, account). Splitting those two worlds fast is the new L1 skill.
  • Recognition terms: SSO via SAML/OIDC for third-party apps, Intune for device management (co-managed with GPO), Windows Hello, self-service password reset (SSPR) — the direction user management is moving.
  • Interview positioning: you don't claim Entra expertise — you say "I understand the hybrid model: AD remains the source of truth, Entra Connect syncs it to the cloud, and I know which side owns which failure." Exactly right for associate level.

State of the art & the horizon — Windows & identity

  • Windows Server 2025 is the current generation, and its headline is operational: hotpatching — security updates applied to a running OS with reboots only quarterly — plus SMB over QUIC (file shares safely over the internet, no VPN) and delegated Managed Service Accounts (dMSA) replacing password-bearing service accounts.
  • NTLM is officially dying: deprecated by Microsoft, with Kerberos extensions (IAKerb, a local KDC) built to replace the last legacy cases. Estates are auditing NTLM usage now — a real project type junior engineers get staffed on. Alongside: built-in LAPS (unique rotating local-admin passwords), SMB signing/encryption by default, and the tiered-admin model with Privileged Access Workstations as the AD-security gold standard.
  • Management went cloud-first: Intune + Autopilot for endpoints (GPO co-management during transition), Azure Arc projecting on-prem servers into cloud management, Windows Admin Center over MMC-era consoles. Identity: passkeys in Entra ID, Conditional Access as the policy brain, cloud Kerberos trust bridging both worlds.
  • Horizon: greenfield companies increasingly skip on-prem AD entirely (Entra-only + Intune); existing AD estates will run for a decade+ (apps depend on it) — which is why AD skills stay employable while the growth skill is the hybrid boundary; AI copilots are landing inside admin consoles (Intune, Sentinel) drafting queries, policies, and remediation scripts; and Kerberos/PKI go post-quantum on the same NIST timeline as everything else (RSA-2048 deprecated by 2030, gone by 2035).
Module 18 · Hardware

Servers, hardware & Dell tools

The physical layer under every VM and every LUN: what is inside a rack server, how it boots, how power, memory and disks fail, and the Dell tools you use to see and fix all of it — iDRAC, Lifecycle Controller, OpenManage and SupportAssist. For a Dell-facing role, this module is where "I know the theory" becomes "I can support your servers".

18.1 Inside a rack server

A rack server is a PC built for 24/7 duty: everything that can fail is doubled and hot-swappable (power supplies, fans, disks), memory corrects its own errors, and a small independent computer — the BMC (Baseboard Management Controller; Dell calls theirs iDRAC) — watches the hardware and lets you manage it remotely even when the main system is off. Dell's server line is PowerEdge; the model name encodes the form: R760 = Rack, 7 = mainstream class, 6 = 16th generation, 0 = Intel (5 = AMD); T = tower, MX = modular blade chassis, XR = rugged edge.

PartWhat it doesWhat you say about it
CPU sockets1 or 2 processors; each owns its own memory channels (NUMA)"A DIMM only works if its CPU is installed — slots belong to a socket."
DIMMs (RDIMM, ECC)Registered, error-correcting server memory"Populate by the slot rules (A1, B1… white tabs first), identical DIMMs per channel, balanced across sockets."
PERCPowerEdge RAID Controller: hardware RAID with a battery- or flash-backed cache"Physical disks go in; the PERC presents virtual disks to the OS."
HBAA controller that passes disks straight through, no RAID"For vSAN, Ceph or ZFS — software that wants raw disks."
BOSSBoot Optimized Storage Solution: two M.2 SSDs in RAID 1"The hypervisor boots from BOSS so the front bays stay free for data."
PSUsTwo hot-swap power supplies, usually 1+1 redundant"Each PSU on a different feed — A-side and B-side PDUs — or the redundancy is fake."
NICsLOM / OCP mezzanine plus PCIe cards"Team or bond two ports across two switches."
iDRACThe BMC, with its own CPU, network port and firmware"My out-of-band way in when the OS is dead" — 18.6.

18.2 BIOS, UEFI and POST — how a server boots

BIOS vs UEFI

The firmware that runs before any operating system. Legacy BIOS (1980s design) boots from the first sector of an MBR disk — limited to 2 TB boot disks and four primary partitions. UEFI (Unified Extensible Firmware Interface) is its modern replacement: boots from a FAT32 EFI System Partition on a GPT disk, has no 2 TB limit, a graphical setup, network boot over HTTP(S), and Secure Boot. People still say "BIOS settings" for both. Every PowerEdge since 14th gen ships in UEFI mode.

POST

Power-On Self-Test: the firmware checks and initialises the hardware — CPUs, memory training, PCIe devices and their option ROMs — before handing over to a boot loader. A server with 1 TB of RAM can spend minutes in POST; that is normal, not a hang. Desktops report POST failures with beep codes; servers use the front LCD/LED, and the iDRAC logs the exact error.

Secure Boot and TPM

Secure Boot lets the firmware run only boot loaders and drivers signed by a trusted key, which blocks boot-level malware (bootkits). The TPM (Trusted Platform Module, a security chip) stores keys and measures each boot stage; BitLocker and Windows 11/Server 2025 rely on TPM 2.0. Classic gotcha: an unsigned third-party driver or an old OS image fails to boot once Secure Boot is turned on.

Setup keys on a PowerEdge — worth memorising: F2 System Setup (BIOS, iDRAC settings, device settings), F10 Lifecycle Controller, F11 one-time Boot Manager, F12 PXE network boot. BIOS settings that come up in tickets: virtualization technology (Intel VT-x / AMD-V) must be on for any hypervisor; the system profile (Performance vs Performance-per-Watt) affects latency; the boot mode (UEFI vs BIOS); and a dead CMOS battery makes the clock drift and settings reset — which then breaks Kerberos logons (Module 12).

18.3 Power: PSUs, redundancy and feeds

  • 1+1 redundant: either PSU alone can carry the full load, so one may fail with no outage. The server raises a redundancy lost alert — the job is still "replace it today", because the next failure is an outage.
  • A/B feeds: PSU 1 to the A-side PDU, PSU 2 to the B-side, each on a different circuit or UPS. Both PSUs on one power strip survives a PSU failure but not a tripped breaker.
  • PSU mismatch: two PSUs of different wattage or type raise a mismatch error. Replace like with like.
  • Sizing: the label is maximum output; real draw is shown live in the iDRAC (watts, history, peak). Power capping in the iDRAC limits a server's draw to fit a rack's power budget.
  • Hot-swap: pull the failed PSU by its release tab with the server running. The LED on the new one should turn green within seconds.

18.4 Memory: ECC, error counts and population rules

Server memory is ECC (error-correcting code): each 64 bits of data carry extra check bits, so the memory controller corrects any single-bit error on the fly and detects multi-bit errors. Cosmic rays and ageing cells flip bits in every large fleet; ECC is why servers don't crash for it.

EventWhat happenedWhat you do
Correctable error (single-bit)Fixed transparently, loggedNothing for one. A rising rate on one DIMM ("correctable error rate exceeded") means it is degrading: schedule a replacement.
Uncorrectable error (multi-bit)Data cannot be trusted; the OS usually halts (Windows bugcheck, Linux kernel panic, ESXi purple screen)Read the SEL for the slot (e.g. DIMM B3), replace that DIMM, run diagnostics.
Less memory than installedA DIMM disabled at POST, wrong slot, or its CPU missingCheck the iDRAC memory inventory and the population rules for that model.

Population rules in one breath: fill slots in the order the lid diagram gives (A1, B1, A2, B2… white release tabs first), keep DIMMs identical within a channel, mirror the layout across both CPUs, and never mix RDIMM with LRDIMM. Get it wrong and the server either refuses to POST or runs with memory silently slower.

18.5 Disks, PERC and hardware RAID

The RAID levels themselves are in Module 9 (9.2). This is the server-side vocabulary for running them:

  • Physical disk (PD) vs virtual disk (VD): you build a VD (say RAID 10 over four PDs) and the OS only ever sees the VD.
  • VD states: Online (healthy), Degraded (a member failed, data still served, no redundancy left in RAID 1/5), Rebuilding, Offline/Failed (too many members lost).
  • Hot spare: an idle disk the PERC rebuilds onto automatically. Global spares serve any VD, dedicated spares one VD.
  • Predictive failure: the disk's SMART counters (reallocated sectors, media errors) cross a threshold before it dies. Replace it then — a planned swap beats a degraded array.
  • Foreign configuration: disks moved from another controller carry its RAID metadata. You import it (keep the data) or clear it (wipe) — clearing the wrong one is a classic way to destroy data.
  • Controller cache: write-back (fast; protected by a battery or flash backup) vs write-through (safe, slow). A failed cache battery silently switches the PERC to write-through, and "the database got slow overnight" follows. See D9.3.
  • Replace a failed disk by its bay (the iDRAC and the blinking amber LED tell you which one). Never pull a healthy disk from a degraded RAID 5: that is two failures.

18.6 iDRAC — out-of-band management

iDRAC (integrated Dell Remote Access Controller) is the BMC built into every PowerEdge: its own processor, firmware, web interface and — ideally — its own dedicated network port on a separate management network. Out-of-band means it does not depend on the server's OS, or on the server being powered on. iDRAC9 runs on 14th–16th generation servers; the 17th generation (2025) introduced iDRAC10.

FeatureWhat it gives you
Virtual console (HTML5 KVM)The server's screen, keyboard and mouse in a browser — including BIOS setup and POST
Virtual mediaMount an ISO from your laptop or a share as if it were a DVD in the server: install an OS remotely
Power controlPower on/off, graceful shutdown, hard reset, power cycle
System Event Log (SEL)Hardware events: PSU, fan, temperature, memory, CPU
Lifecycle LogEverything else: configuration changes, firmware updates, disk and RAID events, who logged in
AlertsEmail, SNMP traps, syslog, Redfish events — so monitoring hears about a failed disk before a user does
Firmware updatesBIOS, iDRAC, PERC, NIC and disk firmware, applied as scheduled jobs
LicensingBasic / Express / Enterprise / Datacenter tiers unlock features; remote console, virtual media and directory login need a higher tier on many models
  • Getting in: the iDRAC IP is set in F2 → iDRAC Settings → Network, or on the front LCD. Out of the box it uses DHCP or the static default 192.168.0.120. Credentials: older servers shipped with root / calvin; current ones ship a unique password printed on the pull-out information tag. Changing a default password is the first hardening step — and it is a security-interview answer.
  • Security: the iDRAC is full control of the hardware, so it lives on an isolated management VLAN, never on the internet, with directory (AD/LDAP) login, role-based accounts and current firmware.
  • The service tag: a 7-character ID on the server (and in the iDRAC) that Dell support uses for warranty, configuration and parts. Have it ready on every call.

18.7 Lifecycle Controller

Lifecycle Controller (LC) is the embedded tool set inside the iDRAC, reached with F10 at boot or remotely. It lets you do the jobs that used to need DVDs: deploy an OS (it injects the right drivers), update firmware from a Dell repository or USB, configure RAID and BIOS, run hardware diagnostics, export or import the full server configuration (a Server Configuration Profile, an XML or JSON file — the way to clone settings to 50 identical servers), and replace a part with automatic restore of its firmware and settings (Part Replacement).

18.8 OpenManage — the fleet view

iDRAC manages one server. OpenManage is Dell's family of tools for managing many:

ToolScopeWhat it is for
OpenManage Enterprise (OME)The whole fleet; a virtual appliance you deployDiscover every iDRAC, inventory, health dashboard, alert policies, firmware baselines and compliance ("which of my 200 servers run an old BIOS?"), template deployment, warranty status
OME ModularMX blade chassisThe same, built into the chassis management
iDRAC Service Module (iSM)Agent inside the OSLets the iDRAC see OS details (hostname, OS-level NIC names), forwards logs, enables automatic OS-side log collection. The modern replacement for…
OpenManage Server Administrator (OMSA)Legacy in-OS agentThe older way to see hardware from inside Windows/Linux. Recognise the name; new deployments use iDRAC + iSM.
IntegrationsYour existing consolesOpenManage Integration for VMware vCenter (hardware health and firmware updates from vCenter, host by host with maintenance mode), Windows Admin Center and System Center extensions, Ansible collection dellemc.openmanage, Terraform provider
OpenManage MobilePhone appAlerts and basic status on the go; Quick Sync to read a server over Bluetooth/NFC at the rack

18.9 SupportAssist — from failure to replacement part

SupportAssist is Dell's automated support link. On a server it is built into the iDRAC: it detects a hardware fault, collects a TSR (Technical Support Report — a bundle of hardware inventory, logs, RAID controller logs and optionally OS logs), and, if the server is registered and under a ProSupport contract, opens a support case with Dell automatically, attaching the TSR. Across a whole site the connection to Dell runs through Secure Connect Gateway (the successor to SupportAssist Enterprise and Secure Remote Services), which also carries storage-array telemetry. Fleet health and predictions show up in CloudIQ (now part of Dell's AIOps service).

18.10 Hardware diagnostics — symptom to first suspect

SymptomFirst suspectWhere you confirm it
No power at allFeed, cable, PDU, both PSUsPSU LEDs, PDU display, iDRAC power history
Powers on, no video, no POSTMemory or CPU seating, a bad DIMM, a new PCIe cardFront LCD, SEL; minimum-config test
Random reboots or crashesUncorrectable memory errors, overheating, PSUSEL timestamps vs the crash times; OS crash dumps
Fans at full speed, thermal alertsBlocked airflow, missing blanks, a failed fan, hot roomiDRAC temperatures (inlet vs exhaust), fan RPMs
Slow disk I/O after a quiet nightA degraded VD rebuilding, or a failed cache battery forcing write-throughPERC status in iDRAC / perccli, Lifecycle Log
Less RAM or fewer CPUs than orderedDIMM disabled at POST, wrong slots, a CPU not detectediDRAC hardware inventory vs the order
NIC link flapsCable/optic, switch port, firmware/driver mismatchSwitch counters (Module 8), iDRAC NIC status, driver versions

The method is the same as Module 8: read the logs before touching anything, change one thing at a time, and prove the fix. Dell adds two habits: run the built-in diagnostics (Lifecycle Controller → Hardware Diagnostics, the ePSA pre-boot test) before asking for a part — support will ask for the result — and check that firmware and drivers match a validated baseline, because a large share of "hardware" faults are fixed by an update.

Interview questions — Module 18

What does the PERC controller’s battery or cache do, and why does a failed one slow the server?

Model answer: "The PERC has cache memory protected by a battery or flash backup. With write-back caching, a write is confirmed as soon as it is in that cache and flushed to disk later, which makes writes, especially RAID 5 and 6 parity writes, much faster. If the battery fails or is relearning, the controller switches to write-through for safety, so every write waits for the disks and performance drops sharply. iDRAC and OpenManage report it; the fix is replacing the battery, not forcing write-back without protection, which risks losing data on a power cut."

What is iDRAC and why does it matter?

Model answer: "iDRAC is Dell's baseboard management controller — a small independent computer inside every PowerEdge with its own network port and standby power. It gives out-of-band management: I can see the virtual console, mount an ISO, power-cycle the server and read the hardware logs even when the OS is hung or the server is off. On any 'server down' ticket the iDRAC is my first stop — the System Event Log and the Lifecycle Log usually tell me whether it's hardware before I touch anything. It belongs on an isolated management VLAN with the default password changed."

A server won't boot. Walk me through it.

Model answer: "First I find where it stops. No LEDs at all is power: PSU LEDs, cables, the PDU. If it powers on, I open the iDRAC and read the SEL and the virtual console. Stuck in POST points at hardware — the LCD or SEL usually names the DIMM or CPU; if not, I strip to minimum config and add parts back. If POST completes but there's 'no boot device', I check the boot mode — UEFI versus legacy — the boot order, and whether the RAID virtual disk or the BOSS card is online. If the OS loader starts and then crashes, it's an OS problem — drivers, boot config — and I move to the OS logs. Each step I note what I checked, so an escalation to Dell includes the evidence."

What's the difference between BIOS and UEFI?

Model answer: "Both are the firmware that initialises hardware and starts the boot loader. Legacy BIOS boots from an MBR disk, which limits the boot disk to 2 TB. UEFI boots from an EFI partition on a GPT disk, has no such limit, supports network boot over HTTP and Secure Boot, which only runs signed loaders. The practical gotcha is boot mode: an OS installed in one mode won't boot if the server is switched to the other."

A memory error appears in the logs. Do you replace the DIMM?

Model answer: "It depends on the type. A single correctable ECC error was fixed in hardware — I note it and watch. If the correctable rate on one DIMM keeps climbing and the iDRAC flags it, the DIMM is degrading, so I schedule a replacement in a maintenance window. An uncorrectable error means the server likely crashed; I take the slot from the SEL, run diagnostics and replace that DIMM. In both cases I attach the logs to the Dell case."

One of the two power supplies shows amber. What's the impact and what do you do?

Model answer: "In a 1+1 configuration the server keeps running on the other PSU, so there's no outage — but redundancy is lost, and the next failure is an outage. I confirm in the iDRAC whether the PSU failed or just lost input — if it lost input it's the cable, PDU or circuit, not the PSU. If the PSU itself failed, I open a case with the service tag and hot-swap it when the part arrives. I also check that the two PSUs are on different feeds, because two PSUs on one strip isn't real redundancy."

What do OpenManage Enterprise and SupportAssist do?

Model answer: "OpenManage Enterprise is the one-to-many console: it discovers all the iDRACs, shows fleet health and inventory, and checks firmware against a baseline so I can update a cluster consistently. SupportAssist is the automated link to Dell support: when hardware fails, it collects a Technical Support Report and opens a case with Dell automatically, so the replacement part is often on its way before anyone calls. Across a site that link runs through Secure Connect Gateway."

A disk in a RAID 5 virtual disk failed. What do you do?

Model answer: "The virtual disk is now degraded with no redundancy left, so I treat it as urgent. I confirm the failed bay in the iDRAC — the amber LED matches — and check whether a hot spare already started a rebuild. I verify the backups are current before anything else, open the Dell case, and when the part arrives I hot-swap only that bay and watch the rebuild to Online. I never pull any other disk during this. Afterwards I'd raise whether large-disk RAID 5 should become RAID 6 or 10."

What is a TSR and when do you collect one?

Model answer: "A Technical Support Report: a SupportAssist collection from the iDRAC with the hardware inventory, the system and lifecycle logs, the RAID controller logs and optionally OS logs. Dell support asks for it on almost every hardware case, so I collect it as soon as I suspect hardware — from the iDRAC web UI or with racadm techsupreport — and attach it to the case."

Level 2 · Deep dive

D18.1 racadm, Redfish and IPMI — the iDRAC from the command line

Every iDRAC task can be scripted. Three interfaces, oldest to newest:

# racadm: Dell's CLI (remote with -r, or locally in the OS / over SSH to the iDRAC)
racadm -r 10.0.99.21 -u admin -p '***' getsysinfo        ← model, service tag, BIOS/iDRAC versions, power state
racadm -r 10.0.99.21 -u admin -p '***' getsel            ← the System Event Log
racadm -r 10.0.99.21 -u admin -p '***' lclog view -n 20  ← last 20 Lifecycle Log entries
racadm -r 10.0.99.21 -u admin -p '***' hwinventory       ← every DIMM, disk, NIC, PSU with part numbers
racadm -r 10.0.99.21 -u admin -p '***' serveraction powercycle
racadm -r 10.0.99.21 -u admin -p '***' techsupreport collect   ← start a TSR (then techsupreport export)
racadm -r 10.0.99.21 -u admin -p '***' racreset          ← reboot the iDRAC only: the host keeps running

# Redfish: the industry-standard REST API (DMTF) — JSON over HTTPS, the modern way
curl -sk -u admin:*** https://10.0.99.21/redfish/v1/Systems/System.Embedded.1 | jq '.PowerState, .Status.Health, .MemorySummary'

# IPMI: the old cross-vendor standard (disable it if you don't need it)
ipmitool -I lanplus -H 10.0.99.21 -U admin -P '***' sel list

Talking point: "racadm reset of the iDRAC doesn't touch the host" — a hung iDRAC web UI is fixed with racadm racreset or by holding the system ID button for about 15 seconds, with zero impact on running VMs. Redfish is what Ansible's dellemc.openmanage modules, Terraform and OpenManage Enterprise use underneath.

Level 2 · Deep dive

D18.2 Firmware updates without an outage

  1. Baseline: pick a validated Dell catalog (or the vendor-certified one for your hypervisor — vSAN in particular has a strict hardware compatibility list).
  2. Compliance report in OpenManage Enterprise: which servers are behind, on which components.
  3. Change request: firmware updates reboot hosts. Plan them like any change, with a rollback (the iDRAC keeps the previous firmware image for rollback).
  4. One host at a time: in a VMware cluster, enter maintenance mode (DRS moves the VMs away), update, reboot, verify health, exit, next host. vSphere Lifecycle Manager with the Dell hardware support manager automates this loop.
  5. Order matters: follow the release notes; typically iDRAC first, then BIOS, then controllers, NICs and disks.
  6. Verify: versions in the inventory, SEL clean, workloads back.
Module 19 · Cloud

Cloud basics & identity (Azure and AWS)

Enough Azure and AWS to hold a confident first conversation: the service models and who secures what, regions and availability zones, a cloud network drawn end to end, the core services side by side, and identity — the part of cloud that causes the most tickets. Module 10 ("From vSphere to cloud") maps VMware ideas to cloud names; this module builds on it.

19.1 What "cloud" means — service models and who secures what

Cloud computing is renting computing on demand: you provision in minutes through an API or portal, pay for what you use, and scale up and down without buying hardware. The three service models differ in how much of the stack the provider runs for you:

  • IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service): you rent VMs, disks and networks — Azure Virtual Machines, AWS EC2. You still patch the OS.
  • PaaS (Platform as a Service): you deploy code or data; the provider runs the OS and runtime — Azure App Service, Azure SQL Database, AWS RDS, AWS Elastic Beanstalk.
  • SaaS (Software as a Service): you just use the application — Microsoft 365, Salesforce, ServiceNow.

Deployment models: public cloud (Azure, AWS, Google Cloud), private cloud (your own VMware or Azure Local estate run cloud-style), and hybrid — both, connected — which is what most enterprises actually run.

19.2 Regions, availability zones and the global map

  • Region: a geographic area with its own set of datacenters — e.g. Azure West Europe, AWS eu-central-1 (Frankfurt). Choose by latency to users, data-residency law, and which services and prices it offers. Microsoft and AWS both run regions in the Middle East (e.g. Azure UAE North and Qatar Central, AWS me-central-1 in the UAE).
  • Availability Zone (AZ): one or more physically separate datacenters inside a region, with independent power, cooling and network, linked by low-latency fibre. Spread VMs across two or three AZs and a datacenter fire does not take the service down.
  • The resilience ladder: one VM (no protection) → several VMs in one AZ (survives a host failure) → across AZs (survives a datacenter failure) → across regions (survives a regional disaster, at real cost and complexity). The higher you go, the more it costs — match it to the RTO and RPO (9.6).
  • Edge: CDN points of presence (Azure Front Door, AWS CloudFront) cache content close to users.

19.3 A cloud network, end to end

The network concepts from Modules 2–7 all reappear in the cloud, with new names. A VPC (AWS) or VNet (Azure) is your private network, with a CIDR range you choose (e.g. 10.20.0.0/16) carved into subnets — the subnetting from Module 2 is used every day here.

ConceptAWSAzureOn-prem equivalent
Private networkVPCVNetYour LAN and its VLANs
Per-VM firewall (stateful)Security groupNetwork Security Group (NSG)Host firewall / ACL
Per-subnet filterNetwork ACL (stateless)NSG on the subnetRouter ACL
Internet access inInternet gateway + public IPPublic IP / load balancerEdge firewall + NAT
Internet access out onlyNAT gatewayNAT GatewayPAT on the firewall
Connect two networksVPC peering, Transit GatewayVNet peering, Virtual WANRouting between sites
Site-to-site VPNSite-to-Site VPNVPN GatewayIPsec tunnel (6.3)

DNSRoute 53Azure DNS (+ Private DNS zones)Your DNS servers
Managed firewallAWS Network FirewallAzure FirewallPerimeter NGFW

Two traps that come up in tickets: cloud routing tables are per subnet — a "private" subnet is just one whose route table has no route to an internet gateway; and overlapping CIDR ranges cannot be peered or VPN-routed, so plan cloud address space so it never clashes with on-prem (the same lesson as merging two companies that both use 192.168.1.0/24).

19.4 Core services side by side

NeedAWSAzure
Virtual machinesEC2Virtual Machines
Scale a group of VMs automaticallyAuto Scaling groupVirtual Machine Scale Sets
Block disks for VMsEBSManaged Disks
