Cost basics interviewers like: pay-as-you-go (on-demand) is the most flexible and most expensive; reservations / savings plans trade a 1- or 3-year commitment for a large discount on steady workloads; spot capacity is very cheap but can be taken back at short notice (batch jobs only). Stopped VMs stop paying for compute but disks keep billing. Azure Hybrid Benefit reuses existing Windows Server and SQL Server licences. Tags (owner, cost centre, environment) are how a bill becomes readable.

19.5 Identity and access — the heart of cloud security

In the cloud there is no locked server room: identity is the perimeter. Every action — starting a VM, reading a bucket — is an API call checked against "who are you, and are you allowed to do this on that?"

ConceptAWS IAMAzure (Entra ID + Azure RBAC)
Directory of peopleIAM users, or better IAM Identity Center (SSO from your corporate directory)Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD) tenant, often synced from on-prem AD (Module 12)
GroupingIAM groupsEntra groups
Permission definitionPolicy: JSON listing allowed or denied actions on resourcesRole definition: Owner, Contributor, Reader, or custom
Granting itAttach the policy to a user, group or roleRole assignment = who + which role + at which scope
Identity for a machine or appIAM role assumed by an EC2 instance (instance profile) or LambdaManaged identity on a VM, function or app
The all-powerful accountThe root user: MFA on, locked away, never used day to dayGlobal Administrator (Entra) and Owner at the top scope: few people, MFA, just-in-time via PIM
Audit trailCloudTrailActivity Log, Entra sign-in and audit logs
  • Least privilege: grant the smallest role at the narrowest scope that does the job, and review it. "Everyone is Owner / AdministratorAccess" is the most common cloud audit finding.
  • MFA everywhere, enforced by policy: Conditional Access in Entra (e.g. "admins need MFA and a compliant device; block sign-ins from unexpected countries").
  • No long-lived secrets in code: use managed identities / IAM roles so applications get short-lived credentials automatically. A leaked access key in a public Git repository is found by bots within minutes.
  • AWS policy evaluation in one line: an explicit Deny always wins; otherwise anything not explicitly allowed is denied.
  • Two kinds of Azure role: Entra roles (Global Administrator, User Administrator) govern the directory — users, groups, licences; Azure RBAC roles (Owner, Contributor, Reader) govern resources such as VMs and storage. A Global Admin is not automatically able to manage VMs.

19.6 How to talk about cloud as an infrastructure associate

  • Your on-prem knowledge transfers: subnets, routing, DNS, firewalls, RAID-like redundancy (zones), backups and RCA work the same way with different names.
  • Typical associate tasks: build or resize a VM, open an NSG / security group rule through a change, attach a disk, check why a VM can't reach the internet (route table, NSG, NAT), restore from a backup, reset access for a user, read the activity log to see who changed what.
  • Entry certifications worth naming as "in progress" or "next": Microsoft AZ-900 (Azure Fundamentals) and AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner; then AZ-104 (Azure Administrator) or AWS Solutions Architect – Associate.

Interview questions — Module 19

What is the difference between Active Directory and Microsoft Entra ID?

Model answer: "Active Directory Domain Services is the on-premises directory: domain controllers, Kerberos and NTLM, Group Policy, OUs, and computers joined to the domain over the LAN. Entra ID, formerly Azure AD, is the cloud identity service for Microsoft 365, Azure and SaaS apps: it speaks modern protocols such as OAuth, OpenID Connect and SAML over HTTPS, adds conditional access and MFA, and has no OUs or Group Policy. Most companies run both, with Entra Connect syncing users from AD so people have one identity everywhere."

How would you connect an office network to Azure?

Model answer: "For most offices a site-to-site VPN: an Azure VPN Gateway in the virtual network and an IPsec tunnel from the office firewall over the internet, with routes for the VNet’s address space and address ranges that do not overlap with the office. Where traffic is heavy or latency must be predictable, ExpressRoute provides a private circuit through a provider, often with the VPN kept as backup. Individual remote users connect with point-to-site VPN instead."

Explain IaaS, PaaS and SaaS with examples.

Model answer: "They differ in how much of the stack the provider runs. With IaaS — Azure VMs or AWS EC2 — I get virtual hardware and still manage the OS, patching and applications. With PaaS — Azure SQL Database or App Service — the provider runs the OS and platform and I bring the data and code. With SaaS — Microsoft 365 — I just use the software. Across all three, the data and who can access it stay my responsibility: that's the shared responsibility model."

What's the difference between a region and an availability zone?

Model answer: "A region is a geographic area, like West Europe or Frankfurt, chosen for latency, data residency and price. Inside a region, availability zones are physically separate datacenters with their own power, cooling and networking, connected by fast links. Spreading VMs across zones behind a load balancer survives a datacenter failure; to survive a regional disaster you replicate to a second region, which costs more and should be driven by the RTO and RPO."

A VM in Azure (or AWS) can't reach the internet. How do you troubleshoot?

Model answer: "Same bottom-up method as on-prem, with cloud names. Is the VM running and does it have an IP in the subnet I expect? Then the route table of that subnet — does 0.0.0.0/0 go to a NAT gateway or internet gateway, or is it forced through a firewall? Then the NSG or security group — outbound rules, and on AWS the subnet's network ACL, which is stateless so return traffic needs its own rule. Then DNS resolution from the VM. Azure Network Watcher's 'IP flow verify' or AWS Reachability Analyzer tells me which rule is blocking."

Security group vs network ACL on AWS?

Model answer: "A security group is attached to an instance's network interface and is stateful — if I allow inbound 443, the replies go out automatically — and it has only allow rules. A network ACL applies to a whole subnet, is stateless, so I must allow return traffic on ephemeral ports explicitly, and it supports explicit deny rules evaluated in number order. Most designs do the real filtering in security groups and keep NACLs simple."

How does access control work in Azure?

Model answer: "Identities live in Microsoft Entra ID, often synced from on-prem AD. Access to resources uses Azure RBAC: a role assignment combines a principal — a user, group or managed identity — with a role like Reader, Contributor or Owner, at a scope: management group, subscription, resource group or single resource, inherited downward. I'd grant the narrowest role at the narrowest scope, assign to groups not individuals, enforce MFA with Conditional Access, and use managed identities so apps don't hold passwords."

What is the shared responsibility model?

Model answer: "It splits security duties between the provider and the customer. The provider always secures the physical datacenters, hosts and the virtualization layer. The customer always owns their data, identities and access configuration. The middle — operating systems, network controls, applications — depends on the model: in IaaS it's mine, in PaaS mostly the provider's. Most cloud incidents happen on the customer's side: public buckets, over-privileged accounts, leaked keys."

Module 20 · Scripting

Scripting: PowerShell & Bash fundamentals

The interview question is rarely "write a program". It is "have you automated anything?" and "what would this script do?". This module gives you the fundamentals of both shells side by side, the one idea that separates them (objects vs text), one worked script in each that you can explain line by line, and the safety habits that make scripts trustworthy. Module 11 has a longer annotated bash script and Module 12 the everyday PowerShell commands.

20.1 Why infrastructure people script

  • Repeatability: the same steps, the same way, on 1 server or 200 — no forgotten step at 3 a.m.
  • Speed: a report across every server in seconds instead of an afternoon of RDP sessions.
  • Evidence: a script's output (a CSV, a log) is proof for a ticket, an audit or an RCA.
  • Use PowerShell for Windows, Active Directory, Hyper-V, Microsoft 365, Azure and VMware (PowerCLI). Use Bash for Linux, ESXi shell basics, network appliances and containers. PowerShell 7 also runs on Linux and macOS.

20.2 The two shells side by side

TaskPowerShellBash
Run a script.\report.ps1 (execution policy must allow it, e.g. RemoteSigned)chmod +x report.sh then ./report.sh, or bash report.sh; first line #!/usr/bin/env bash
Variable$name = "web01"name="web01" (no spaces around =)
Use it in a string"Host: $name" — double quotes expand, single quotes don't"Host: $name" — the same rule
Argumentsparam([string]$Path, [int]$Days = 7) → -Path C:\logs -Days 3$1, $2, all: "$@", default: ${1:-7}
Ifif ($pct -lt 15) { … } elseif (…) { … } else { … }if [[ $pct -lt 15 ]]; then … elif …; then … else … fi
Compare-eq -ne -lt -gt -le -ge, -like "web*", -match (regex)numbers: -eq -ne -lt -gt; strings: == !=; regex: =~
Loop over a listforeach ($s in $servers) { … } or $servers | ForEach-Object { $_ }for s in "${servers[@]}"; do … done
Read a file line by lineGet-Content servers.txt | ForEach-Object { … }while read -r line; do … done < servers.txt
Functionfunction Get-Free { param($Drive) … }get_free() { local drive=$1; … }
Did the last command work?$? (True/False); $LASTEXITCODE for external programs$? — 0 means success, anything else is an error code
Handle errorstry { … -ErrorAction Stop } catch { $_.Exception.Message }set -euo pipefail; cmd || echo "failed"
Find helpGet-Help Get-Service -Examples, Get-Command *dns*, … | Get-Memberman df, df --help, type, which
Comment# line, <# block #># line

PowerShell commands are Verb-Noun cmdlets (Get-Service, Restart-Service, Get-ADUser); Get-Verb lists the approved verbs, so you can often guess a command's name. Bash strings together small programs (grep, awk, sort, cut), each doing one job.

20.3 The big difference: objects vs text

20.4 One worked script in each — a low-disk report

The same job in both shells: check free space and report anything below a threshold. Be ready to explain every line.

# disk-report.ps1: list fixed disks below a free-space threshold, on one or many servers
param(
    [string[]]$ComputerName = @($env:COMPUTERNAME),   ← default: this machine
    [int]$MinFreePercent = 15
)
foreach ($c in $ComputerName) {
    $query = @{ ClassName = 'Win32_LogicalDisk'; Filter = 'DriveType=3'; ErrorAction = 'Stop' }   ← DriveType 3 = fixed disk
    if ($c -ne $env:COMPUTERNAME) { $query.ComputerName = $c }    ← remote: over WinRM, on by default on Windows Server
    try {
        $disks = Get-CimInstance @query                   ← "splatting": pass the hashtable as parameters
    } catch {
        Write-Warning "$c unreachable: $($_.Exception.Message)"
        continue                                          ← one dead server must not stop the report
    }
    foreach ($d in $disks) {
        $pct = [math]::Round($d.FreeSpace / $d.Size * 100, 1)
        if ($pct -lt $MinFreePercent) {
            [pscustomobject]@{ Computer = $c; Drive = $d.DeviceID; FreePct = $pct }   ← output objects, not text
        }
    }
}

# run it, and because the output is objects, export straight to CSV:
.\disk-report.ps1 -ComputerName SRV01,SRV02 -MinFreePercent 20 | Export-Csv low-disk.csv -NoTypeInformation
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# disk-report.sh: warn about filesystems above a usage threshold; exit 1 if any
set -euo pipefail                      ← stop on errors, unset variables and failed pipes
max_used=${1:-85}                      ← first argument, default 85 (%)
status=0
while read -r pct avail mount; do        ← mount last: it absorbs any spaces in the path
  pct=${pct%\%}                        ← strip the % sign: "91%" → 91
  if (( pct > max_used )); then
    echo "WARN $mount is ${pct}% full ($avail free)"
    status=1
  fi
done < <(df -h --output=pcent,avail,target -x tmpfs -x devtmpfs | tail -n +2)
                                       ↑ pick the columns by name, skip the header and RAM-backed filesystems
exit "$status"                         ← 0 = all fine; monitoring or cron can act on 1

Both scripts were run as shown here (the Bash one with GNU coreutils df). What to point out in an interview: both take a parameter with a sensible default, both handle failure deliberately (try/catch and continue; set -euo pipefail), and both produce output another tool can use — PowerShell objects into a CSV, Bash an exit code that cron, a monitoring agent or a CI job can test.

20.5 Safety habits that make scripts trustworthy

  • Dry run first: PowerShell's -WhatIf shows what Remove-Item, Stop-Service or Set-ADUser would do; -Confirm asks each time. In Bash, echo the command before running it for real.
  • Quote your variables in Bash: rm -rf "$dir/", never rm -rf $dir/ — an empty or space-containing variable turns the second into a disaster.
  • No passwords in scripts: use Get-Credential, the SecretManagement module or a vault; on Linux, SSH keys and root-only config files. A password in a script ends up in Git, backups and screenshots.
  • Test on one machine, then a small group, then everyone — the change-management habit applied to code.
  • Log what you did: Start-Transcript in PowerShell; exec > >(tee -a /var/log/myjob.log) 2>&1 in Bash.
  • Version it: scripts live in Git, not on someone's desktop.

20.6 Running scripts on a schedule and remotely

NeedWindows / PowerShellLinux / Bash
Run on a scheduleTask Scheduler (Register-ScheduledTask)cron (crontab -e: 0 7 * * 1-5 /opt/disk-report.sh = 07:00 on weekdays) or systemd timers
Run on remote machinesInvoke-Command -ComputerName SRV01,SRV02 -ScriptBlock { Get-Service spooler } over WinRM (ports 5985/5986)ssh admin@web01 'df -h'; a loop over hosts; Ansible for fleets
Interactive remote shellEnter-PSSession SRV01ssh admin@web01
Who may run scriptsExecution policy (Get-ExecutionPolicy; RemoteSigned is the usual server setting) — a safety catch, not a security boundaryFile permissions: the execute bit (chmod +x), owner, and sudo rules

Interview questions — Module 20

How would you check free disk space on 100 servers?

Model answer: "Not by logging in to each one. On Windows, Invoke-Command against the list of servers, from a file or from Get-ADComputer, runs Get-Volume or Get-CimInstance Win32_LogicalDisk in parallel, and I filter for volumes under, say, 15 percent free and export to CSV. On Linux, an Ansible ad-hoc command or a loop over SSH running df -h does the same. Then I schedule it, or better, make sure monitoring alerts on it, so it is not a manual check at all."

How would you write a script that is safe to run on production servers?

Model answer: "Make it idempotent so a rerun does no harm; support -WhatIf or a dry-run flag that prints what would change; fail loudly with set -euo pipefail in Bash or $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop' and try/catch in PowerShell; log what it did with timestamps; keep secrets out of the script, pulling them from a vault or credential store; and roll it out gradually: one test machine, a pilot group, then everyone. And it lives in Git, reviewed like any other code."

Have you automated anything with scripts?

Model answer: "Yes — in my lab I wrote a small PowerShell script that checks free disk space across a list of servers and exports anything under 15% to a CSV, with try/catch so one unreachable server doesn't stop the report. I wrote the same check in Bash for Linux, returning a non-zero exit code so cron or monitoring can alert on it. The pattern I follow: a parameter with a default, deliberate error handling, test on one machine first, and keep it in Git."

What's the main difference between PowerShell and Bash?

Model answer: "PowerShell passes objects down the pipeline, so I can sort or filter by property names — Sort-Object WS — and pipe straight into Export-Csv. Bash passes text, so I combine small tools like grep, awk and sort and have to know which column holds what. PowerShell is the natural choice for Windows, AD, Hyper-V and Azure; Bash for Linux and network or storage appliances."

What does set -euo pipefail do?

Model answer: "It makes a Bash script fail safely. -e exits when a command fails instead of carrying on with bad state, -u treats an unset variable as an error — which prevents things like rm -rf on an empty path — and pipefail makes a pipeline fail if any command in it fails, not just the last one."

How do you run a command on 50 Windows servers at once?

Model answer: "With PowerShell remoting: Invoke-Command with a list of computer names — for example read from a text file or from Get-ADComputer — and a script block. It runs in parallel over WinRM and returns objects tagged with each computer's name, so I can filter the failures and export the result. I'd test against one server first, and use -WhatIf on anything that changes state."

A script runs fine by hand but fails from the scheduler. Why?

Model answer: "Usually the environment differs. The scheduled task or cron job runs as a different account — with different permissions or no network-share access — and from a different working directory, with a minimal PATH, so relative paths and commands that aren't fully qualified fail. In PowerShell the execution policy may block it. I fix it by using absolute paths, running under a service account with the right rights, and logging output to a file so the scheduler's failures are visible."

Module 13 · Operations

IT operations & ITIL

The service-management vocabulary in the job description — "incidents and service requests within defined service levels" — decoded, plus how a delivery center actually runs.

13.1 ITIL and the ticket types

ITIL (the IT Infrastructure Library) is the standard framework for running IT as a service (ITSM). Capgemini's managed services run on it, so using its words correctly signals you'll fit right in:

TermDefinitionExample
IncidentUnplanned interruption or degradation of a service — restore it fast"Email is down", "Wi-Fi slow on floor 3"
Service requestA standard, pre-approved ask — no breakage involved"Create a mailbox", "access to shared folder", "new laptop"
ProblemThe underlying cause of one or more incidents — root cause analysis, slower track"Why does the branch VPN drop every Monday?"
ChangeA controlled modification to infrastructure, risk-assessed and approved (CAB), with a rollback plan"Upgrade the core switch firmware Saturday 02:00"
WorkaroundTemporary fix that restores service while the problem is investigated"Move users to the guest SSID while AP is replaced"
Known error / KBDocumented problem with a documented workaround; knowledge-base articlesThe article you write after solving something new
CMDBConfiguration Management Database — inventory of assets (CIs) and their relationships"Which VMs sit on the host we're patching?"
The distinction they will test: incident vs service request ("something broke" vs "I need something"), and incident vs problem ("restore service now" vs "find the root cause so it stops recurring").

13.2 SLAs and priority

  • SLA (Service Level Agreement) — the contract with the customer: e.g. "P1 incidents: respond in 15 min, restore in 4 h; 99.9% availability." OLAs are the same promises between internal teams.
  • Priority = Impact × Urgency. Impact: how many users/how critical a service. Urgency: how fast it hurts. A CEO's mouse is low impact; a dead core switch is P1 even at night.
  • Typical matrix: P1 critical outage, all hands, hourly comms → P4 minor, scheduled. Breaching an SLA has financial penalties in managed services — that's why ticket timestamps and updates matter so much.
  • Escalation: functional (L1 → L2 → L3 — more expertise) vs hierarchical (to management — visibility for big/breaching incidents). Escalating on time with good notes is a skill they hire for: say what you tried, what you ruled out, and attach the evidence.
  • Support tiers: L1 triage/known fixes, L2 deep technical work (this role grows into it), L3 engineering/vendors.

13.3 The operations rhythm

  • Monitoring — tools like Zabbix, Nagios, PRTG, SolarWinds, vRealize/Aria watch device health (SNMP, agents, ping) and raise alerts before users call. A NOC (Network Operations Center) watches the dashboards 24/7 in shifts — this role can include that.
  • Patching cycle — monthly windows, test group first, change record, rollback plan, post-checks. (Windows: Patch Tuesday/WSUS; Linux: dnf/apt via schedules; VMware: Lifecycle Manager with vMotion evacuations; network gear: firmware in maintenance windows.)
  • Backups — daily job checks are a standing L1/L2 duty: failed jobs are tickets, restores get tested.
  • Documentation — runbooks (step-by-step operational procedures), network diagrams, the CMDB, and post-incident KB articles. The job description lists this explicitly — mention that you like documenting; it's rarer than it should be.
  • Handover — shift-based teams live and die by clean handovers: open incidents, their state, next actions.

13.4 Ticket lifecycle done right

  1. Acknowledge within SLA; set correct category/priority.
  2. Triage: scope, quick wins, known-error lookup.
  3. Work & log: every action and result in the ticket — the next engineer (or you at 3am) must be able to continue.
  4. Communicate: user updates at promised intervals; no silent tickets.
  5. Escalate with evidence when stuck or out of scope — before the SLA clock forces it.
  6. Resolve → confirm with the user → close with root cause and fix recorded; new knowledge → KB article.

13.5 Customer handling & communication

In support roles, soft skills are scored as hard as subnetting. The customer rarely judges the fix — they can't see it — they judge how they were treated and whether they knew what was happening. Two habits cover most of it: acknowledge the person before the problem, and never leave a customer without a next update time.

  • Explain to non-technical people impact-first: what they will notice, what they need to do, and when it will be normal — not the protocol. "The branch's internet line is down, so the tills can't reach the payment server; card payments are offline until about noon, cash still works."
  • "I don't know" is fine with a plan attached: "I don't know yet — I'll check with the storage team and update you by 3 p.m." Guessing and being wrong costs more trust than admitting a gap.
  • Remote sessions: ask before taking control, ask them to close personal or confidential windows, say what you're doing as you do it, and hand control back at the end.
  • Writing tickets and emails: facts, times and actions, no emotion or blame; someone else (or an auditor) will read it later. One topic per email, the request in the first line.
  • Saying no: offer what you can do and the proper route. "I can't give local admin rights — that needs a security approval. I can raise the request now, and meanwhile I'll install the software for you remotely."
  • Escalating without losing the customer: a warm handover — tell the customer who will contact them and when, and give the next team the whole story so the customer never repeats it.
Instead of…Say…
"That's not my department.""That's handled by the network team — I'll pass it to them with everything you've told me and stay on the ticket."
"It works on my side.""I can't reproduce it yet — can you show me exactly what you see?"
"You must have changed something.""Has anything changed recently — updates, new equipment, a move?"
"It'll be fixed soon.""We're working on it; I'll update you by 2:30, or sooner if it's fixed."
"Calm down.""I understand this is stopping your work. Let's get it sorted."

The incident update format for a wider audience — managers, a whole office — has four lines: what is happening (impact in plain words), who is affected, what we are doing, and when the next update comes. Send it on time even when nothing has changed.

Interview questions — Module 13

What is the difference between an incident and a problem?

Model answer: "An incident is a single interruption, and the goal is to restore service as fast as possible, even with a workaround such as a reboot. A problem is the underlying cause of one or more incidents, and the goal is to find it and remove it so the incidents stop recurring. A known error is a problem whose cause and workaround are documented. In practice, when the same incident shows up several times, I raise a problem record and link the incidents to it."

A change you made last night caused an outage this morning. What do you do?

Model answer: "Restore service first: if rollback is the fastest safe path, roll back, following the change's back-out plan, and tell the incident manager and affected users what is happening. Once service is back I say plainly that my change caused it, open a problem record, and do the root cause analysis: why testing did not catch it and why the back-out was or was not quick. Then I fix the process, for example a pre-change check or a smaller pilot group, and update the runbook. Owning it quickly is what builds trust."

What's the difference between an incident and a service request? And incident vs problem?

Model answer: "An incident is something broken or degraded — the goal is restoring service as fast as possible, even with a workaround. A service request is a standard ask for something new — an account, access, equipment — nothing is broken. A problem is the underlying cause behind one or more incidents: incident management asks 'how do we get users working again now', problem management asks 'why did this happen and how do we stop it recurring'. Example: the VPN dropping today is an incident; investigating why it drops every Monday is a problem; the firmware upgrade that fixes it is a change."

What is an SLA and how does it affect your daily work?

Model answer: "It's the agreed service commitment with the customer — response times, resolution targets, availability percentages, per priority level. Practically it drives everything: I acknowledge tickets within the response window, prioritize by impact and urgency rather than by who shouts loudest, keep the ticket updated so the clock and the customer both see progress, and escalate early with good notes when something risks breaching. In managed services SLA breaches can cost the company money, so treating the ticket queue with discipline is part of the engineering job."

When do you escalate, and how?

Model answer: "I escalate when the issue is beyond my access or knowledge, when the SLA clock is at risk, or when the blast radius grows — and I'd rather escalate fifteen minutes early than sit on a P1. A good escalation is a package: symptoms, scope, exact steps already tried with their results, what I've ruled out, logs or screenshots attached, and the business impact. Then I stay engaged and learn from the fix — following through to resolution is in this job's description, and it's also how juniors become seniors."

You have three tickets at once: a director can't print, a floor lost internet, a new-hire account request. Order them.

Model answer: "Priority is impact times urgency. The floor outage is first — dozens of users down is the highest impact, likely a P2; I'd check scope immediately and engage it. The director's printer is one user — high visibility but low impact; a quick acknowledgment buys goodwill: 'received, on it right after a floor-wide outage'. The account request is a service request with a due date, not an interruption — scheduled last. And I'd communicate expected times to all three, because silence is what actually generates complaints."

Level 2 · Deep dive

D13.1 The priority matrix with real SLA numbers

PriorityExampleTypical responseTypical resolutionBehavior
P1 CriticalSite down, ERP down, security breach15 min4 hAll hands; bridge call; comms every 30–60 min; hierarchical escalation immediate
P2 HighDepartment down, no redundancy left30 min8 hPrioritized over queues; updates every 2 h
P3 MediumSingle user degraded, workaround exists4 h2–3 daysNormal queue
P4 LowCosmetic, questions, future requests1 day5+ daysScheduled

Availability math (memorize one row and derive the rest): 99.9% = 8h 46m downtime/year · 99.99% = 52 min · 99.999% = 5 min. "Three nines vs four nines" is the difference between a maintenance window and full redundancy — good vocabulary for SLA talk.

D13.2 Major incidents & RCA — how grown-up ops behaves

  • Major Incident process: declare early → incident manager owns coordination → separate technical bridge from business comms (engineers must not spend the outage writing emails) → workaround first, elegance later → post-incident review within days.
  • RCA / 5 Whys example you can retell: Users lost email → mail VM paused → datastore full → snapshot grew for 3 weeks → backup job's snapshot deletion had been failing → and nobody watched that alert. Root cause isn't "disk full"; it's "failed-job alerting wasn't actionable." Fixes at every level: free space (correct), alarm on snapshot age (better), review alert routing (systemic).
  • Blameless culture: RCAs name process gaps, not people — say this phrase; delivery centers live it.
  • Change types: standard (pre-approved, low risk — password resets, cert renewals), normal (CAB-assessed), emergency (break-glass during incidents, reviewed after). Every P1 postmortem asks "what change caused this?" — ~70% of incidents trace to changes, which is why change control exists.

D13.3 Monitoring that works (and the KPIs on your dashboard)

  • Monitor layers: ping/SNMP up-down → interface errors & utilization → service checks (port 443 answers, DNS resolves) → synthetic transactions (login actually works) → log alerts (SIEM). A green ping with a dead application is why service checks exist.
  • Alert hygiene: every alert must be actionable — alert fatigue (hundreds of ignored emails) is how the real one gets missed (see the RCA above). Thresholds with duration (">90% for 10 min"), maintenance windows suppressed, escalation chains if unacknowledged.
  • KPIs you can name: MTTR (mean time to restore), MTBF, FCR (first-contact resolution), SLA compliance %, ticket reopen rate (quality signal), backlog age. Saying "I'd care about reopen rate because it measures fix quality, not just speed" is a differentiator.
  • On-call etiquette: acknowledge fast, stabilize (workaround > root cause at 3 a.m.), document while fresh, hand over cleanly — and update the runbook so the next person sleeps.
Level 4 · State of the art & the horizon — how elite operations teams run

What the best run today

  • SRE thinking crossed over from Google into enterprise ops: define SLOs (service level objectives — "99.9% of logins under 2 s") and spend the error budget deliberately — if you're within budget, ship changes; if you've burned it, freeze and stabilize. Toil gets measured and automated away; postmortems are blameless artifacts, not punishments.
  • The tooling stack: ServiceNow (with Now Assist AI) as the ITSM backbone in big delivery organizations; PagerDuty/Opsgenie/incident.io orchestrating on-call and incident comms; OpenTelemetry-based observability; runbook automation (Ansible Automation Platform, Rundeck) turning "the 2 a.m. procedure" into a button; ChatOps — incidents run in a Teams/Slack channel with bots posting diagnostics.
  • AIOps in production: event correlation collapsing alert storms, anomaly detection on golden signals, and — the 2025–26 wave — agentic AI on L1: password resets, disk-space clears, known-error matching, and first-draft diagnosis handled by AI agents with human approval gates. Capgemini itself sells AI-augmented operations; expect your interviewers to be living this shift.
  • Platform engineering: internal developer platforms (Backstage-style portals) where standard requests — a VM, a database, access — are self-service and policy-checked, killing whole categories of tickets. FinOps (cloud cost engineering) became a first-class ops discipline next to performance and availability.

The horizon — and what it means for your career

  • Trajectory: self-healing infrastructure (detect→remediate loops), LLM-drafted RCAs reviewed by engineers, autonomous NOC functions for routine faults — with humans owning novel failures, risk decisions, customer trust, and the automation itself.
  • The honest career read to carry into the interview: the ticket work this role starts with is exactly what AI is absorbing — so the winning move is to be the associate who learns the automation, writes the runbooks the bots execute, and grows toward the judgment work. Saying a version of that, unprompted, is a differentiator: it shows you see where the industry is going and you're running toward it, not from it.

14.2 "Why Capgemini?" — model answer

Model answer (adapt the bracketed parts to your story)

"Three reasons. First, the learning curve: Capgemini's Cairo delivery center supports major European clients across exactly the technologies I want to build my career on — networks, virtualization, cloud infrastructure — and it invests seriously in certifications and training; as someone starting out, being around L2 and L3 engineers on real enterprise estates is the fastest way to grow. Second, the scale and stability: a 420,000-person global leader that's still expanding in Egypt — the center is growing toward thousands of engineers — means real career paths, not a dead-end seat. Third, the culture fits me: Capgemini's values like Team Spirit, Honesty, and Modesty describe the kind of colleague I try to be — [one-line personal example, e.g. 'in my graduation project I was the one keeping the team documentation and helping teammates debug']. I want to start where the fundamentals are taken seriously, and a global delivery center is exactly that."

14.3 The classic HR questions — model answers

"Tell me about yourself." (60–90 seconds, structure: present → past → why here)

Template: "I'm a [Computer Science/Engineering] graduate from [university], focused on IT infrastructure and networking. [Present:] Recently I've been building hands-on skills — I've studied [CCNA-level networking / Linux administration], set up [home lab / virtual lab with VMware or VirtualBox], and practiced [subnetting, configuring VLANs, managing Linux servers]. [Past proof:] During [internship/project], I [one concrete achievement — 'supported X users', 'built a small network', 'automated Y']. [Why here:] I'm looking to start my professional career in infrastructure support, and this role matches exactly what I've prepared for — networks, VMware, Linux — at a company where I can learn from a large engineering organization. That's why I applied."

Rules: no life story, no repeating the CV line by line, end pointing at the role.

"What are your strengths and weaknesses?"

Strengths — pick two the role needs and prove them: "I'm systematic under pressure — I troubleshoot in layers instead of guessing, which I practiced in [lab/project]. And I document what I fix; I keep notes others can follow." Weakness — real, non-fatal, plus the fix: "Early on I'd spend too long trying to solve something alone before asking for help — I've learned that in support, escalating with good notes at the right time is a strength, not a failure, so I now timebox myself." Never say "I'm a perfectionist" and never name a core requirement (communication, teamwork) as the weakness.

"Where do you see yourself in five years?"

Model answer: "Growing inside this track: first mastering the associate role and earning certifications — CCNA, then VMware VCP or RHCSA depending on where the team needs depth — then moving toward L2/L3 engineering, and eventually specializing, likely in cloud infrastructure or network security. Capgemini is somewhere that path visibly exists, which is part of why I applied." (Says: ambitious, loyal, realistic — without "I want your job" or "I'll start my own company.")

"Are you willing to work night shifts / weekends / on-call?" (they WILL ask)

Model answer: "Yes — I understand the center supports clients in other time zones on a 24/7 model, and shift work is part of infrastructure operations everywhere. I'd expect a fair rotation, and I'm comfortable with it." If you have a genuine constraint, state it honestly now, not after the offer — Honesty is literally one of their values.

"What are your salary expectations?"

Model answer: "As a fresh graduate, my priority is the learning and the growth path. I'd expect the standard range for this role at Capgemini Egypt — I'm sure your range is fair, and I'm flexible within market rates." If pushed for a number, give a researched range for associate infra roles in Cairo, not a single figure, and say it's negotiable. Don't anchor yourself below market or price yourself out over a first job.

"Do you have any questions for us?" (never say no — ask 2–3 of these)
  • "What does a typical shift look like for this team — mostly monitoring and tickets, or also project work?"
  • "Which clients or regions would this team support, and what does the escalation path to L2/L3 look like?"
  • "How does Capgemini support certifications — is there a training path for CCNA or VMware for associates?"
  • "What separates the associates who grow fastest here?"
  • "What are the next steps in the process?"

14.4 Behavioral questions — STAR + the seven values

Answer behavioral questions ("tell me about a time…") with STAR: Situation (one line of context) → Task (what you had to achieve) → Action (what you did — the longest part) → Result (outcome + what you learned, with a number if possible). Prepare four stories from projects/internships/university and map them to their values:

They ask…Value testedYour story should show…
"A time you worked in a team / handled a difficult teammate"Team Spirit, TrustYou shared credit, unblocked others, communicated early
"A time you made a mistake"Honesty, ModestyYou owned it immediately, fixed it, changed your process — never "I don't make mistakes"
"A time you had to learn something fast / took initiative"Boldness, FreedomSelf-taught skill under deadline with a concrete result
"A time you handled pressure / an angry user or customer"Team Spirit, TrustStayed calm, communicated status, prioritized by impact, escalated properly
Example STAR answer — "Tell me about a time you solved a problem under pressure"

"S: In my graduation project, our demo server stopped responding the morning of the presentation. T: I had 90 minutes to get the system back before our slot. A: Instead of panicking and rebooting things randomly, I worked it in layers: the VM was up, SSH worked, so the network was fine; systemctl status showed our app service failed; the log showed the disk was 100% full from debug logging we'd left on. I cleared the logs, disabled debug mode, added a size limit, restarted the service, and verified the app end-to-end. R: We presented on time and got an A. It taught me two habits I still keep: check the logs before touching anything, and after every fix, remove the root cause — not just the symptom."

14.5 Rapid-fire drill — 40 one-liners across all four topics

Cover the right column and answer aloud. These are the short-form questions technical screeners fire in sequence; the goal is a crisp first sentence, not an essay.

Networks — 14 rapid answers

Port of HTTPS / SSH / RDP / DNS? 443 · 22 · 3389 · 53.

Layer of a switch? A router? L2 (MACs) · L3 (IPs).

What does DHCP stand for and do? Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol — leases IP/mask/gateway/DNS automatically (DORA).

What's 255.255.255.192 as a prefix? /26 — 64 addresses, 62 usable.

Private ranges? 10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16.

What's APIPA? 169.254.x.x self-assigned = DHCP unreachable.

ARP does what? Resolves IP → MAC on the local LAN.

TCP vs UDP in one line? Reliable ordered connection vs fast connectionless datagrams.

What is a VLAN? Logical L2 segment = its own broadcast domain on a shared switch.

Native VLAN? The untagged VLAN on a trunk — must match both ends.

Why STP? Blocks redundant L2 paths so loops can't cause broadcast storms.

Default route? 0.0.0.0/0 — matches when nothing more specific does.

OSPF metric? Cost, inversely proportional to bandwidth; Dijkstra shortest path.

Ping by IP works, by name fails — culprit? DNS.

Storage — 9 rapid answers

RAID 1 vs RAID 5? Mirror (50% capacity, survives 1) vs striping+parity (n−1 capacity, survives 1, write penalty).

Minimum disks for RAID 10? Four.

NAS speaks…? SAN speaks…? Files: SMB/NFS · Blocks: FC/iSCSI.

What's a LUN? A block volume the array presents to hosts.

iSCSI port and roles? TCP 3260; initiator = host, target = array.

IOPS vs throughput? Operations/sec (random) vs MB/s (sequential).

Thin provisioning risk? Oversubscribed pool hits 100% → all thin volumes stop.

Incremental vs differential? Since last any backup vs since last full.

3-2-1? 3 copies, 2 media, 1 offsite/offline.

VMware — 9 rapid answers

ESXi vs vCenter? Hypervisor on the host vs central management server.

vMotion needs? Shared storage, vMotion network, compatible CPUs (EVC), matching port groups.

HA vs FT? Restart on another host (minutes) vs lockstep shadow VM (zero downtime).

DRS does? Automatic load balancing via vMotion.

Snapshot = backup? No — delta on the same datastore; short-term undo only.

VMFS is? VMware's clustered filesystem multiple hosts mount at once.

VMware Tools gives? Drivers, heartbeat, graceful shutdown, balloon driver.

vCenter dies — VMs? Keep running; you lose central management/vMotion/DRS.

Type 1 vs Type 2? Bare-metal (ESXi) vs app on a desktop OS (Workstation).

Linux — 8 rapid answers

Check disk space? df -h; find usage with du -sh.

Service status/logs? systemctl status X · journalctl -u X.

chmod 644 means? Owner rw, group r, others r.

Follow a log live? tail -f /var/log/…

Show listening ports? ss -tulpn.

IP and routes? ip a · ip r.

Root's UID? Superuser practice? 0; use sudo, not root logins.

Where are configs? Logs? /etc · /var/log.

14.6 A simulated technical interview (read it aloud, both parts)

15-minute mock transcript with commentary — how a strong associate sounds

Interviewer: Walk me through the OSI model briefly.
You: "Seven layers, bottom up: Physical is the medium itself — cables, fiber, radio. Data Link moves frames inside a LAN using MAC addresses — that's where switches work. Network is IP addressing and routing between networks — routers. Transport is TCP and UDP with port numbers — reliability versus speed. Session, Presentation and Application handle sessions, encryption and formatting, and the protocols users actually touch, like HTTP and DNS. Day to day it gives us a shared language — 'layer 2 problem' means switching, not routing." ← 30 seconds, ends with a practical hook.

Interviewer: A user says the internet is down. Go.
You: "First I'd ask two things: is it just you, and what changed? If it's one user, I start at their machine: link light, then ipconfig /all — do they have a valid address or a 169.254 one, which would mean DHCP failed. Then the ping ladder: gateway, then 8.8.8.8, then a name. Each step isolates a layer — gateway fails, it's local; IP works but names fail, it's DNS. If many users are down, I skip to shared infrastructure — the floor switch, the DHCP scope, the uplink — and I'd check monitoring and recent changes before touching anything." ← method first, tools second, scope-awareness throughout.

Interviewer: What's the difference between vMotion and HA?
You: "vMotion is planned, zero-downtime live migration — memory is copied while the VM runs, used for maintenance and balancing; DRS automates it. HA is unplanned failure recovery — if a host dies, its VMs restart on surviving hosts, so there are a few minutes of downtime. And if even that's too much, Fault Tolerance runs a lockstep shadow copy — zero downtime but expensive."

Interviewer: Have you worked with SAN storage?
You: "Not in production yet — honestly. I understand the concepts well: block storage presented as LUNs over iSCSI or Fibre Channel, zoning and masking to control visibility, multipathing for redundancy, and I've practiced the iSCSI initiator flow in my lab with TrueNAS. I'd expect to ramp up quickly on your arrays." ← honest "no" + concept fluency + lab proof + confidence. This is the template for every gap.

Interviewer: A Linux service is down. What do you do?
You: "systemctl status for the state and last log lines, then journalctl -u on the unit for the real reason — usually a config error, a port conflict, permissions, or disk full. Fix the cause, restart, verify with curl or a port check, and make sure it's enabled so it survives reboots. Then document it in the ticket."

Interviewer: Why should we hire you with no commercial experience?
You: "Because the fundamentals this role needs are exactly what I've built: I can subnet on paper, explain and troubleshoot along the OSI model, administer Linux at the command line, and I've practiced vSphere and AD in my lab. What I lack — your clients' environments and processes — is precisely what a delivery center teaches fast, and I document well, escalate cleanly, and genuinely like this work. I'll return the investment quickly."

14.7 Say it smoothly — phrase bank for a non-native interview

Buying thinking time

"That's a good question — let me structure my answer." · "There are two parts to that…" · "Let me start with the definition, then how I'd use it."

When you don't know

"I haven't used that in practice yet; my understanding is that…" · "I'd rather not guess — but here's how I'd find out." · "I know its role at a high level: …"

Clarifying

"Just to confirm — is this one user or many?" · "Do you mean the site-to-site case or remote access?" · "Should I go deeper on that part?"

Structuring

"First… second… and finally…" · "The short answer is X; the reason is Y." · "In a support context, that matters because…"

Recovering from a mistake

"Actually, let me correct myself — I said X, it should be Y." (Interviewers rate self-correction highly.)

Closing an answer

"…and that's also how I'd verify the fix." · "Does that answer what you were looking for?"

14.8 What NOT to say — anti-patterns that fail interviews

  • "I'd just reboot it / reinstall Windows." → You skipped diagnosis. Always show the method first; restarts are a step, not a strategy.
  • Bluffing acronyms. One follow-up question exposes it, and it poisons trust in your correct answers too. Use the "honest no + concepts + lab" template.
  • "That's not my job / L1 doesn't do that." → Delivery centers hire flexibility. Say what you would do up to your access, then how you'd escalate.
  • Blaming users ("the user is probably stupid"). Empathy for users is scored, sometimes explicitly.
  • Answering a different question than asked. If they ask TCP vs UDP, don't recite the OSI model. Answer, stop, offer depth: "want me to go into the handshake?"
  • Memorized-speech tone. Interviewers derail scripts on purpose. Practice ideas, not word-for-word paragraphs — this course's model answers are skeletons to make your own.
  • Trash-talking a previous employer/university/team — signals a future problem, whatever the story.

14.9 Interview-day checklist

  • Re-verify: employee count, CEO, latest quarterly headline (60 seconds on capgemini.com/investors), and re-read the job description.
  • Be ready to answer entirely in English — practice your "tell me about yourself" aloud; delivery centers screen communication hard.
  • Rehearse the six set pieces: OSI in 60 seconds · "user can't reach the internet" · TCP vs UDP · "what happens when you type a URL" · NAS vs SAN · vMotion vs HA.
  • Prepare your 4 STAR stories, your questions to ask, and your salary range.
  • Honesty rule for technical rounds: if you don't know, say "I haven't worked with that yet — my understanding is [educated guess], and here's how I'd find out." Bluffing fails instantly against senior engineers; structured honesty scores.
  • Logistics: ID, arrive/log in 10 min early, camera on, quiet room, phone silent, CV copies.
  • Using the Level-4 material safely: frontier knowledge is seasoning, not the meal. Deploy it in one sentence, framed as curiosity — "I've been reading about the post-Broadcom migration wave / ZTNA replacing VPNs / post-quantum TLS rollouts" — then stop. If they bite, discuss; if not, move on. Never let buzzwords outrun your fundamentals: an interviewer forgives not knowing eBPF, never a wrong subnet mask.

Module 15 · Quick reference

Cheat sheets

The night-before page. If you can reproduce everything here from memory, you're ready.

The 60-second summaries

OSI in one breath

Physical bits → Data Link frames/MAC (switches) → Network packets/IP (routers) → Transport TCP/UDP+ports → Session → Presentation/encryption → Application (HTTP, DNS). PDUs: bits, frame, packet, segment, data.

DHCP

DORA — Discover, Offer, Request, ACK. Broadcasts; relay/IP-helper for remote subnets; failure = APIPA 169.254.x.x.

DNS

Name→IP. Recursive resolver → root → TLD → authoritative; cached per TTL. Records: A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, PTR, TXT, SRV (AD!).

TCP vs UDP

TCP: handshake (SYN/SYN-ACK/ACK), reliable, ordered, flow control — web, mail, SSH. UDP: connectionless, fast — DNS, VoIP, video.

NAT

Private → public at the edge; PAT = many-to-one by ports; static NAT publishes servers.

VLAN

Logical L2 segmentation = separate broadcast domains; access vs trunk (802.1Q tags); inter-VLAN via L3 switch SVIs.

STP

Blocks redundant L2 paths to prevent broadcast storms; root bridge election; RSTP is fast; PortFast for edge ports.

Routing

Longest prefix wins; AD ranks sources (C 0, S 1, eBGP 20, EIGRP 90, OSPF 110, RIP 120); 0.0.0.0/0 = default; OSPF inside, BGP between organizations.

NAS vs SAN

NAS = files over LAN (SMB 445 / NFS 2049). SAN = blocks/LUNs over FC or iSCSI (3260). RAID ≠ backup; snapshot ≠ backup; 3-2-1 rule.

RAID

0 stripe (fast, fatal), 1 mirror (50%), 5 single parity (n−1, rebuild risk), 6 dual parity, 10 mirror+stripe (fast+safe, 50%).

VMware

ESXi = hypervisor, vCenter = management, cluster pools hosts. vMotion = live move (zero downtime); HA = restart on host death (minutes); DRS = auto-balance; FT = lockstep zero-downtime; snapshots = short-term undo only.

Linux firsts

Service down → systemctl status + journalctl -u. Disk → df -h/du -sh. Net → ip a, ip r, ss -tulpn. Perms: 4r 2w 1x → 755/644/600.

AD

Forest → domain → OU → objects; DCs replicate; Kerberos + DNS SRV records; GPO order LSDOU; security vs distribution groups.

ITIL

Incident (restore) vs service request (provide) vs problem (root cause) vs change (controlled). Priority = impact × urgency. SLA drives the queue.

The troubleshooting reflexes

  • Scope first: one user → device; many → shared infra. Always ask what changed?
  • Ping ladder: 127.0.0.1 → gateway → 8.8.8.8 → name. Fails at name only = DNS.
  • Ping OK, app dead = check the port/service, not the network.
  • 169.254.x.x = DHCP unreachable. Duplicate IP = flapping ARP. Slow + errors on port = duplex mismatch.
  • VM fine but no network after migration = VLAN not trunked to new host.
  • df full but du can't find it = deleted file held open (lsof | grep deleted).
  • AD weirdness (logon, GPO, shares) with healthy network = check DNS and time first.
Module 16 · Vocabulary

Glossary

Every technical term in this course, A–Z. Skim it the day before — being fluent in the vocabulary is half the interview.

ACL
Access Control List — ordered permit/deny rules on routers/firewalls; top-down, first match, implicit deny at the end.
AD / AD DS
Active Directory (Domain Services) — Microsoft's central directory of users, computers and groups, hosted on domain controllers.
Administrative distance
A router's trust ranking between route sources (connected 0, static 1, OSPF 110…). Lowest wins.
APIPA
169.254.x.x self-assigned address = the host couldn't reach DHCP.
ARP
Address Resolution Protocol — resolves an IP to a MAC on the local LAN via broadcast.
Broadcast domain
All devices that receive each other's L2 broadcasts; bounded by routers/VLANs.
BGP
Border Gateway Protocol — the internet's routing protocol, policy-based, between autonomous systems (TCP 179).
CIDR
Classless addressing written as prefix length: /24 = 255.255.255.0.
CIA triad
Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability — the three security goals.
CMDB
Configuration Management Database — asset/CI inventory and relationships.
Datastore
VMware storage container for VM files (VMFS on LUNs, NFS, or vSAN).
Default gateway
The router a host sends traffic to for destinations outside its subnet.
DHCP
Auto-assigns IP/mask/gateway/DNS via DORA (Discover-Offer-Request-ACK); UDP 67/68.
DMZ
Firewall zone for internet-facing services, isolated from the internal LAN.
DNS
Domain Name System — resolves names to IPs via root → TLD → authoritative hierarchy; port 53.
DRS
VMware Distributed Resource Scheduler — auto-balances VMs across cluster hosts via vMotion.
Duplex mismatch
One side full-, one side half-duplex — link works but is terribly slow with errors.
EtherChannel / LACP
Bundling multiple links into one logical link for bandwidth + redundancy.
ESXi
VMware's type-1 hypervisor installed on each physical host.
FSMO
Five special single-owner roles among AD domain controllers.
FT
VMware Fault Tolerance — lockstep shadow VM, zero downtime on host failure.
Firewall (stateful)
Tracks connections; return traffic of allowed sessions passes automatically.
GPO
Group Policy Object — centrally enforced settings linked to domain/OU; order LSDOU.
HA
VMware High Availability — restarts VMs on surviving hosts when a host fails.
HBA
Host Bus Adapter — a server's Fibre Channel interface card.
Hypervisor
Software that runs VMs on physical hardware; Type 1 bare-metal, Type 2 hosted.
ICMP
Control/diagnostic protocol — ping (echo), traceroute (TTL exceeded), unreachables.
IOPS
I/O operations per second — storage's random-performance metric (with latency and throughput).
IPsec
VPN protocol suite: IKE negotiates, ESP encrypts; tunnel vs transport mode.
iSCSI
Block storage (SCSI) over TCP/IP, port 3260; initiator → target, names are IQNs.
ITIL
The standard IT service management framework: incidents, requests, problems, changes, SLAs.
Jumbo frames
MTU ~9000 for storage/vMotion networks — must match end-to-end.
Kerberos
AD's ticket-based authentication protocol; breaks if clocks drift >5 min.
LACP
See EtherChannel.
LAN / WAN
Local network you own vs wide-area links between sites/the internet.
Latency / jitter
Delay and variation of delay; jitter kills voice/video.
LUN
Logical Unit Number — a block-storage volume presented by a SAN array.
LVM
Linux Logical Volume Manager — PV → VG → LV; grow filesystems online.
MAC address
48-bit hardware address of a NIC; local to the LAN segment; FF:…:FF = broadcast.
MFA
Multi-factor authentication — password plus token/app/biometric.
MPIO / multipathing
Multiple redundant paths from server to storage array.
MPLS
Carrier-managed private WAN with QoS between sites.
MTU
Max frame payload (1500 default); mismatches cause "ping works, app hangs".
NAT / PAT
Translating private to public addresses; PAT = many-to-one via ports.
NAS
Appliance serving files over SMB/NFS on the LAN.
NFS
Network File System — Unix/Linux/VMware file-sharing protocol (2049).
NIC teaming
Multiple physical NICs backing one logical interface for redundancy.
NTP
Network Time Protocol (UDP 123) — clock sync; stratum hierarchy.
OSI model
7-layer framework: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application.
OSPF
Link-state interior routing protocol; cost metric, areas, Dijkstra SPF.
OU
Organizational Unit — AD folder for objects; GPO link point.
PDU
Protocol Data Unit — data/segment/packet/frame/bits per layer.
PoE
Power over Ethernet — powers APs/phones/cameras over the data cable.
Port group
VMware vSwitch port profile (VLAN, policies) that VMs connect to.
PSK / 802.1X
Wi-Fi auth: shared passphrase vs per-user RADIUS authentication.
RAID
Disk redundancy schemes: 0 stripe, 1 mirror, 5/6 parity, 10 mirror+stripe.
RADIUS / TACACS+
AAA servers for network authentication (802.1X, device admin).
RDP
Remote Desktop Protocol, TCP 3389.
RPO / RTO
Max acceptable data loss / max acceptable downtime — the two backup design numbers.
SAN
Storage Area Network — shared block storage over FC/iSCSI fabric.
SD-WAN
Software-defined WAN steering traffic over multiple links per app, centrally managed.
SLA
Service Level Agreement — contractual response/resolution/availability targets.
SMB/CIFS
Windows file-sharing protocol, TCP 445.
Snapshot
Point-in-time image (VM or storage); short-term undo, never a backup.
SNMP
Monitoring protocol (161/162); polls OIDs, sends traps; use v3.
SSID / BSSID
Wi-Fi network name / an individual AP radio's MAC.
SSH
Encrypted remote shell (22); key-pair authentication.
STP / RSTP
Spanning tree — blocks redundant L2 paths to prevent loops/broadcast storms.
Subnet mask
Marks the network vs host bits of an IP address.
SVI
Switch Virtual Interface — an L3 switch's routed interface for a VLAN.
systemd / systemctl
Linux service manager and its control command; journalctl reads its logs.
TCP / UDP
Reliable connection-oriented vs fast connectionless transport.
Thin/thick provisioning
Allocate storage on demand vs up front; thin pools need monitoring.
TLS / SSL
Encryption layer under HTTPS; certificates signed by CAs.
Trunk (802.1Q)
A link carrying multiple VLANs with tags; access ports carry one untagged.
TTL
Time To Live — hop counter in IP (traceroute's trick); also DNS cache lifetime.
vCenter
VMware's central management server; enables vMotion/HA/DRS; VMs run fine without it.
VLAN
Virtual LAN — logical L2 segmentation; one broadcast domain each.
vMotion
Live migration of a running VM between hosts, zero downtime.
VMkernel port
ESXi host's own IP interface for mgmt/vMotion/storage/vSAN traffic.
VMFS
VMware's clustered filesystem on shared block storage.
VMware Tools
In-guest drivers/agent: performance, heartbeat, graceful shutdown.
VPN
Encrypted tunnel over untrusted networks; site-to-site or remote-access; IPsec or SSL.
vSAN
VMware hyper-converged storage pooling hosts' local disks.
vSwitch (vSS/vDS)
ESXi virtual switch, per-host standard or vCenter-managed distributed.
WLC
Wireless LAN Controller — central AP management.
WPA2/WPA3
Wi-Fi encryption standards; Enterprise mode = 802.1X per-user auth.
WSUS
Windows Server Update Services — central Windows patching.
WWN
World Wide Name — Fibre Channel's hardware address (zoning uses it).
Zoning / LUN masking
Fabric-level and array-level controls over which hosts see which storage.

Deep-dive terms (Levels 2–3)

ALUA
Asymmetric LUN access — multipath prioritizes the owning controller's paths.
APD / PDL
All Paths Down (array vanished, hosts retry) vs Permanent Device Loss (array declared it gone) — vSphere storage failure states.
BPDU Guard / Root Guard
STP protections: err-disable an edge port that hears a switch / block an uplink claiming root.
CBT
Changed Block Tracking — hypervisor marks changed disk blocks so backups copy only deltas.
CGNAT
Carrier-grade NAT — ISP-level shared public IPs (100.64/10 inside).
CRC / late collisions
Port error counters; both together scream duplex mismatch or bad cabling.
DAVG / KAVG / GAVG
esxtop storage latencies: array / host queueing / what the guest feels.
D-state
Uninterruptible I/O sleep — inflates Linux load average; unkillable until the I/O returns (dead NFS classic).
DPD / NAT-T
IPsec dead-peer detection / ESP wrapped in UDP 4500 to survive NAT.
DSCP / EF
QoS markings in the IP header; Expedited Forwarding = the voice queue.
EVC
Enhanced vMotion Compatibility — masks CPU generation differences within a vendor so vMotion works cluster-wide.
FSMO / PDC Emulator
AD's five single-owner roles; PDCe handles time, password forwarding, lockouts — the one you feel when it breaks.
Global Catalog
DC with a partial replica of all domains — forest-wide search and universal group logons (3268).
Inode exhaustion
Disk "full" with free space — out of file entries (df -i); millions of tiny files.
MSS clamping
Shrinking TCP's segment size on tunnels so full packets fit the reduced MTU — fixes "ping works, transfers hang".
OOM killer
Linux kernel killing the biggest process when memory runs out — check dmesg when apps "randomly die".
PSOD
ESXi's purple diagnostic screen — hypervisor kernel panic, usually hardware/driver.
SPAN / mirror port
Switch port that copies traffic for capture/IDS.
SYN cookies
Defense that lets servers survive SYN floods without a half-open queue.
URE
Unrecoverable read error rate — the math that killed RAID 5 on big disks.
VSS / application-consistent
Windows Volume Shadow Copy — apps flush before the backup snapshot; required for DBs/AD.
vCLS
Tiny agent VMs vSphere 7+ deploys per cluster to keep DRS working — leave them alone.
Zero-window
TCP receiver advertising 0 buffer — the capture signature of a slow application, not a slow network.

Frontier terms (Level 4)

AIOps
AI-driven operations — alert correlation, anomaly detection, natural-language ops assistants (Mist Marvis, Dynatrace Davis).
Agentic AI
AI agents that execute multi-step ops/security tasks (triage → diagnose → remediate) with human approval gates.
CXL
Compute Express Link — fabric letting servers pool and tier memory; blurs the RAM/storage boundary.
Confidential computing
CPU features (AMD SEV-SNP, Intel TDX) encrypting VM memory even from the hypervisor/cloud operator.
DPU / SmartNIC
A NIC with its own cores running networking, storage, and security offloads (NVIDIA BlueField, Pensando).
eBPF
Safe programs injected into the Linux kernel — powers modern networking (Cilium), security (Falco), observability (bpftrace).
ECH
Encrypted Client Hello — hides even the destination site name inside TLS.
Error budget / SLO
SRE practice: an objective ("99.9%") and the allowed failure it implies, spent deliberately on change velocity.
Firecracker / microVM
Millisecond-boot minimal VMs (runs AWS Lambda) — VM isolation at near-container speed.
GitOps / IaC
Infrastructure defined as code in Git (Terraform/Ansible), applied by pipelines — the config is the repository.
GPUDirect Storage
NVMe-to-GPU data path bypassing the CPU — feeding AI clusters.
HAMR
Heat-assisted magnetic recording — 30 TB+ hard drives.
Harvest-now-decrypt-later
Recording encrypted traffic today to decrypt with a future quantum computer — the reason PQC migration already started.
KubeVirt / OpenShift Virtualization
Running VMs as Kubernetes objects — one platform for containers and VMs.
Leaf-spine / VXLAN / EVPN
Modern DC fabric: routed underlay, tunneled L2 overlay, BGP EVPN control plane — the successor to big STP domains.
ML-KEM / ML-DSA (PQC)
NIST's post-quantum key-exchange and signature standards (FIPS 203/204); hybrid ML-KEM already default in major browsers/CDNs.
NVMe-oF / NVMe-TCP
NVMe over networks — the modern SAN protocol replacing iSCSI.
OpenTelemetry
The vendor-neutral standard for metrics, logs, and traces.
Passkeys / FIDO2
Phishing-resistant cryptographic sign-in replacing passwords.
Platform engineering / IDP
Productizing infrastructure as self-service "paved roads" (Backstage portals) instead of ticket queues.
Private 5G / CBRS
Dedicated cellular networks for campuses/factories complementing Wi-Fi.
QUIC / HTTP-3
Transport over UDP 443 with built-in TLS 1.3 — much of today's web and modern VPN-like traffic.
RPKI / ROV / MANRS
Cryptographic validation of BGP route origins + operator hygiene norms — how internet routing gets trustworthy.
SASE / SSE / ZTNA
Cloud-delivered network security edge; zero-trust per-app access replacing "on the VPN".
SONiC
Open-source switch OS on white-box hardware — hyperscaler networking.
SRv6
Segment routing over IPv6 — path programmed in the packet; MPLS's successor in carriers.
Streaming telemetry / gNMI
Devices pushing per-second state over gRPC (OpenConfig models) — replacing SNMP polling.
Talos / immutable OS
Image-based, no-shell Linux replaced rather than patched — config drift made impossible.
Ultra Ethernet (UEC)
Ethernet re-engineered for AI training fabrics — the InfiniBand challenger.
VCF 9
Broadcom's subscription bundle of vSphere+vSAN+NSX+Aria — the center of the 2026 "migrate or commit" decision.
Wi-Fi 8 (802.11bn)
"Ultra High Reliability" — same speed as Wi-Fi 7, engineered for determinism; ratification ~2028.
XDR / SIEM / SOAR
Correlated detection across endpoint/identity/cloud; the SOC's log brain; automated response playbooks.
